title: The Lantern City Beneath the Waves
subtitle: A Bedtime Journey to the Hidden Ocean Below
description: When a curious child stumbles upon a secret doorway in the sea, they discover a luminous city hidden far beneath the waves. Guided by new friends—some fish, some human, some delightfully in-between—they uncover an ancient mystery that only someone with a brave heart and fresh eyes can solve. Along the way, they learn what it means to belong in more than one world at once.

characters.name: Mara Bright
characters.description: Mara is a thoughtful, stubbornly curious ten-year-old who asks questions until adults surrender entire encyclopedias out of self-defense. She loves sketching strange machines in the margins of her homework and believes that if something is labeled “Do Not Open,” it is obviously addressed to her specifically. While she sometimes worries that she doesn’t quite fit in on land—too quiet, too odd, too fascinated by the sea—she has a deep well of kindness, a sharp, sideways sense of humor, and a talent for noticing small details that other people miss.

characters.name: Captain Thimble Kelp
characters.description: Captain Thimble is an elderly, semi-retired sea captain who now runs a creaky little seaside museum that appears to be held together by dust, string, and sheer narrative momentum. He has wild gray hair that looks like it was styled by a storm, a wooden leg carved with tiny waves and ships, and a habit of addressing the ocean as “Madam.” Behind his comic grumbling and exaggerated tall tales lies a genuine knowledge of forgotten sea-lore and a quiet guilt about a long-ago voyage that first revealed the hidden city—knowledge he has never dared share with anyone until Mara arrives.

characters.name: Liora of the Glass Tides
characters.description: Liora is a mer-child from the hidden city of Pelagoria, with iridescent scales along her arms, dark curving hair that drifts like seaweed, and eyes the color of tide pools at dusk. Half-human and half-oceanic, she can breathe both water and air, though neither world entirely trusts her. Clever and cautious, she is quick with dry, sardonic commentary but fiercely loyal once she decides someone is a friend. Liora secretly dreams of seeing the surface sun up close, believing it might answer the questions she can’t ask in Pelagoria’s strict, shimmering halls.

characters.name: Professor Barnaby Finn
characters.description: Professor Finn is an absent-minded, enthusiastic marine inventor who lives in Pelagoria and wears a patchwork diving suit like a waistcoat. His beard floats like a small, dedicated cloud when he talks, which is almost always about improbable machines: bubble-elevators, current-catchers, and translation shells. Although he tends to get lost in his own ideas and forget things like meals, doors, and which way is “up,” he has a gentle heart and becomes a kind of eccentric uncle to Mara and Liora, trusting their instincts when the adults around them hesitate.

characters.name: Queen Nerissa of Pelagoria
characters.description: Queen Nerissa is the regal, tired, and endlessly patient ruler of the hidden city. Draped in robes that ripple like sea-silk and crowned with living coral, she carries the weight of old promises made between the sea and the surface. She is cautious about surface-dwellers, having seen their ships and nets and careless pollution, yet she remembers a time when the two worlds traded stories instead of fear. Her love for her people and for her daughter, Liora, often pulls her in different directions, and she must decide whether to cling to old protections or trust a child from above.

characters.name: The Lantern Whale
characters.description: The Lantern Whale is a vast, ancient creature that glows softly with drifting lights along its sides like floating lanterns. It moves with dreamlike slowness through the deepest trenches, carrying memories of shipwrecks, storms, and old songs in the language of currents. Neither wholly animal nor entirely myth, it seems to understand speech in any tongue if it is spoken kindly. Its mournful, echoing calls shape the tides around Pelagoria, and its mood has the power to calm or stir the ocean itself.

chapters.chaptershortdescription: Where Mara discovers a shabby seaside museum that is much larger on the inside than on the outside and meets Captain Thimble Kelp.
chapters.chapterdetails: One blustery evening near closing time, Mara ducks into the crooked door of the Kelp & Curiosities Maritime Museum to escape a sudden squall, expecting little more than postcards and dust. Instead, she finds a cavern of glass cases, strange glows, and the smell of old salt-water stories, as if the whole building once tried to be a ship and never quite got over it. Captain Thimble Kelp hobbles out from behind a pile of brass instruments, muttering about “unseasonable weather” and “persistent children,” but his twinkling eyes betray his curiosity about this solitary girl with the sea-spray in her hair. As he gives her a rambling tour past ship-in-bottles that seem to move on their own and maps whose coastlines shift when she looks away, Mara notices that one battered diving helmet in the corner is still dripping wet. When she asks about it, Thimble goes abruptly quiet, then tells her, too casually, that some doors stay open even when we pretend they’re shut. The museum’s floorboards creak like someone breathing underneath, and when Mara presses her hand against a particular patch of wall, she feels—not wood—but a slow, cold pulse, like the heartbeat of the sea itself.
chapters.chapterText:
The storm arrived the way most good storms do: all at once, as if it had been waiting just around the corner for someone to open a door and let it in.

One moment the beach was a stretch of damp sand and scattered shells under a sulking grey sky; the next, the wind decided it had opinions. It came rolling over the sea and along the promenade, snatching at umbrellas, shoving at the swings in the empty playground, and whipping Mara Bright’s hair into her face so thoroughly she could taste salt and loose strands.

She had been walking the long way home on purpose. The short way meant crowded streets and people who asked what a ten-year-old was doing out alone so late, and then you had to look at your shoes and mumble about knowing the way and having a phone and all the other things grown-ups needed to hear to unclench. The long way meant the sea and the rattle of shells and the feeling that the horizon was a question nobody had finished answering yet.

Then the sky cracked open and dropped a sheet of rain onto her head.

Cold needles of water found the gap between her collar and her neck and raced down her spine. The second gust of wind shoved the rain sideways, right into her eyes. Mara squinted, hunched her shoulders around her backpack, and scanned the row of crooked seafront buildings for somewhere that didn’t look like it would collapse if you breathed too hard.

That was when she saw the sign.

It was hanging from a rusted bracket between a fish-and-chips shop and a boarded-up arcade, swinging wildly in the wind like it was trying to escape. The paint was peeling, the wood was warped, and half the letters were the colour of old teeth. It read:

KELP & CURIOSITIES  
MARITIME MUSEUM  
SINCE, MORE OR LESS, 1879

A spray of painted seaweed curled around the words, and a cartoon squid peered over the top with an expression that suggested it had seen things and would very much like to un-see them.

The door underneath the sign was painted the particular flaking green of doors that have given up on being impressive and are just trying to get through the day. It was also slightly crooked, as if it were leaning away from the fish-and-chips shop on one side and the abandoned arcade on the other and didn’t trust either of them.

Mara hesitated for a heartbeat. Then the next blast of wind threw a faceful of rain at her. She ducked her head, grabbed the tarnished brass handle, and slipped inside.

The door closed with a shuddering thump, like something enormous had just exhaled.

For a moment, Mara could hear only the storm raging outside, muffled by the walls, and the echo of her own breathing. The air was cool and full of dust and something else—salt, she realised, and a faint, lingering tang of old rope and rust and that particular dampness that belonged to things that had been wet a long time ago and never entirely forgiven anyone for it.

She pushed her wet hair back from her face and blinked into the dim interior.

From the street, the museum had looked like it couldn’t hold more than a single narrow room: a cramped little corridor with some postcards, maybe, and a rack of souvenir tea towels featuring whales that looked like bloated sausages. Instead, Mara found herself standing at the edge of what felt like a cavern.

The floorboards stretched away in all directions, uneven and dark with age. Glass cases sprouted from them like stalagmites, each one crowded with objects: coils of rope, barnacle-encrusted compasses, bits of coral, carved figureheads with flaking paint and blank, judging eyes. Nets hung from the ceiling in loops and drapes, catching dust instead of fish. Lanterns—actual lanterns, with thick glass and metal frames—hung from chains, glowing with a soft yellow light that clearly wasn’t electricity but also didn’t seem very committed to being fire.

The museum smelled like the underside of a pier and the pages of a very old book had gotten together and agreed to share their best features.

Mara took a cautious step forward. The floorboard under her foot creaked with a long, complaining note, then settled into a steady, almost rhythmic ticking, like someone tutting in the distance.

Her eyes adjusted slowly. The gloom resolved into more detail, and then more, and then she realised that either she was imagining things or she was in a building that was bigger on the inside.

From the outside, Kelp & Curiosities was wedged in like an afterthought between the other shops, barely the width of a bus. From the inside, the room stretched out in a long, meandering hall that bent away into shadows, with alcoves branching off to the left and right. There was a vague awareness at the edges of her vision of more staircases, more galleries above, iron railings, ladders leading… sideways?

At the far end, a staircase spiraled up and then down, though how it managed both at once was not entirely clear.

Mara frowned. She was good with spaces. She liked maps. She could usually tell if a room made sense. This room did not make sense. It did something to her sense of distance, pulling it long like chewing gum.

“Hello?” she called out, because that was what one did, apparently, when one found oneself mysteriously alone in an impossibly large museum that smelled like secrets and salt.

Her voice disappeared into the rafters and came back a moment later, thinner and more dubious.

There was a small bell on the counter by the entrance labelled PRESS IF YOU MUST in wobbly handwriting. Mara considered it. The bell looked like it resented being asked to do anything without proper notice. She decided to let it sulk in peace and wandered further in instead.

To her left, a row of glass cases held ships in bottles. This was ordinary enough, except that these ships did not appear to be entirely aware they were made of wood and glue and were supposed to stay put. Tiny white sails twitched, catching invisible breeze. A miniature wave slapped against a glass bottleneck. One ship, which appeared to be perpetually caught in the moment just before capsizing, creaked ominously and then… didn’t.

Mara leaned close to one of the bottles, fogging the glass with her breath. Inside, a crew of tiny figures scurried about, hauling ropes no thicker than a thread, adjusting sails no bigger than postage stamps. One even seemed to turn, shading its hand over its eyes, to peer back at her.

She jerked back so fast she nearly knocked over the next case. The floor complained loudly. Somewhere deeper in the museum, something metal clanged in protest.

Mara’s heart thumped in her ears. Then she laughed—just once, a small, breathy sound—because she was wet and cold and clearly tired enough to imagine things moving in bottles. Still, she decided, she didn’t need her face quite that close to the glass.

The next case held maps, laid out under glass like flattened, sleeping beasts. Some were yellowed with age; others were dark and stiff, ink faded to a ghostly grey. Waves were drawn with the obsessive detail of someone who loved water but did not entirely trust it. Sea serpents lounged in curling corners. Islands bristled with palm trees and alarming annotations in spidery handwriting: HERE THERE BE WHISPERS. DO NOT PROMISE ANYTHING ON THIS SHORE. ASK THE ROCKS PERMISSION FIRST.

Mara pointed to one coastline that curled like a question mark. “You are not there,” she murmured, because it definitely hadn’t been there when she’d first looked.

The coastline in question had shifted again, subtly, like someone changing their mind halfway through a sentence. A peninsula that had reached bravely out into the sea was now a stub. Two islands had slid closer together and were, in her opinion, definitely plotting something.

She pressed her nose almost to the glass, watching. The lines stayed stubbornly still.

“Fine,” she whispered. “I won’t look away, then.”

Something behind her coughed.

It was the sort of cough that had barnacles on it. It sounded as though it had weathered several storms on its own and come out the other side mildly offended. It also sounded distinctly human.

Mara spun around.

A man stood in the gap between two towering cabinets of sextants and brass tubes. At first glance, he looked like a pile of coats and scarves someone had left there by accident. Then the pile moved, revealing a face tanned to old leather, lined in the way maps were lined, with deep creases at the corners of the eyes from squinting into too many distances.

His hair was wild and grey, sticking out in ruffled waves as if it had tried very hard to be a storm and then, halfway through, forgotten what it was doing. A beard of the same unruly colour clung to his chin, threaded with the occasional glint of copper or brass, as though small bits of hardware had become permanently lost in it.

One leg was solid and booted. The other, from the knee down, was carved from wood the colour of old ship’s hulls, polished smooth by years of use, with tiny waves and ships and sea creatures etched along it. When he shifted, the carvings seemed to ripple.

He leaned on the counter with the familiarity of years, eyeing Mara as if she were an interesting new species of crab that had washed up uninvited.

“Closed,” he said. His voice had the rough-edged quality of someone who had spent a great deal of time shouting over wind and waves and now could only speak in varying degrees of grumble. “Or near enough as makes no odds. Didn’t you see the sign on the door?”

Mara glanced back over her shoulder. From this side, the door was farther away than it had any right to be. The small glass panel set into it did, indeed, have a painted sign hung behind it. It read: CLOSED-ISH.

“Oh,” she said. “I thought that meant ‘probably open if you’re polite about it.’”

The man huffed, which might have been a laugh that hadn’t quite committed. “Hnh. Modern children. Can’t read, but can argue with punctuation.”

“I can read,” Mara said, because this was important. “I just disagreed with your use of the suffix.”

His eyes, which were an unexpected sharp blue, crinkled. “Suffix. Is it. And what, in your expert professional opinion, does ‘ish’ mean, then?”

“It means the boundary is negotiable,” she said promptly. “Like when grown-ups say ‘bedtime-ish’ if it’s the holidays. Or ‘we’ll see’ when they’re going to say no, but they don’t want a discussion yet.”

The man snorted. “Hnh. She’s got you there, Thimble,” he muttered, apparently to himself, and then straightened with the creak of old bones and older wood.

He wiped his hands on his coat, which did not become appreciably cleaner for the effort, and squinted at her. “Right, then. What’ll you be, missy? Lost? Runaway? Wayward school group broke loose and you’re the clever one who found the door?”

“I’m not lost,” Mara said automatically, which was only partially true. She knew where she was on the map; it just felt as though the map had stretched when she wasn’t looking. “I just came in because of the rain. The storm. The unseasonable weather.”

“Unseasonable,” the man repeated, with the air of someone who had been personally affronted by the forecast. “That’s the word for it, right enough. Shouldn’t be blowing like that this time of year. Madam’s in one of her moods.”

Mara glanced instinctively toward the door, as if she might see Madam herself out there, rattling the windows. “Madam?”

He jerked his head toward the general direction of the sea. “Madam Ocean. Great wet temperamental lady out there. Changes her mind every five minutes, then pretends she meant to do that all along. You know her work: tides, storms, swallowing people who annoy her.” He gave her a narrow look. “And leaving others on the doorstep who ought to be in bed.”

“I’m not—” she started, then stopped, because actually she was very likely supposed to be on her way home. “My house isn’t far,” she amended instead. “And my parents know I like to walk by the water. It helps me think.”

“Hnh.” That sound again, somewhere between a grunt and a skeptical gull. “Thinking. Dangerous hobby at your age.” His eyes flicked to the droplets of seawater still clinging to the ends of her hair. “You’ve got the sea on you.”

“It’s raining,” Mara pointed out.

“Not that.” He waved a hand dismissively, then seemed to realise he was being mysterious and frowned at himself. “Never you mind that. What you need is a towel and five minutes to drip somewhere that isn’t my compass drawer. Captain Thimble Kelp, at your service, or at least at your mild inconvenience. Proprietor, curator, reluctant janitor, and general dogsbody of this illustrious establishment. And you are?”

“Mara,” she said. “Mara Bright.”

“Bright, eh?” He tilted his head, as if testing the word. “We shall see about that. Right now you look a bit more like Mara Damp.”

He limped—no, not limped, exactly; he walked with the determined uneven rhythm of someone who had long ago decided that every step was a small argument with gravity and he intended to win them all—around the counter and rummaged in a crate. After a moment of clinking and muttering, he produced a towel that might once have been white but was now the exact unplaceable shade of fabric that has seen too many adventures and not enough detergent.

He handed it to her. “Here. Don’t drip on anything that looks like it might disintegrate. Which is most of it.”

“Thanks,” Mara said, rubbing at her hair. The towel smelled faintly of rope and lemons, as if someone had made a half-hearted attempt to make it pleasant and then been distracted by something involving pulleys.

Captain Thimble watched her for a moment, his head cocked. “So. You wandered in. You could have stayed by the door. Instead you made it all the way to the maps. Hnh. Maps are for people who want to go somewhere they haven’t quite admitted to yet.”

“I like maps,” Mara said, because that felt safer than admitting she liked the feeling of being out of place and yet exactly where she was supposed to be.

“Of course you do. Curious sort, are you?” His eyes twinkled. “The dangerous kind.”

“Is there a safe kind?” Mara asked.

“Not in my experience,” he said cheerfully. “Right. Since you’re in here and I haven’t got the heart to chuck you back into Madam Ocean’s tantrum, you may as well have a look round. Properly, mind. None of this ‘in, out, ooh look a souvenir keyring’ nonsense. You stand still and listen to things. They’ll talk if you give ‘em half a chance.”

“Things talk?” Mara said, delighted despite herself.

“Well, not in words,” Thimble said. “Mostly they mutter. Or vibrate. Or fall on your head at interesting moments. But that’s as may be. This is the Kelp & Curiosities Maritime Museum. Everything in here’s got a story. Some of ‘em are even true.”

“Which ones?” she asked.

He grinned, showing a row of teeth that looked like they’d had disagreements with several hard biscuits and at least one mast. “If I told you that, where’d be the fun?” He gestured broadly with one arm, nearly smacking a hanging net full of glass floats. “Come on, then. I’ll give you the short tour.”

“This is the short tour?” Mara said, glancing again at the impossible length of the hall.

“Short-ish,” he said, with a wink.

He set off between the cases, cane tapping, wooden leg thudding, the rhythm as much a part of the place as the creaking floor. Mara followed, towel draped around her shoulders like a very unimpressive cape.

As they walked, he talked—rambling, sideways narratives that looped and doubled back on themselves like tangled rigging.

“This here,” he said, stopping by a glass case in which a length of rope lay coiled, fatter than Mara’s arm and stiff with age, “is a piece of the Great Rope of Arelia. Strongest rope ever woven. They say it was spun from the hair of the Storm Sisters, three witches who lived on a cliff and argued with thunder. Anchored the biggest ship ever built. Ship still sank, mind you. Turns out you can’t tie a knot in a promise.”

Mara peered closer. The rope did look like it might have been spun from something once alive; tiny threads of silver glinted in the rough fibres, catching the lantern light.

“Why did the ship sink?” she asked.

“Captain promised too much,” Thimble said, almost absently. “Sea remembers.” He shook himself slightly and moved on.

They passed a collection of figureheads: women with hair that had once been bright gold or red now flaked down to muted streaks, men with proud carved chins, beasts with open mouths frozen mid-roar. One mermaid’s eyes were inlaid with tiny chips of what might have been mother-of-pearl; they seemed wet.

“Do they watch people?” Mara asked, not entirely joking.

“Only the liars,” Thimble said. “So you’re safe if you keep your fibs small and your truths big.”

They turned a corner that shouldn’t have existed, given the shape of the building as seen from outside. The air grew cooler, and the smell of salt was stronger here, less memory and more presence. The floor felt not just old but… layered, as if many floors had been piled on top of each other until no one could remember where the first one had started.

Mara slowed. “How… big is this place?” she asked, unable to keep the wonder out of her voice.

“Oh, you know,” Thimble said vaguely. “Big enough to hold what it needs to. Small enough the council doesn’t notice.” He squinted up at the ceiling, where several rafters were doing their best impression of a ship’s hull turned inside out. “Buildings expand if you put enough stories in ‘em. Never seen a bookshelf that stopped at the wall, have you? They just keep going up in your head. Same principle. Now, over here we’ve got the starboard annex—”

“Starboard?” Mara said. “Isn’t that… ships?”

“Everything’s ships if you argue hard enough,” Thimble said. “Walls, floors, people. Some just haven’t grown their sails yet.”

The starboard annex contained, among other things, a brass instrument taller than Mara, bristling with levers and lenses and little glass bulbs that glowed with an eerie blue light. It hummed faintly, the sound prickling against her teeth. A small hand-painted sign at its base read: EXPERIMENTAL TIDE CALCULATOR (DO NOT ASK IT ABOUT THURSDAYS).

“What happens on Thursdays?” Mara asked.

“Nothing you need to see before you’ve had algebra,” Thimble said firmly.

They wandered on. The storm outside faded into background growls and occasional flashes of light through high, grimy windows. Time stretched, loosening at the edges. Mara lost track of how long they’d been walking. It could have been ten minutes; it could have been an hour. The museum felt like the sort of place where clocks forgot their jobs.

Every now and then, Thimble glanced sideways at her, as if checking she was still there and hadn’t dissolved into a puddle of seawater and curiosity.

“You’re a quiet one,” he observed eventually. “Most children I get in here, they’re all fingers and noise. Pick up everything, ask if it’s haunted, then demand a gift shop. You look instead. You listen.”

Mara shrugged, uncomfortable under the attention. “People talk a lot,” she said. “But they don’t always say anything.”

He barked a laugh. “Oh, you’re trouble. I can tell.”

They came at last to a corner of the museum that was less well lit. The nearest lantern flickered uncertainly, casting wavering shadows. Here, things were piled more haphazardly: crates stacked on crates, tarps thrown over bulky shapes, barrels with stencilled words too faded to read. It felt less like an exhibition and more like the attic of someone with a very specific obsession.

Mara’s gaze snagged on a shape half-hidden behind a crate of cracked glass buoys.

A battered diving helmet sat on a low wooden stand. It was the old-fashioned kind she’d seen in pictures in books: big and round, made of dulled copper, with thick glass portholes like watchful eyes. Tubes emerged from the sides, snaking down toward a coil of hose on the floor. Bolts ringed the neck where it would fasten to a suit. A faint green tinge crawled over the metal where sea and oxygen had quarrelled.

All of that was ordinary enough, for certain values of ordinary.

The not-ordinary thing was that water was dripping from it.

A slow bead of clear seawater formed at the rim of the front porthole, swelled, and then dropped with a soft pat onto the warped floorboards below. Another drop was already forming behind it, patient and inevitable, as if there were an entire ocean contained inside the helmet and it had decided to leak.

Mara stepped closer, captivated. The air around the helmet felt cooler, damp but not unpleasantly so, like the breath of a cave mouth in summer. Her skin prickled with goosebumps that had nothing to do with the damp towel now hanging forgotten over her arm.

“Careful,” Thimble said sharply. His cane came down with a thud that had more to it than wood on wood, as if it were a warning to the floor as well as to her.

“It’s dripping,” Mara said, unable to keep the wonder out of her voice. “Why is it still wet?”

Thimble’s face did something complicated. The lines at the corners of his mouth deepened. His eyes, which had been full of mockery and half-amusement, shuttered slightly, as though he were pulling a curtain behind them.

“Old leak,” he said, too casually. “Pipes in this place have a mind of their own. Get condensation, that’s all. Nothing to bother about.”

He was lying.

Mara knew the taste of lies. Adults lied the way they put on coats: casually, because the weather demanded it. Some lies were big and clumsy, like “It won’t hurt” before injections, or “We’ll talk about it later,” which translated to “We will never talk about this again and I hope you forget.” Some were small and papery, like “We’ll see.”

This lie felt different. It felt heavy, weighted down with something unsaid. It sat between them like another person.

“If it’s just condensation,” she said, picking her words with careful innocence, “why does it smell like the sea?”

She didn’t mean the general salt-and-must of the museum. There was, around the helmet, a different smell: cold and deep and clean, the scent of water far below where the waves broke, where things were old and slow and listening.

Thimble’s hand tightened on his cane. For a moment, he looked not like an old man in a shabby coat in a too-big museum, but like someone who had once stood on a deck in the middle of an unending night, listening for something in the swell of the waves and hoping it wouldn’t answer.

“Some doors,” he said, after a too-long pause, “stay open even when we pretend they’re shut.”

The words hung in the air, heavier than they should have been.

Mara tore her gaze away from the helmet to stare at him. “Doors?” she echoed.

“Mm.” He blew out his cheeks, as if annoyed with himself for saying even that much. “Places you can go. Places that can come to you. Holes worn through in the world, like in an old net. You patch ’em as best you can, but the sea…” He trailed off, shook his head. “The sea doesn’t always agree with your idea of a good patch.”

“That’s not a very reassuring answer,” Mara said quietly.

“Wasn’t trying to reassure you,” Thimble said. “Reassurance’s how people get themselves eaten by metaphors.” He opened his mouth as if to add something, then thought better of it. “Anyway. The helmet’s an old piece. Relic. Leftover. Not for climbing into. Not for poking. Not for—” He caught the look in her eyes and pointed a finger at her. “Not for curious children to put on their heads and go exploring. Clear?”

Mara bristled, torn between indignation and the thrill of being seen through so completely. “I wasn’t going to—”

“You were absolutely going to,” he said. “Could see it in your shoulders. All set to lean just that bit too far. You’ve got that look.” His gaze softened, just for a moment. “The one that asks ‘What if?’ louder than it asks ‘Should I?’.”

He turned away abruptly, as if annoyed with his own softness. “Come on. Enough of that,” he said more briskly. “There’s other things to see that don’t drip or sulk or tempt you into trouble.”

He moved off, but Mara lingered for one more heartbeat, drawn to the slow, steady drip. She watched another bead of water form and fall. The tiny splash sounded too loud in her ears.

The floor beneath the helmet was damp, darker than the surrounding boards. She could see faint salt crystals blossoming where drops had evaporated, pale and sharp-edged. A small puddle had collected in a shallow dip; the surface trembled, as if something far away had moved.

She swallowed and turned to follow Thimble.

They took another path now, looping back—or maybe deeper in; distance was unreliable here—past a display of bottles filled with sand from beaches all over the world. Each was labelled in careful ink: PORT SAINT-LOUIS, FINE AS FLOUR; SKAGERRAK, SHARP AS TEETH; NARROW STRAND, DO NOT OPEN.

“Never open bottled sand,” Thimble advised. “You think you’re tipping out a nice little souvenir, next thing you know you’re ankle-deep in someone else’s shoreline and arguing with their crabs.”

Mara murmured something that might have been agreement. Her thoughts were still back with the dripping helmet and the idea of doors that didn’t quite close.

They reached a long wall lined with framed photographs: ships in harbours, the sea in all its disguises, people in stiff old clothes squinting into the sun. Thimble paused before one of them: a black-and-white image of a younger version of himself standing on the deck of a ship, hair only marginally less wild, arm slung around another sailor whose face had been damaged by time or by something else—the features were blurred, the outline smudged.

He looked at it only briefly, then moved on without comment. Mara filed that away in the part of her mind labelled Things Adults Don’t Say Because They Think You’ll Break.

After a while, the echo of her own footsteps started to sound strange to her, as if there were someone walking almost in time with her, half a beat out of sync. The floor creaked and settled. Somewhere, something that might have been a clock chimed a time that didn’t correspond to anything on her watch.

They passed a display of shells arranged in spirals and lines. As they drew near, Mara could swear she heard a faint susurrus, like distant whispers. When she leaned closer to a large conch, the sound sharpened into something almost like words in a language she didn’t know but nearly understood.

She straightened quickly. “Do you ever feel like the building is… listening?” she asked.

Thimble’s mouth twitched. “Building?” he said. “Oh, no. This isn’t a building. This is a story that got too big to stay on a shelf, so it grew walls to keep the rain out.” He tapped his cane twice on the floorboards. The wood answered with a hollow, resonant thump. “She creaks when the tide changes,” he added, almost fondly. “Makes her own weather sometimes, too, when Madam gets moody.”

As if on cue, a low groan sounded under their feet, followed by a ripple of movement that ran through the floor like a breath. Mara stumbled, catching herself on the edge of a glass case. The boards felt, for a moment, less like wood and more like ribs.

“Did you feel that?” she whispered.

“Old place,” Thimble said lightly, though his gaze flicked down, measuring. “Settling. Remembering. Might be the storm outside nudging her nerves. She doesn’t entirely approve of gales. Says they’re show-offs.”

Mara wasn’t satisfied with that answer. The sensation had been unmistakable: the slow rise and fall underfoot, as if something enormous and patient lay beneath the museum, sleeping. For a second, the thought of the ocean—not the polite fringe of waves on the beach, but the deep, dark weight of it far out—rose in her mind, and she felt very small.

She wandered toward a patch of wall between two display cases. It was an unremarkable section of wooden planking, painted the same tired off-white as the other walls, scuffed where people had brushed past over the years. But her skin prickled as she neared it.

Mara reached out, almost without thinking, and laid her palm flat against the wood.

The museum’s noises dwindled. The creak of boards, the dim mutter of Thimble talking about something behind her, the distant rumble of the storm—all of it faded to a muffled hush, as if she had put her head underwater.

Beneath her hand, the wall was cool. Not the cool of shade or unheated buildings, but a deeper cold, the kind that seeped into rocks at the bottom of the sea. The wood, which should have felt solid and unchanging, seemed to flex, infinitesimally, against her skin.

Thump.

It was slow, so slow that if she hadn’t been concentrating she might have missed it entirely. A pressure, a subtle outward push, like a pulse.

Thump.

Her own heartbeat answered, quick and startled. The wall’s pulse remained unhurried, immense, indifferent.

“That’s not—” she began, her voice strange in her own ears, and then stopped, because she didn’t know how to finish that sentence. That’s not possible? That’s not wood? That’s not just a building?

From somewhere behind her: “Mara? Best not touch—”

She pressed her hand more firmly against the wall. The cold deepened, but it wasn’t unfriendly. It reminded her of being a small child standing ankle-deep in the surf, feeling the pull of the tide around her feet, the sense that something enormous and restless was moving beneath the surface, paying no attention to her and yet holding her up.

Images flooded her mind, not sharp enough to call visions, but more than imagination: green light filtering down through water; shapes drifting in the blue; the glimmer of something far below, like a city made of lanterns; silence, and then a sound like a whale’s call stretched into forever.

Her breath hitched. Her fingers tingled. For a heartbeat—hers or the wall’s, she couldn’t tell—the world narrowed to that point of contact.

“Enough,” Thimble said, closer now, voice low but edged. A warm, calloused hand closed gently but firmly around her wrist, lifting her palm away from the wood.

The connection broke with a sensation like surf withdrawing from sand. The noises of the museum rushed back in: the creak, the distant rattle, the hum of some unseen machine complaining about the damp. Mara swayed, trying to reorient herself.

She looked up at Thimble. For the first time since she’d met him, he looked genuinely unsettled.

“You felt that,” she said, more statement than question.

He released her wrist slowly. His fingers left faint impressions in her skin, like the memory of a rope.

“Some stories,” he said, choosing his words with care, “are meant to rock you to sleep. Some are meant to wake you up. And some aren’t meant for children who ought to be home by supper.”

“That wall is—” She groped for the right word and fell, inevitably, on the obvious. “—alive.”

He snorted, but there was no real humour in it. “Everything’s alive if you look close enough. Stones. Seas. Maps. Old men.” He glanced at the wall, then away again, as if looking at it too long hurt his eyes. “This place sits where it sits,” he went on. “Here and… not entirely here. There are currents in wood as well as water. Sometimes they… syncopate.”

“Syncopate,” Mara repeated softly. She knew the word from music lessons she’d once had and abandoned, when the piano teacher had become far more interested in telling Mara to sit up straight than in the strange stormy piece Mara had wanted to learn. Syncopation: the stress on the weak beat, the shift where you didn’t expect it.

She thought of tides. Of doors that refused to stay shut.

“I thought this was just a museum,” she said, but what she really meant was, I thought this was solid.

Captain Thimble Kelp regarded her with those sharp blue eyes that had seen too much sea and not enough sleep.

“Nothing is ‘just’ anything,” he said. “Not if you stare at it long enough. This place…” He gestured vaguely around them. “This place remembers more than it ought to. Some of it’s mine. Some of it’s Madam’s. Some of it belongs to other folk. Folk who live…” He inclined his head slightly toward the wall she’d touched, toward the hidden world beneath the waves. “…elsewhere.”

Mara’s heart thumped too fast. Images from that strange moment of contact eddied at the edge of her mind: glimmers of light, slow shadows in deep water.

“You mean—” she began.

“I mean,” he interrupted briskly, “that it’s late. And you’re wet. And if I let you stay any longer, you’ll sink roots into my floor and Madam Ocean will knock a hole in the foundations to come see what I’m doing with her favourite sort of creature.”

“Favourite sort?” Mara said.

“Curious,” he said simply. “She likes the ones who lean over edges.” He nodded toward the door, which was now, without warning, only a short distance away. Mara blinked. She was certain they had been deeper inside the museum a moment before, but the entrance was right there: the glass panel, the CLOSED-ISH sign, the brass handle beaded with condensation from the storm outside.

“How did we get…?” she started.

“Short cut,” Thimble said, with the air of someone who wasn’t going to explain how he’d folded space because then he’d have to draw diagrams and he’d never get his tea. “Museum knows when to take pity on small drippy humans. Off you go, Miss Bright. Come back when it’s not trying to rain sideways and your parents won’t send the coastguard out after you.”

Mara stood still. The towel felt heavy on her shoulders. Her palm still tingled faintly where it had touched the wall. There were a thousand questions pressing against her teeth, jostling to be first: What did you mean, ‘other folk’? What’s behind the wall? Why is the helmet dripping? Have you been there? Can I go?

Instead, she heard herself say, “Is it all real?”

Thimble paused with his hand on the back of a chair that definitely hadn’t been there before. His shoulders slumped a fraction, as if someone had let air out of them.

“Depends what you mean by real,” he said at last. “Is the tide real, if you only believe in land? Are stories real, if you can’t trip over them? You’ve seen ships in bottles that remember how to move. Maps that forget to stay put. A wall that pulses like a heart. You tell me.”

“I…” Mara swallowed. “I don’t know yet.”

He smiled, a quick sideways thing that looked almost shy. “Good answer. The moment you’re sure of everything, you stop seeing the bits that don’t fit. And those are the important bits.”

“Will you be here tomorrow?” she asked, surprising herself.

“Unless Madam decides to relocate the whole enterprise to the bottom of the bay out of spite,” he said. “I open at ten-ish. Close at five-ish. Same rules as the tide: entirely unpredictable unless you pay attention.” He tilted his head. “You’ll come back?”

It wasn’t a demand. It wasn’t even really a question. It was curiosity, offered like a rope.

“Yes,” Mara said. The word felt like a promise—not made to him, or even to herself, but to the strange deep something that had pulsed beneath her hand. “I’ll come back.”

He nodded, as if this confirmed some private theory. “Mind your step on the way out,” he said. “She’s a bit twitchy when the weather’s like this.”

Mara nodded and reached for the doorknob. As her fingers closed around the cold metal, she hesitated and glanced back one last time.

The museum stretched away into dimness; the lanterns swayed gently, as though under the influence of some current. The dripping helmet sat in its shadowed corner, just visible between two stacks of crates. Even from here, she could see a tiny flicker of reflected light in its glass, like the suggestion of something moving behind it.

Captain Thimble Kelp stood beside the counter, one hand resting on the worn wood, his wooden leg bent just so, his storm-tousled hair creating its own minor weather system around his head. He lifted a hand in a small salute.

Outside, the storm roared.

Mara opened the door. Wind slapped her in the face, wet and wild. For a moment the world was all grey and noise. She stepped out, pulling the door shut behind her with both hands.

It shut with that same deep, shuddering thump, like a heart closing around a secret.

She stood on the slick pavement, immediately soaked again, hair plastered to her cheeks, shoes squelching. The promenade was almost empty; a single gull hunched on a lamppost, looking miserable. The fish-and-chips shop’s neon sign buzzed and flickered. The boarded-up arcade sighed.

Mara turned to look at the museum. From the outside, it was as it had been: a narrow little building squeezed between its neighbours, leaning slightly sideways. The sign creaked in the wind. The windows were small and murky. Light glowed faintly behind the glass, but it was the sort of light that belonged to one tired bulb, not to a cavern full of lanterns and moving maps.

She reached out and touched the peeling green paint of the door. It was just a door. Chilly under her fingers, rain-slick, but no pulse.

Still, her own heart beat a little faster, echoing something she had felt inside.

She glanced down. At the edge of her thumbnail, a tiny white salt crystal clung, glittering faintly.

Mara smiled, a little unevenly, and curled her hand into a fist around it.

The storm tugged at her, urging her home. She set off along the promenade, the wind at her back, the taste of salt on her lips, and the knowledge that somewhere, just a few feet and a world away, there was a shabby seaside museum with a heartbeat in its walls and a door that didn’t entirely know the meaning of closed.

Behind her, in the Kelp & Curiosities Maritime Museum, water dripped—steadily, patiently—from a battered diving helmet, forming a growing puddle on the floor. And far beneath the town, beneath the sand and rock and restless waves, something vast and luminous turned in its sleep at the faint touch of a child’s hand against its distant, wooden skin.

chapters.chaptershortdescription: Where Mara returns to the shore, follows a trail of impossible clues, and discovers a hidden door in a tidepool that leads downward instead of in.
chapters.chapterdetails: The next day, unable to stop thinking about the dripping helmet and the pulsing wall, Mara returns to the rocky beach below the museum just as the tide is going out. The sky is clear but the water seems to whisper, hissing secrets between the stones, and a line of faintly glowing shells leads her to an isolated tidepool she’s never noticed before. Leaning over, she sees not pebbles and seaweed but an uncanny reflection: an archway of light, rippling beneath the surface where her face should be. Remembering Captain Thimble’s half-muttered warning about doors, she hesitates—then her curiosity, which is larger than most people’s common sense, wins. She reaches in, and her hand passes through the water with hardly any resistance, feeling a cool, spiraling tug. The reflection ripples, the world tilts sideways, and Mara finds herself slipping feet-first through the pool as if it has become a vertical tunnel, shafts of blue-green light stretching below her like a staircase made of water. Above, the shore recedes into a shimmering circle; below, something bright and distant flickers like a city of fireflies trapped in glass.
chapters.chapterText:
By morning, the storm had remembered it had other places to be.

The sky over the town was scrubbed clean and pale, streaked with wisps of cloud that looked like they’d been left behind by a distracted painter. The sea, having shouted itself hoarse all night, lay sprawled along the shore in a mood that might generously be called “apologetic,” ruffling the edge of the sand with small, guilty waves.

None of this helped Mara Bright’s concentration in the slightest.

Her cereal had gone from crisp to soggy in record time while she stared past it, seeing not the kitchen window with its view of the neighbour’s thoroughly uninteresting shed, but a dim museum hall, a dripping helmet, and a wall that had pulsed like a slow, enormous heart under her hand.

“Eat,” said her mother, without looking up from the tablet propped against the sugar jar. “You’ll be late.”

“I am eating,” Mara said automatically, though what she was doing could more accurately be described as prodding. “Technically.”

Her father lowered his newspaper just enough to peer at her over the edge. “You’re quiet,” he observed. “Even for you.”

“I’m thinking,” Mara replied, because that was easier than saying I touched a building and it thought back at me.

“About what?” her mother asked, still skimming headlines with the intensity of someone hoping the news might, just once, be about something pleasant like kittens winning the lottery.

Mara hesitated. “Maps,” she said finally. It wasn’t untrue. “And… museums.”

“The one on the front?” her father said, brightening. “Captain Something Kelp? They used to have a very stern octopus in a jar. I don’t know what happened to it.”

“Legislation, probably,” her mother murmured. “Or ethics.”

Mara chewed, swallowed, and found that “Captain Thimble Kelp” caught on something inside her. She turned the name over in her mind the way she might turn over a shell, checking for hidden patterns. The memory of his lined face, his storm-tossed hair, the way his fingers had tightened on her wrist—those clung like salt to skin.

“Are you going out after?” her mother asked. “You can, just—stay where there are people, all right? No wandering off down strange alleys or climbing derelict piers or befriending seals. They carry diseases.”

“You can’t get diseases from befriending seals,” Mara said.

“Emotional diseases,” her father put in. “Attachment. Separation anxiety. Fish breath.”

“Ha,” said her mother, entirely without humour. “Anyway, text if you change locations. Please. That’s all I ask.”

It was not all she asked. There was also Eat vegetables and Don’t lick strange things no matter what your cousin dares you, and the evergreen favourite Don’t go swimming alone. But she didn’t say those, because she trusted repetition to have carved them into Mara’s brain already.

“I’ll stay on the beach,” Mara said. Which again, was not exactly a lie. The beach was, after all, technically people-adjacent. “Tide’s going out. It’s nice.”

Her father made a thoughtful noise. “Watch out for jellyfish,” he said. “Those pink ones have an agenda.”

Mara finished the last of the now thoroughly unpleasant cereal, grabbed her jacket, and slung her backpack over one shoulder.

On her way to the door, her mother called, “Mara? Phone!”

Mara patted her pockets and came up with the small, scratched rectangle. “Got it!”

“On,” her mother added. “And not on silent.”

“You’re ruining my mysterious loner aesthetic,” Mara muttered, but she flicked the volume up anyway. It gave a small, startled chirp, as if it hadn’t been allowed to speak in days.

Outside, the air tasted like rinsed glass. The world had that particular brightness it only ever had after storms, when every surface was freshly washed and the colours hadn’t had time to fade back to normal levels of disappointment. Puddles still collected in the dips of the pavement, reflecting slices of sky. A gull strutted along the railings in the firm belief that it owned all horizons.

Mara’s feet knew the way even without her thinking about it: down the road that sloped toward the sea, past the cluster of souvenir shops still shuttered, their postcards trembling in their racks; across the car park that always smelled faintly of fried onions no matter the time of day; and onto the promenade, where the sea spread out before her, blue and deceptively simple.

The museum crouched in its familiar place between the fish-and-chips shop and the dead arcade, its flaking green door and KELP & CURIOSITIES sign looking no more or less improbable than the day before. If she squinted, Mara could believe that the walls bulged slightly, as though holding in more space than their dimensions should allow.

She slowed as she approached, half expecting the doorknob to twitch, the CLOSED-ISH sign to flick over to OPEN of its own accord. It didn’t. The windows were dull and faintly reflective. A hand-painted note had been wedged against the glass, scrawled in a hasty, spidery script.

BACK IN A BIT  
TIDE BUSINESS  
—C.T.K.

“Tide business?” she murmured. “Is that like monkey business, but wetter?”

The note stared back, unhelpful.

Mara felt an immediate, sharp pinch of disappointment. Her plan—such as it was—had been to march in, ask Captain Thimble Kelp as many questions as he could withstand, and hope that somewhere between “accidental” and “annoying,” some answers would leak out.

Instead, the museum was stubbornly, smugly shut.

She turned away, toward the sea.

The tide had retreated considerably since dawn, dragging the waterline back to reveal a long stretch of wet sand and, beyond that, the darker, jagged scatter of rocks that made up the lower beach. Normally, she avoided that part; it was full of treacherous algae and sharp edges and the sort of crannies that invited ankles to twist.

Today, the exposed rocks gleamed like the slick backs of strange, sleeping animals. Seawater puddled in hollows, catching the sunlight. The hiss and susurrus of the waves was broken up now by the smaller sounds of the revealed shore: trickles, drips, the occasional plop of something dropping back into somewhere.

Mara hopped down the concrete steps from the promenade to the sand. Her shoes sank slightly; the sand was firm but damp, a cool give under her soles. The air here smelled more strongly of salt and less of chips. Gulls wheeled overhead, arguing.

She pulled in a lungful of sea air. It felt… different.

Not bad. Just… crowded. As if she’d stepped into a room mid-conversation and everyone had gone silent in exactly the way that meant they were still talking, just at a pitch she couldn’t hear.

The waves, sliding in and out over the sand, hissed like someone whispering secrets through clenched teeth.

Mara frowned, tilting her head, the way you do when you’re sure you heard your name and then realise you didn’t. The sound of the water seemed almost patterned. Not quite speech—but not quite random, either.

“You’re being weird,” she informed the sea. “Again.”

A small, entirely ordinary wavelets lapped at her toes in what might have been an indifferent shrug.

Fine. If the museum was closed and the sea was being cryptic, she would do what she always did when adults were unhelpful: look around more carefully.

Her gaze drifted along the line where rock met sand. There were the usual things—kelp draped like abandoned scarves, limpets clinging like tiny stubborn helmets, the occasional ruined crab exoskeleton (someone’s dinner, someone else’s warning). Tidepools caught the sky in their still surfaces, hosting small universes of weed and shell and darting, suspicious fish.

And there—just at the edge of where the beach tilted down into the more serious rocks—something glimmered.

Not the bright glare of sun on wet stone. This was a softer glow, pale and uncertain, the colour of old pearls or quiet moonlight.

Mara narrowed her eyes and stepped closer.

Shells.

They were arranged in a line along the sand, leading away across the uneven terrain like a string of beads dropped in a hurry. Each one was about the size of her thumb, delicately curved, their ridges smooth and intact. They were also, undeniably, faintly luminous.

Not enough to be dramatic. If she’d been out here at noon, she might not have seen it at all. But in the slant of late morning light, each shell seemed to hold a tiny smear of its own radiance, a ghost of glow that didn’t quite match the direction or colour of the sun.

The line of shells started a few feet from where she stood, as if whoever had laid them had begun well out of stomp-range. They wound between rocks, up over a small outcrop, and then disappeared from view behind a larger, weed-draped boulder.

She looked around, half expecting to see a child sprinting away giggling, or an artist lurking behind a dune waiting to see if anyone noticed their installation.

The beach was mostly empty. An old man with a metal detector was sweeping patient, hopeful arcs closer to the waterline. Two teenagers sat on a concrete breakwater, headphones in, mutually pretending the other didn’t exist. No one was paying her the slightest attention.

Mara’s scalp prickled.

She crouched to pick up the nearest shell.

It was cool, slick with a film of saltwater. The glow, up close, was more a suggestion than a fact—the faintest luminescence along the inner spiral, as if someone had breathed starlight into it and then mostly changed their mind. When she turned it over in her fingers, the sheen followed no logic of light source she understood.

“It’s bioluminescence,” she told herself. “Probably. Some tiny organisms. Or a trick of the angle. Or—”

The shell vibrated, very slightly, in her hand. Just a shiver, the way a cat’s skin twitches in a dream.

She nearly dropped it.

“Okay,” she said aloud, because sometimes sound steadied things. “New plan. We do not explain everything immediately, because that way lies headaches. We… observe.”

She set the shell back in its place in the line and straightened up.

The shells continued onward, their ghostly glow just enough to mark a path. It was such a deliberate arrangement. Too tidy for nature’s usual chaos, too random for the sort of pattern human children made when they were bored.

“Captain Thimble,” she muttered. “If this is one of your ‘interactive exhibits,’ I’m going to… continue to follow it, actually, because who am I kidding.”

She adjusted her backpack strap and stepped after the shells.

The rocks here were irregular, jutting and pocked. The sea’s retreat had left them slick in places, dry and rough in others. Mara picked her way carefully, feeling for stable footholds, testing each step. The line of shells twined ahead of her, occasionally disappearing behind a stone and then reappearing on the other side like a thought she kept almost losing.

As she moved farther from the main stretch of sand, the sound of the waves shifted in her ears, becoming more muffled, bounced and chopped by the surrounding rocks. Other noises rose in its place: the gurgle of trapped water, the clack of shells knocking together, the tiny fizz of dissolving foam.

And underneath all of that, something else.

A whispering, again—but closer now, clearer. Not in words she recognised, but with an intonation that felt like question, like invitation, like Come see.

She paused near a low ridge of stone. The shells led up and over it, their glow brightening just a fraction as the rock’s shadow fell across them. On the other side, she caught a glimmer of open water.

The ridge itself rose to around her waist. Seaweed had draped itself along its crest, drying to a dark, crackling fringe. Small barnacles clustered on its seaward face, the barnacle equivalent of a metropolis.

Mara put one hand on the rough rock for balance and scrambled clumsily up.

On the far side, the ground fell away more steeply than she’d expected, turning into a tangle of boulders worn into curves and channels by centuries of water. At the bottom of this tumble lay an isolated hollow, a basin scooped out of the stone.

A tidepool.

Plenty of tidepools dotted the lower beach, but this one was oddly set apart, as if the rest of the ocean had politely looked the other way when it reached this spot. The walls around it rose higher, making a little amphitheatre of stone. The pool itself was roughly oval and surprisingly still; even from here, Mari could see it wasn’t agitated by the usual patterns of surface ripples. It was a mirror punched into the world.

The line of shells descended the slope toward it, then circled its edge almost protectively, forming a loose, glowing halo.

Mara slid down the inner side of the ridge, catching herself with a hand against the rock. Her shoes skidded on patches of algae; tiny drops of cold water splashed her ankles. When she reached more level ground, she stood for a moment, just looking.

The pool’s water was clear, the colour of glass just before it takes on a tint. Bits of seaweed clung to the sides, swaying gently in water that did not appear to be moving. Sunlight slanted in, cutting clean lines on the stone.

She stepped closer until her toes edged the wet ring of stone at the pool’s lip. Instinctively, she expected to see the usual: sand and pebbles at the bottom, maybe a crab or two, perhaps a small fish darting about with paranoid efficiency.

Instead, the water held—her.

Her reflection stared back: damp curls escaping her ponytail, jacket hood shoved back, yesterday’s salt-scrubbed trainers, the faint smudge of pencil on her right hand that never quite went away. Above her, the same clear sky; around her, the same stones.

For a second, it was entirely ordinary.

Then the world shifted, very slightly. Like a picture behind glass catching a different angle of light.

Her reflection wavered, as if someone had breathed on the inside of the water.

The Mara in the pool blurred at the edges, colours smudging. The stones around her melted into softer, darker shapes. The sky behind her dimmed and—not blackened, exactly, but deepened, like the blue of the sea when you look straight down from a boat and remember there’s more below you than you like to think about.

Her reflected face peeled away, drifting, the features separating into ripples. For a breathless instant, there was nothing there but the suggestion of movement, the hint of depth.

Then something else resolved, where her reflection should have been.

It was not a simple picture. It had perspective, distance. It had light.

An archway hung there, made entirely of glow.

Not built of stone or metal, but of brightness itself: pale, wavering lines that traced the outline of a door with no apparent support. It was as if someone had drawn an opening in the air using phosphorescent ink.

The archway hovered a short distance “behind” the surface—behind, under, below; the directions were suddenly suspect—and beyond it, instead of more rock or sand, was darkness laced with faint threads of greenish light, moving slowly like currents or hanging weeds.

Every time the tidepool’s surface shivered, the arch’s outline flickered. It wasn’t a reflection of something above her; it was a window to something else.

Mara’s scalp prickled. Her breath had gone shallow without her noticing. She blinked twice, hard, then leaned closer, elbows against her knees, until her face was only a handspan above the water.

The arch remained.

She could make out the rough idea of a space beyond it—a sense of “downward,” of more water, of distance. Like looking down a well or a long, deep shaft.

The whispering at the edges of her hearing grew clearer. It felt like a sound you couldn’t hear with your ears, only your bones: the soft shiver of water over stone, the far-off thrum she’d felt in the museum wall, the echo of whale song thinned out for shore.

“Some doors stay open even when we pretend they’re shut,” Captain Thimble Kelp had said.

Her knees went weak.

“Door,” she whispered. The word tasted strange in this place. “You’re a door.”

The tidepool, being a tidepool, said nothing. But the arch seemed to brighten, just by a shade, as if someone had adjusted the contrast.

Mara’s mind did an unhelpful thing then: it offered her a series of perfectly sensible options.

You could go back, it suggested. You could go back up the rocks and onto the sand and pretend you never saw this. You could wait until the museum opens and tell Captain Thimble and let him deal with it. You could take a photo and think about it later. You could—

Her curiosity, which had never listened particularly well to reason and was currently very large and humming like a tensioned wire, overruled the list.

“Don’t you dare climb into that helmet,” Thimble had warned. He hadn’t said anything about tidepools.

“Mum is going to say I went looking for trouble,” she murmured. “It’s not my fault. Trouble left me a glowing trail of shells.”

Her hand hovered over the water.

It looked like water. It shone like water. A faint breeze from the sea ruffled its surface, distorting the view of the archway beneath. She could see, if she looked carefully, tiny bits of debris suspended in it: sand, the ghost-lace threads of plankton, a stray bubble.

“Just touch it,” she told herself. “That’s all. Touch the weird impossible thing and then… reassess.”

Captain Thimble’s voice echoed in the back of her mind: Some doors aren’t meant for children who ought to be home by supper.

Mara thought of the kitchen table. Of soggy cereal and the neighbour’s shed. Of homework waiting on her desk like a pile of folded, uninteresting storms. Then she thought of the slow, unfathomable pulse under her palm in the museum, the way her skin had prickled with something that was not fear exactly, but its cousin.

She dipped her fingers into the pool.

There was no splash. No chill shock. No resistance.

Her hand went through the surface as if through the thinnest layer of cool mist. For an instant, she felt only temperature—the same neutral cool of seawater.

Then something took hold of her.

Not in the sense of fingers or teeth. It was more like the sensation of a current catching your legs when you step into the shallows: that sly, sideways tug. A spiral of motion wound around her wrist, pressing inward and around, like a long, clear ribbon of stream pulling her in the direction it wanted to go.

She gasped.

The pull was not violent. It did not yank. It invited with steady, insistently growing pressure.

She tried to pull her hand back.

Her arm moved—slowly. There was a stretch, like trying to drag your hand through very thick syrup, but colder and impossibly smooth. The more she thought about resisting, the more the spiral seemed to tighten, coaxing rather than grabbing.

“Okay,” she said aloud, voice a little higher than she liked. “Okay, this is… different. This is new.”

The archway in the pool flared brighter, its edges sharpening. The darkness beyond it deepened to a richer blue-green, as if someone had turned the saturation up on an image of the sea at midnight.

Her balance shifted.

She realised, with a weirdly detached fascination, that the tug was no longer just around her wrist. It had crept up along her forearm, around her elbow, threading through her shoulder. It was rearranging which way was “down” for her, adjusting the labels on gravity.

The rocks under her feet felt less solid. The world tilted, not like slipping on ice, but like the moment in a dream when you step onto a stair that isn’t there and your stomach swoops.

Mara grabbed for the lip of the pool with her free hand. Her fingers found stone, rough and wet, barnacles biting shallow marks into her skin. She clung, breathing hard.

The water around her submerged arm felt… vast. That was the only word she had. Vast, as if what she’d plunged into was no longer a shallow bowl of trapped seawater but something that went on and on.

“Stop,” she whispered, though she wasn’t sure if she meant the current, or herself.

The sea hissed softly against the more distant shore. A gull called overhead, a harsh, mundane cry that sounded abruptly far away, as if shouted down a long tunnel.

Beneath her, through the strange bending of perspective in the pool, she saw it.

Below the glowing arch, below the plane of the water that wasn’t just water, something shimmered in the depths.

Lights.

Tiny ones, dozens, hundreds of them, scattered in three dimensions like fireflies that had learned to swim. They pulsed and drifted, some bright, some dim, arranged along what her mind insisted were structures: lines, gentle curves, vertical drops. A city seen from above at night, but instead of streets, the lights traced out something more organic, like veins or branches.

The sight twisted something in her chest. Awe, mostly. And a small, sharp spike of fear that pointed in entirely the wrong direction.

Down, it said. Down there.

“Of course,” Mara said hoarsely. “Of course there’s a glowing… whatever that is… under the weird door pool. Why not. Why be normal.”

Her hold on the stone lip slipped half an inch. Her submerged arm tugged harder, like a dog that has finally realised you really are going for a walk.

Captain Thimble’s voice came back, clear and exasperated in her memory: You’ve got that look. The one that asks ‘What if?’ louder than it asks ‘Should I?’.

“What if,” she said, “I don’t?”

The spiral of cool around her limbs pulsed, once. The lights below flared, then settled, patiently gleaming.

She pictured herself letting go. The current would pull. She would go through the arch. She might drown. She might not. She might fall forever. She might land.

She pictured turning back. Climbing up over the rocks, trying to explain to Captain Thimble later that she’d found a door and she’d… left it. The idea tasted like regret already, like a missed flavour she would never quite be able to describe.

“I am supposed to text if I change locations,” she muttered. “Does ‘somewhere under the ocean in a possibly imaginary glowing city’ count as a location?”

The universe, characteristically, did not provide clarification.

Her fingers hurt where they gripped the stone. The barnacles were not kind. The practical part of her brain, the one that liked safety and rules and oxygen, screamed something about foolishness and risk and lung capacity.

Her curiosity opened its mouth and swallowed that part whole.

“Fine,” she told the pool. “Fine. But if this goes badly, I’m haunting that museum.”

She took a careful breath, filling her chest, counting to three the way she did before jumping off the high diving board in the community pool that one summer when she’d decided she would not be the sort of person who always watched from the side.

One.

She loosened her grip on the stone.

Two.

She let her knuckles unclench, feeling the roughness slide past her fingertips.

Three.

She let go.

The world responded, not with a dizzy plummet, but with a decisive, impossible rearrangement.

Down was no longer the ground beneath her feet. Down was where her arm disappeared through the shining mirror of the tidepool. Gravity rotated ninety degrees like a dial being turned. Her stomach swept sideways. The edge of the pool, the rocks rimming it, the sky—they all tilted, sliding out of place.

Her feet left the rock with a sensation like stepping off a stair she hadn’t known was the last one. For a jagged instant she hung in a directionless space where up and down argued.

Then the water took her.

It was like being folded neatly but very quickly.

One moment, she was kneeling on the familiar, wet stone, half her arm submerged, sun on the back of her neck. The next, the world pivoted; her legs lifted; her body followed the line of her arm.

The pool’s surface wasn’t something she passed through so much as something that rotated around her. It slid from horizontal to vertical, a cold, slick curtain that wrapped and unwound.

There was no shock of plunging. No involuntary gasp, no rush of freezing. The temperature simply matched itself to her skin and went past it. Her hair lifted around her head, moving like seaweed. The little sounds of the beach—the gulls, the shush of waves on sand—stretched, thinned, and then snapped off, replaced by a deeper, more muffled hush.

Mara flailed for a second, instinctively reaching for something to hold. Her fingers closed on water and light.

She was not falling. Not exactly. She was… moving.

Down.

Above her—behind her?—the circular frame of the tidepool shrank, a bright, wavery disc. Through it, she saw, impossibly, the inverted image of the shore: rocks and sand and a wedge of sky, all turned wrong-side-up and far away, as if she were looking up from the bottom of a very deep well.

She kicked experimentally. Her legs met a medium that clung but did not drag, like swimming through silk. There was resistance, but it was gentle, more like someone’s hand on her back guiding her than water trying to hold her.

Her lungs, she realised with a jolt of alarm, were still full of air. She had taken that breath before letting go and… kept it. No water had rushed in. Her nose and mouth felt damp, but not flooded. The panic that had been coiling, waiting for the sudden need to breathe, faltered, confused.

Carefully, cautiously, she exhaled a little.

Tiny silver bubbles slipped from her lips, spinning lazily away. The sight was so strange and beautiful that she almost laughed, which would have been an excellent way to waste the rest of her air.

The tunnel around her glowed with its own, soft colours. The walls weren’t solid; they were water, all of it water, but denser, somehow, where the light thickened. Shafts of blue and green stretched downward, striped with paler bands like bars of sunlight reaching through clouds. Here and there, darker shapes swam—no, drifted—in the periphery of her vision: curtains of weed, perhaps, or shoals of fish that chose not to come too close.

The spiraling sensation hadn’t been an illusion. The current that held her turned, ever so slightly, around an axis she couldn’t see. She felt it in the way her orientation kept shifting: the distant circle of the surface moving from above her head to just behind her shoulder, then off to one side. She was descending and slowly corkscrewing, like a leaf in a gentle vortex.

Her backpack tugged at her shoulders, suddenly heavy, then oddly weightless. Its straps pressed reassuringly into her collarbones.

“Okay,” she thought, because talking out loud felt dangerous, as if words might be fragile in this place. “You’re going down through a tidepool. You are currently in a vertical tunnel made of water. This is either the best hallucination or the worst safety lecture.”

Below her, the lights she’d glimpsed from above grew bigger, brighter. They weren’t just dots anymore; they were clusters, lines, points of radiance strung along forms that suggested architecture, or at least organisation. Some glowed steady and soft; others blinked in slow pulses, like signals passed along a chain.

Her fear, which had been doing its level best to keep up with events, found itself outpaced.

In its place came a wonder so fierce it hurt.

Images tumbled through her thoughts: the dripping helmet in the museum, the maps with their shifting coastlines, the professor-sounding machines that had hummed with unspent questions, the pulse in the wall that had matched itself to her hand. The glowing door under the tide. The shells.

This is connected, she thought. This is all the same story.

The tunnel widened.

She felt it more than saw it—the subtle change in pressure, the way the current’s embrace loosened around her arms and legs. The blue-green light opened up ahead, growing less tubular and more… spacious.

Mara tilted her head back to look one last time.

Far, far above—or behind, or what used to be above—the circle of the tidepool was now no bigger than a coin held at arm’s length. Through it, she saw a smudge of sky and the faint suggestion of a human world, smaller and less certain than it had ever appeared from the beach.

Her chest ached, but not yet with need for air. With something else.

“Don’t close,” she thought at the shrinking circle of light. “Not yet. Please don’t close.”

It flickered, once, as if in acknowledgement. Or it might have been her own vision blurring.

Then the tunnel opened under her like a mouth.

The water around her thinned in that particular way that means space, the way the air in a high-ceilinged room feels different from that in a closet. The gradient of light shifted; blue gave way to softer teals, streaked with muted gold and the faint, translucent pink of phosphorescent creatures shifting in clusters.

The city lay below her.

There was no other word for it, not now that she could see it properly. It sprawled across the seafloor in a pattern that obeyed rules entirely its own.

Structures rose from the depths, some tall and narrow like chimneys, others broad and low like sleeping beasts. None of them were quite straight. They curved and flowed, built from what looked like a blend of coral and glass and something else altogether, something that carried its own light. Bridges arched between them in delicate, filigreed spans, studded with lanterns that dripped pale fire.

The lights she’d seen before were windows, doors, tiny bulbs on the tips of swaying fronds. They traced out streets that weren’t streets exactly, more like paths in three dimensions: up, across, through.

And all of it moved.

Not crumbling, not unstable, but… breathing. The buildings flexed in the almost-imperceptible way of living coral, opening and closing minuscule pores, shedding and renew­ing. Curtains of algae and strange, translucent banners fluttered in currents that she was only now beginning to feel teasing at her fingers.

Shapes darted between the glowing pillars—fish, yes, in flashes of silver and black and ridged blue, but also other forms: silhouettes that suggested arms as well as fins, tails that ended in fans instead of points, hair that drifted like seaweed.

Something huge and slow passed far below, its side dotted with soft lanterns, like a fragment of night sky deciding to go for a swim.

Mara hung there for a heartbeat in the gentle hold of the vertical current, suspended between the world she’d known and the one below. The circle of the shore above had grown smaller, paler, less persuasive by the second.

Her lungs gave a more assertive twinge. The thought rose again: breathe.

She looked down at the city of lights, heart pounding, and understood in some quiet, startled part of herself that whatever happened next, whoever she was when she returned—if she returned at all—would not be exactly the same girl who’d peered into a tidepool an hour ago, careful not to get her shoes too wet.

“Hello,” she thought at the luminous sprawl, at the impossible architecture and the drifting shapes within it. The word formed in her mind like a bubble.

Then, with the shore a shrinking coin above and the unknown blazing beneath, Mara loosened the last of her grip on the idea that doors should only open sideways, surrendered to the spiraling pull, and let herself be carried feet-first into the glowing ocean city waiting in the depths below.

chapters.chaptertitle: Pelagoria, City of Glass and Currents
chapters.chaptershortdescription: Where Mara arrives in the hidden city beneath the ocean and is both welcomed and arrested by its wary inhabitants.
chapters.chapterdetails: Mara plunges gently out of the tunnel into a huge bubble of air suspended in the sea, landing on a walkway made of fused white sand that arches toward a breathtaking city encased in translucent domes. Schools of fish flicker by like living confetti while spirals of coral buildings rise and dip, connected by bridges that ripple as if woven from water itself. Before she can decide whether to be awed or terrified, a group of armored guards with opalescent scales and sharp-looking tridents surrounds her, their expressions a mixture of alarm and fascination at the appearance of a dry-land child in their protected realm. They speak in lilting, burbling syllables until a tall woman in sea-silk robes—Queen Nerissa—arrives, her gaze cool and assessing. Mara tries to explain that she simply found a door and fell through it, which sounds precisely as suspicious as she feared it might. As the Queen orders that this “surface trespasser” be brought to the palace for questioning, a figure watching from the shadows of a coral balcony—a girl with fin-fringed arms and human-brown eyes—murmurs to herself that finally, finally, one of the old stories might be true.
chapters.chapterText:
Mara hit the air like a dropped feather.

One second, she was sliding down the glowing throat of the ocean, her hair floating around her in lazy, dark clouds and the weight of all that water holding her in a cool, constant embrace. The next, something invisible and elastic snapped around her, and she found herself tumbling—gently, but with conviction—through a space that was not water and was not exactly land.

Her stomach did a small, dignified somersault. Her shoes, which had been feeling very smug about being above all this wet nonsense, suddenly remembered gravity. She flailed, windmilling, as the tunnel of water above her sealed like an eye closing.

She fell perhaps three metres.

It was enough to make her yelp and, at the very last moment, to jam her eyes shut and think of every terrible thing that might be waiting for her at the bottom: sharp rocks, abandoned anchors, the historically inevitable skeleton.

Instead, she landed on something that felt like glass pretending to be stone.

Her knees buckled. She skidded, hands slapping down with a flat, ringing sound. Pain flared in her palms, sharp and clean, and then she was still, panting, her backpack thumping down beside her with a sullen flap.

For a moment, she stayed exactly where she was, folded over her elbows, breathing hard, trying to work out if she was alive or several interesting new pieces.

The surface under her palms was cool and faintly textured, like frosted glass. When she finally cracked one eye open, she saw—through the film of adrenaline and confusion—that it was pale as bleached bone, shot through with faint, glimmering lines where individual grains of sand had been melted and fused together. The pattern reminded her of waves frozen mid-crest.

She lifted her head.

The walkway she’d landed on arched gently away in both directions, a pale ribbon suspended in a space that should not exist.

Above her, there was no ceiling—not in any traditional, health-and-safety sense. Instead, the air ended abruptly in a curved, invisible surface that bulged outward in all directions, like the inside of a glass sphere. Beyond that thin, perfect boundary, the ocean pressed close.
