Mara could see it as clearly as if she were standing inside a colossal, exquisitely clean fishbowl: endless blue-green, streaked with dim shafts of light from some faraway surface; shoals of tiny silver fish that fluttered past like handfuls of thrown confetti; larger, slower shapes gliding at the edges of visibility, careful and watchful. Dark fronds of kelp rose and swayed, their tips brushing the outside of the bubble as if testing it.

The bubble itself—this bubble of air she was breathing—hung in the water like a pearl. It didn’t wobble. It didn’t leak. It simply… was.

Mara’s mouth went dry. Which was impressive, given where she was.

The walkway beneath her continued, one end vanishing into a luminous haze, the other curving toward something that filled her field of vision when she dared to look.

The city.

Pelagoria.

It rose from the seafloor in a sweep of geometry that ought to have been impossible and, she felt instinctively, refused to care.

She could see domes—dozens of them, hundreds, some small as houses, some vast as stadiums—clustered together like bubbles of glass, each one holding its own pocket of stolen sky. Their surfaces caught and refracted the underwater light, turning it into shifting rainbows that slid across their curves. Between them, bridges arched and coiled: some as solid and pale as the walkway beneath her, others more translucent, rippling and flexing with the lazy grace of water tamed into shapes.

Spirals of coral rose among the domes: towers that curled like nautilus shells, walls riddled with windows that shone from within. Some grew straight from the rock; others appeared to be anchored to nothing at all, held in place by braids of living seaweed and beams of pale light.

Long, trailing banners of some thin, shimmering fabric fluttered from the tallest structures, stirring in invisible currents. They were the colours of deep ocean things: midnight blues, soft greens, the flushed pink of certain shells. Symbols were stitched along their lengths in thread that caught the light like fish scales.

It was not a neat city. It hadn’t been laid out with straight lines and obedient grids. It swooped and dipped, squabbled with itself, piled buildings up in haphazard layers that still, somehow, made sense. It looked like it had grown, like coral or a particularly ambitious story, adding bits over centuries wherever there was the slightest space.

Tiny lights pricked its depths: lanterns hung in windows, glowing nodes along the bridges, clusters of luminescence in garden-like pockets where tall, translucent plants waved slowly. Schools of fish threaded themselves through its alleys, flashing silver and blue. Far beneath, a shadow the size of a cathedral coasted past, lanterns along its flank winking solemnly as it moved.

Mara’s brain threw words at the sight like pebbles into deep water: incredible, unbelievable, impossible. None of them made a dent.

She realised dimly that she was still on her hands and knees on the walkway and that her mouth was, in fact, hanging open.

She shut it, because some inner voice reminded her that one ought to appear at least slightly composed when arriving in a hidden undersea city in a bubble.

Her lungs were starting to protest the breath she’d taken before leaving the tunnel. She gingerly tried inhaling.

Air filled her chest. Cool, crisp, faintly tasting of salt and something metallic, like it had passed over a lot of rock and science on its way to her.

She coughed once, half in surprise.

“Right,” she said, out loud, because if you could talk, then things were probably not as terrible as they might otherwise be. Her voice rang oddly, bouncing back and forth in the bubble. “Okay. So. Not dead. That’s… that’s good.”

The walkway vibrated, a subtle tremor under her palms, as if something large had just stepped onto it some way off.

Mara froze.

The tremor became a rhythm: a series of approaching, uneven thuds and lighter, scraping sounds. Not the randomness of distant movement. Footsteps. Several sets of footsteps. Armoured ones.

She pushed herself unsteadily to her feet. Her knees wobbled. The bubble’s air felt suddenly thinner.

At first, all she could make out was motion at the cityward end of the walkway: a ripple of darker shapes against the brilliance beyond. Then, out of that haze, five figures resolved, striding toward her in a loose formation that gave the impression of people who had absolutely done this before and were not expecting to enjoy it.

They were… people. Mostly.

They walked upright, on two legs, with the broad-shouldered, purposeful gait of guards everywhere. They wore armour that caught the light in sudden, startling flashes: plates and scaled pieces that curved over torsos, shoulders, and thighs, made of something that looked like mother-of-pearl forged into discipline. It was pale in some places, darker in others, patterned with faint ripples that moved when they moved.

Where their skin showed at elbows, throats, and cheeks, it gleamed faintly. Scales, Mara realised. Tiny, overlapped like the finest chain mail, in colours that shifted between green and blue and the soft, bruised purple of storm clouds over water.

Their hair flowed behind them like streamers, unfurling in the slight currents of air inside the bubble: some dark as Mara’s, some pale as sand, some a startling, nacreous white. Here and there, thin fins protruded delicately from forearms or along jawlines, twitching as if tasting the air.

In their hands, they carried tridents.

Mara had seen tridents in pictures: the sort of thing drawn in the hands of gods who were fond of storms and boundary issues. Those had looked theatrical. These did not.

These were long and slender, made of some pale, gleaming metal that was not quite silver, their three tines tapering to points that looked perfectly capable of conducting a strong moral argument directly to someone’s spleen. Veins of faint, bluish light ran along the shafts, pulsing gently, in time with nothing Mara could identify.

As they came closer, their faces resolved: high cheekbones, wide eyes set a little farther apart than humans’, irises in improbable colours—sea-glass green, sunburst gold, stormy grey. Their expressions were a fascinating mixture of alarm, wariness, and the particular sort of excitement that came from a day suddenly deciding not to be boring after all.

The one in front raised a hand. The others fanned out, forming a half-circle around Mara with smooth, practised efficiency.

Mara’s first thought, which arrived with the shrill clarity of panic, was that she had been here all of thirty seconds and she was already surrounded by heavily armed fish-people.

Her second thought was that they were not, in fact, fish-people. They were something else. Something in-between.

Her third thought was, unhelpfully: They’re very shiny.

The lead guard—taller than the others, with a crest of short, silvery fin along one temple and a long scar trailing from the corner of their mouth down under their jaw—levelled their trident. Not quite at her, but close enough that Mara became acutely aware of how soft and entirely un-scaled her own throat was.

They spoke.

The words came out in a rush of sound that was both familiar and utterly alien. There was a cadence to it, a rolling rhythm that made her think of waves breaking on different kinds of shore: some syllables short and bright, like pebbles; others long and burbling, full of swallowed consonants and round vowels that seemed to curl back on themselves.

Mara’s ears heard: “Kesh thalan varu’ith? Sel a’se, sel a’se!”

Her brain heard: seabirds and bubble streams, someone humming through a snorkel.

She blinked. “I’m sorry?”

The guard frowned. The fin along their jaw twitched. They tried again, more slowly, stabbing the air with one word in particular and punctuating it with a jab of the trident in her direction.

“Sur-fa-ce.”

That, at least, made it through the translation barrier. The way they said it made it sound like a diagnosis.

“Yes,” Mara said cautiously. “Surface. Me. Hi.”

She lifted one hand in what she hoped was a non-threatening, universal gesture of greeting and not, in this place, some horrible insult involving sea cucumbers.

The guard’s eyes flicked to her fingers, then back up. Their nostrils flared, their pupils tightening for a fraction of a second. They barked a word over their shoulder. Two of the other guards shifted their grip on their tridents, sliding half a step closer, as if she’d just brandished a small nuclear device instead of five calloused fingers and bitten-down nails.

One of them muttered something that was probably not “Oh good, a child, what a relief.”

Mara swallowed.

“Right,” she said, words coming out faster, higher. Nervous babbling, her old friend. “So. You don’t know what I’m saying, I don’t know what you’re saying, and if this is anything like human security, that means eventually someone is going to start shouting, and I don’t—I really don’t think we need to shout. I didn’t mean to—”

She cut herself off as another voice cut through the bubble.

This one was clearer, firmer, threaded with the sort of authority that made people straighten their backs without consulting their opinions.

“Stand down. She’s not armed.”

The guards shifted as one, tridents lowering just a fraction, not enough to stop being a threat, but enough to admit that perhaps stabbing the small, dripping stranger might not be the immediate first step.

A new figure approached along the walkway from the city’s direction.

Even among people with opalescent skin and hair that behaved like the dream of shampoo advertisements, she stood out.

She moved with a slow, assured grace, as if every step was a decision worth making properly. Her robe—if robe was the right word for the garment that draped from her shoulders in ripples of colour—was made of something that looked like liquid light woven into cloth. It clung and flowed and never seemed quite to agree on what hue it wanted to be. At one angle it was deep-sea green; at another, the pale blue of shallow water; in the corner of Mara’s eye, she could have sworn it flashed with the fiercer blue-white of breaking waves.

Around her shoulders, strands of living coral coiled in delicate loops, forming a collar and then flowing upward into a crown. Tiny polyps along their lengths opened and closed rhythmically, their minuscule tentacles tasting the air. Here and there, small, bioluminescent creatures—perhaps symbiotic, perhaps adornment, perhaps both—glowed softly, studded in the coral like jewels.

Her skin was a deep, resonant brown under the sheen of fine, almost invisible scales. Her hair floated in a steady halo around her head, dark and thick, threaded with the occasional glint of shell or tiny silver fish that had decided it was the safest place in the ocean.

Her eyes, when they fixed on Mara, were the dark, complex colour of tide pools at dusk: layers of greens and blues and flecks of gold shifting behind a cool surface.

Mara did not need an introduction to know who she was.

Some people wore authority like a badge or a uniform. This woman wore it the way the sea wore waves: as a default condition.

The lead guard straightened, thumping the butt of their trident lightly against the walkway. The sound rang out, a clean, bell-like note.

“Your Majesty,” they said, in their rolling, burbling tongue. Even without translation, the title was clear.

Queen Nerissa of Pelagoria regarded the child who had fallen into her city as if she were a particularly complicated tide chart.

Up close, Mara became acutely aware of how small and scruffy she must look. Her jacket was damp and patched at one elbow. Her jeans were scuffed and bore the faint ghosts of old grass stains. Her shoes were, as ever, betraying their cheapness around the seams. Salt had dried in pale streaks on her cheeks. Her hair, which she had optimistically tied back that morning, had rebelled and formed a small, drifting cloud around her head.

She pulled herself up as straight as she could, for no other reason than that slouching felt like losing.

Queen Nerissa stepped to the front of the half-circle of guards. She did not reach for a weapon. She did not snap commands. She simply stood and looked.

Mara, who knew full well what it was to feel like an odd piece in a puzzle no one else could see, held that gaze.

For a moment that stretched long and taut, nothing moved. Even the ever-present fish beyond the bubble seemed to have paused, hanging in the water like commas.

Then Nerissa spoke.

Her voice was lower than Mara had expected, softer, like the sound of distant surf heard from inside a cave. The language was the same as the guards’, full of burred consonants and liquid vowels, but there was an oldness in it, a gravity.

She said several words. Mara caught, unmistakably, “surface” and something that was probably “child.”

The lead guard answered, adding a series of phrases punctuated with expressive hand gestures: a fall, a door, a tunnel, a this-just-came-out-of-the-sky-and-we-are-not-thrilled.

Queen Nerissa’s eyes never left Mara’s face. She tilted her head slightly, considering. Then, with a small, abrupt gesture, she flicked her fingers in front of her throat, as if snapping an invisible thread.

Something in the air hummed.

It was faint, like the crackle before lightning, or the sound old televisions used to make when they were on in the next room. A prickle ran along Mara’s arms, raising goosebumps. She became acutely aware of her tongue, her teeth, the shape of her own mouth.

Nerissa spoke again, this time slowly, each syllable deliberate.

“Can you understand me now, child of the dry lands?”

The words were in clear, precise English. They sat oddly in the Queen’s mouth—not clumsy, but as if each had been picked up, turned over, and chosen for weight as well as sound.

Mara’s jaw dropped a little. She shut it again.

“Yes,” she said. Her own voice sounded thin compared to Nerissa’s. “I—I can. What was—how—?”

Nerissa made a small, graceful gesture with one hand, as though batting the question aside like a drifting piece of seaweed.

“Translation shell,” she said. “A net for meaning. It sits in the air between your words and ours, if I will it. There are… old agreements.” A faint, wry twist touched the corner of her mouth. “They assumed more polite visits than this.”

She took a step closer, the coral of her crown glinting.

“You fell through one of our doors,” she said. It wasn’t quite a question.

Mara wet her lips, suddenly very aware that every movement she made was being watched by five armed guards and a ruling monarch.

“Yes,” she said. “I mean—I didn’t mean to. I was on the beach. There was a tidepool. With a… sort of glowing arch thing? And shells, that were kind of… luminous? And I touched it, and then it—well, it decided I was coming, I think, because I tried not to, but currents are very insistent and—”

She heard herself and clamped down hard before the babbling reached high tide.

“I found a door,” she said, forcing the words to line up neatly. “And I fell through it. I didn’t know it led here. I didn’t even know ‘here’ was… was real.”

Nerissa’s eyes narrowed the smallest fraction. “And yet,” she said, “you walked into it.”

Mara opened her mouth. Closed it again. Honesty, she suspected, would not make her look better. Nevertheless, it came out.

“Yes,” she admitted. “I… I was curious.”

One of the guards made a small, incredulous noise. Another said, in their own language, something that the translation net rendered in Mara’s head as, “Of course she was.”

“Curious,” Nerissa repeated, tasting the word. “Curious. That is a dangerous current.”

Mara bristled, just a little. “It’s not a bad thing,” she said. “Not by itself.”

Nerissa tilted her head, and for a heartbeat, something almost like humour flickered behind her eyes. “No,” she said quietly. “By itself, it is only movement. But currents reshape coasts.”

Her gaze travelled over Mara from head to toe, noting details: the cheap, worn clothes, the ink smudges on her fingers, the stubborn set of her jaw. Her eyes lingered, briefly, on the faint white salt-crystal still caught at the edge of Mara’s thumbnail, a relic from the museum floor that had survived storms, tunnels, and transitions.

“You came from the surface without a suit,” Nerissa said. “Without a guide. Without so much as a breath-stone.” She shook her head slowly, a small ripple passing through her hair. “You should not be here. And yet… here you are. Alive.”

“That wasn’t entirely my idea,” Mara muttered. “The door was very… persuasive.”

Nerissa’s mouth tightened. “The door should not have opened at all,” she said. “Not to one of you.”

She turned slightly, addressing the lead guard without taking her attention off Mara for long.

“Captain Tideglass. How long from the first alarm-shell until her arrival?”

The guard—Tideglass—shifted, trident held against their shoulder with practised ease.

“Three hundred heartbeats, Majesty,” they replied. “Give or take the panic.”

“Long enough for her to drown or be crushed,” Nerissa said. “Yet she is neither. Long enough for the Tunnel to close.” She flicked a glance upwards, to where the vertical gouge of water that had delivered Mara was now a faint shimmer in the ceiling of the bubble, already knitting itself closed like a wound. “And yet it did not. It held for her.”

The way she said “her” made Mara feel simultaneously very important and very much like a problem.

“I didn’t mean to trespass,” Mara said, because the word surfacer had come wrapped in an accusation. “I didn’t know. I was just—on the beach. I saw the shells, and the light, and I followed, and—”

“And the sea opened her hand to you,” Nerissa finished softly, eyes darkening. “When she has been keeping her fists tight for years.”

She was silent for a moment, weighing something invisible. The guards shifted slightly, the faint chime of their armour a delicate percussion.

“This city,” Nerissa said, her voice carrying more than just sound now, “is hidden for a reason, child from above. We live in the cracks between your world and the deep. We walk in air and swim in water. We exist because we are forgotten. That forgetting is our safety. The last time a door like that yawned wide, we nearly lost all of this.”

Her hand swept out, encompassing the domes, the spirals, the tiny, gleaming lives drifting through them.

Mara’s chest clenched. “Then why—”

“Why did it open for you?” Nerissa’s gaze speared her. “That is precisely what I intend to find out.”

There was a rustle among the guards. One of them, shorter than the rest, their scales edged with a faint rose-gold sheen, murmured, “Your Majesty, she is only a child.”

“Children drown as easily as their elders,” Nerissa said, not unkindly. “And innocent feet trample coral just the same as guilty ones.” She let out a breath, the sound of a tide retreating over pebbles.

“But,” she added, and there was a subtle shift in the air, a loosening of something, “children also see what the old have trained themselves to ignore.”

Her eyes returned to Mara’s face with a new, sharper intent.

“Tell me your name,” she said.

Mara had to stop herself from giving the name in full, with middle, as she would if a teacher or doctor asked. This was not a form. This was a queen.

“Mara Bright,” she said. Her voice was steadier now than she felt. “From… well, from up there.”

She jerked her chin toward the vague direction of the surface, or at least where she thought the surface ought to be. In Pelagoria, the concept of “up” had already started to feel negotiable.

Nerissa repeated the name quietly, as if hooking it into memory.

“Mara Bright from Above,” she said. “You stand in Pelagoria without leave or knowledge. You have crossed boundaries older and deeper than you can yet understand. By our laws, that makes you a trespasser.”

The word hung in the air, heavy as an anchor.

Mara swallowed. “I—”

“However,” Nerissa went on, overriding whatever Mara had been about to say with the effortless authority of someone who had never in her life had to shout to be heard, “by those same laws, a trespasser who arrives by way of the Queen’s Door”—she nodded upward, toward the now-faded scar in the bubble—“is under my protection until I know what to do with them.”

That was… better? Possibly? Mara’s experience with legal phrasing was limited to terms and conditions she did not read before clicking, but “protection” seemed preferable to “immediate imprisonment” or “feeding to enormous symbolic fish.”

Nerissa turned to Captain Tideglass.

“Captain, you and your squad will escort this surface-child to the palace,” she said. “Gently. No points, no chains. She is not to be harmed unless she proves herself a danger.”

Tideglass inclined their head. The scar along their jaw pulled tight. “Majesty,” they said, the syllables crisp and reluctant.

“And send word to Professor Finn,” Nerissa added, almost as an afterthought, though the slight roll of her eyes suggested it was not as simple as that. “Tell him the sea has delivered him a… puzzle. He may wish to contain his excitement until after I’ve spoken with the girl. But he won’t.”

She looked back to Mara, and for the first time, something softened in her expression. It was not quite kindness. It was more like recognition.

“You will come with us,” she said. “You will answer our questions. You will not run, or shout, or touch anything that looks like it took more than ten years to grow.”

Mara had an unhelpful flash of herself tripping and taking out an entire cultural landmark. “I didn’t come here to hurt anything,” she said. “I just… wanted to see.”

“Yes,” Nerissa murmured. “That is what I am afraid of.”

She gave a small, almost imperceptible signal with two fingers. The guards shifted, their formation loosening just enough to fall into an escort rather than a threat.

Two fell in beside Mara, one on each side, their tridents now held upright, the faint glow along the shafts dimming as if in response to a change of mood. Tideglass took point; another guard brought up the rear, casting occasional, quick glances at Mara as if half expecting her to suddenly explode into teeth.

“Walk,” Tideglass said tersely.

Mara hesitated, casting one more look upward.

The tunnel she had come through was nearly gone, its once-bright shaft blending back into the blue ceiling of the bubble. Beyond that, through the curved transparency, the sea stretched away in all directions, vast and unreadable.

Somewhere very far above, there was a shore with a little town and a green, flaking door to a museum that shouldn’t exist. Somewhere even higher, there was sky.

She squared her shoulders, the way she did when stepping into classrooms that smelled of marker pens and other children’s noise.

“Okay,” she said quietly, more to herself than anyone else. “Palace. Questions. Not touching anything.”

She walked.

The fused-sand walkway had a faint give to it, like very dense rubber. It curved toward the city in a gentle, confident arc, the pale path leading her past wonders she had no vocabulary for yet.

As they advanced, the scale of Pelagoria shifted. What had been an impressionistic sweep of domes and towers resolved into detail.

She saw people moving within the nearer bubbles: children racing along narrow walkways, their bare, scale-sheened feet slapping rhythmically; an older figure perched on a low wall, mending a net that shivered and reformulated itself with each knot; someone hanging a string of glowing shells along the edge of a balcony, whistling a tune that made Mara’s skin pebble even through the translation net.

Bridges of water arched beneath and above her: shimmering bands that looked like streams plucked up and stitched between platforms. Within them, fish moved in both directions, some darting through the thin layer of liquid as if it were a highway, others pausing to hover and then shoot off at sudden angles. The bridges adjusted themselves minutely as currents changed, flexing but never breaking.

Closer to the domes, the walkway branched. One spur dipped downward toward a great, transparent arch embedded in the side of the largest bubble, through which Mara could see an enormous open space, full of movement and colour. Another spur curled up to a smaller, more ornate entrance, flanked by tall columns of living coral carved—or grown—together into spirals.

They took the upward path.

As she walked, Mara felt eyes on her.

People—Pelagorians? Pelagori?—had come to the edges of their bubbles and balconies, drawn by the sight of the guards and their unlikely prize. Some peered through the clear walls of the domes, their faces flattened slightly by the curvature, like fish in reverse. Others leaned against railings of braided shell and kelp, their expressions variously wary, fascinated, or unmistakably disapproving.

Mara caught snatches of their speech, the translation shell doing its best.

“…it’s true, a surface-child…”

“…after all these years…”

“…Queen’s Door, they say…”

“…should have been sealed…”

“…maybe the stories—”

A younger voice, bright with unfiltered excitement: “Do you think she’s got gills hiding under that cloth?”

“No, idiot, they can’t breathe properly down here. Look, her lips are going pale.”

Mara resisted the urge to clap a self-conscious hand over her mouth. She could feel the thinness of the air now—the way each breath filled her lungs, but not as easily as on land. There was something… thinner about it. Like air up a mountain, maybe, she thought, though she’d only ever seen mountains in books.

The escort turned onto the last curve of the walkway, leading toward the ornate entrance.

Above it, carved into the fused-sand arch in curling, flowing lines that almost looked alive, were words in that same flowing script she’d seen on the museum’s strange maps. The translation net murmured in her ear: PELAGORIA HIGH HALL. HOUSE OF THE TIDEBORN QUEEN.

Mara had just enough time to think that this was a lot to live up to before the world shifted perspective again.

High above the archway, half-hidden in curving shadows and the leaves of some enormous, fanlike plant, a small balcony jutted from the side of a coral tower.

On it, a girl pressed herself against the railing, fingers curled around the smooth, ridged surface. Her hair, dark and heavy, drifted around her head, refusing to decide which way was down. Faint iridescent scales glittered along her arms, where the light caught them under the thin weave of her tunic. Delicate fins fringed the outsides of her forearms, held tight against her skin for now; another thin crest ran from just behind one ear, disappearing into her hair.

Her eyes, though—her eyes were human-brown, deep and watchful.

She had been there for some time, pretending, to anyone who glanced up, to be admiring the banners or checking the condition of the higher coral. In reality, she had been listening.

The words carried differently up here, fuzzed and bent by the curve of the bubble, but the tone—especially Nerissa’s—came clear. The guards’ alarm. The word surfacer, hissed with old fear. Her mother’s measured anger.

The girl had heard the name too: Mara Bright. It did not sound like the names she knew. It sounded like someone trying to start a story mid-sentence.

She squinted down now at the little procession making its way across the final span of walkway. The child at its centre was smaller than she’d expected. All the stories made surfacers sound huge, loud, the sort of people you could hear coming three currents away. This one looked… ordinary. Off-balance. Her clothes hung wrong, made for air that pressed differently.

But there was something in the way she held her shoulders, as if every part of her wanted to flinch and refused to.

The girl’s fingers tightened on the balcony rail until the knuckles blanched faintly under the thin scale-sheen.

“So,” she whispered to herself, so softly even the nearest fish could not quite catch it. “You made it through a door that shouldn’t open.”

Her voice had the dry edge of someone used to not being believed and making peace with that through sarcasm.

“Finally,” Liora of the Glass Tides murmured, human-brown eyes very wide as she watched Mara vanish into the cool, gleaming shadow of the palace entrance. “Finally, one of the old stories decided to be true.”

chapters.chaptertitle: Liora and the Library of Whispers
chapters.chaptershortdescription: Where Mara meets Liora, the mer-child who has been secretly studying surface legends in a hidden library and decides Mara is the key to an ancient prophecy.
chapters.chapterdetails: Taken to a chamber that seems halfway between a throne room and an aquarium, Mara is left to sit anxiously under the watchful gaze of carved coral guardians while the palace hums with rumors outside. A hidden panel in the wall suddenly slides open and in slips Liora, dripping saltwater and mischief, her hair floating around her like a dark halo. She introduces herself briskly, as if she’s been expecting Mara for years, and urges the confused surface girl through a maze of narrow passages into a secret library carved inside a hollow cliff, where shelves of shell, stone tablets, and transparent algae-sheets glow with stored bioluminescent ink. Liora confesses that she has been collecting forbidden tales about the surface—the sun, boats, rain that falls down instead of up—and about a legend that says a child from above will come when Pelagoria’s greatest protection begins to fail. She believes Mara’s arrival through the old door means something is wrong with the city’s defenses, even if the adults are too afraid to say it. As they pore over a swirling map of currents and listen to the faint echoes of whale-song stored in crystal jars, the girls begin to trade questions, jokes, and wary trust, realizing that together they might be able to see what neither the sea nor the land can see alone.
chapters.chapterText:
Pelagoria’s throne hall looked as if someone had tried to build a cathedral and an aquarium in the same spot, lost patience with both, and then decided to let the sea finish the job.

Mara sat on a smooth, pale bench that had grown out of the floor in a vague attempt at being a chair. It was too high for her feet to reach the ground properly, so her heels hovered, making her feel even more like a small child in a very large, very important waiting room.

The chamber was vast, oval, its high ceiling lost in dim, wavering light. The walls were not walls in the strict, comforting sense. They were thick, curved glass or something like it, banded with pale ribs of calcified coral. Beyond them, the ocean pressed close—an endless, rippling, blue-green presence just beyond the transparent shell. Fish the size of her hand darted past in bright flickers. Shadows of larger shapes drifted slowly in the middle distance, like thoughts too big to surface.

The floor was a pale, fused-sand mosaic in swirling patterns, the lines echoing waves and currents. At the far end of the hall, a raised platform curved gently up from the floor, supporting a broad, low seat that was more grown than carved. It was made of coral in shades from cream to deepest red, polished smooth where a person might sit but still bristling with delicate, living outgrowths elsewhere, tiny polyps questing at the water-scented air.

Queen Nerissa had taken that seat when they’d brought Mara in, her coral crown catching the light. She’d asked more questions, measured and precise, each one sinking hooks into Mara’s story: the tidepool, the shells, the museum-that-wasn’t, the man called Thimble Kelp. The name had made Nerissa’s nostrils flare, just slightly.

“You will remain here,” the Queen had said at last, her gaze like a weight. “Until I decide your place in this.”

This had not been encouraging.

Then she and her retinue had swept out through an arched doorway behind the coral throne, leaving Mara with two guards at the distant entrance, a lingering sense of having accidentally become a state secret, and a room full of carved coral guardians.

They lined the sides of the hall, ten on each curve: figures half again as tall as Mara, grown from stone and coral and some glassy substance that caught the light inside itself. Their faces were stylised—eyes large and slightly slanted, mouths composed, hair fanning back like waves. Their arms folded across their chests, each held a different object: a trident, a scroll, a shell, a coiled rope. Fins and scaled patterns edged their limbs.

At first, Mara had thought they were just elaborate decorations. Then she’d noticed the eyes.

They were not painted. They were not carved. They were little ovals of some dark, translucent stone—or maybe something alive, trapped or resting—and they caught every shift in the light. When she shifted on her bench, she was almost sure that a couple of those glossy pupils tracked the movement.

“Hello,” she told the nearest statue under her breath, because politeness cost nothing. “If you’re going to come to life dramatically, can you at least warn me first? Maybe do a little stretch? Rattle your coral? No? All right then.”

The statue sent her the blank, patient stare of things that had been asked much better questions.

The palace hummed around her.

It wasn’t a sound, exactly, more a layered thrum that she felt in her ribs rather than her ears. The faint, constant vibration of pumps and flows, the quieter murmur of many voices beyond the closed doors, all braided together. The air tasted faintly charged, like the moment before thunder when the sky holds its breath.

Occasionally, faint, warped snippets of conversation reached her through the heavy doors at the far end, carried on little eddies of air. The translation shell Nerissa had snapped into being still fluttered in the space around her head and ears, turning the burbled Pelagorian syllables into meaning.

“…fell straight through…”

“…Queen’s Door…”

“…hasn’t opened since—”

“…Professor Finn will—”

The last was cut off by a sound that was either a choked laugh or a groan.

Mara swung her feet, heels thudding softly against the bench’s side. Her brain, ever helpful, began producing worst-case scenarios in a neat, escalating list. She was going to be locked in a tower. Or sent back through the door in pieces. Or politely erased. Or—

The wall to her left sighed.

It was a soft, almost embarrassed sound: stone shifting against stone, coral flexing. Mara froze, halfway through inventing a fate involving being fed to something with too many teeth.

A narrow section of wall—between two of the carved guardians, where a vertical pattern of shell inlay had looked purely decorative—slid sideways. It moved silently once the initial shudder had passed, like a well-oiled secret.

Behind it, a low, dark gap yawned.

Out of that slot in the wall, as if she had just swum through an invisible skin of water and popped into air, stepped a girl.

She was dripping, but in a considered sort of way, like a painting of someone mid-surfacing. Droplets of water clung to her skin and clothes, running in tiny rivulets to pool at her bare feet. Her hair—long, dark, and thick—floated around her head in a slow, untidy halo, only half-subject to gravity. When she moved, it lagged a split-second behind, like it was deciding whether to come along.

Her tunic reached mid-thigh, woven from some pale, supple material that clung when wet. It was edged with faintly iridescent bands where scales showed along her shoulders and arms. Delicate fins fanned from the outer edges of her forearms like translucent sleeves tucked back. A faint spray of tiny, opalescent scales dusted her cheeks and temples, catching the light when she tilted her head.

Her eyes were the first thing Mara really processed: they were a deep, human brown, not the pale, uncanny colours of some of the guards. They were also bright with a particular brand of mischief that Mara recognised from every time she had been told not to touch something and then absolutely, definitely touched it.

The girl slipped fully into the hall, reached back, and eased the panel closed with practised fingers. The seam vanished, leaving only the unbroken pattern of shell inlay and stone.

Then she turned to Mara and smiled like they were old co-conspirators.

“There you are,” she said briskly. “Took you long enough.”

Mara stared. “I—what?”

The girl snorted, planting her hands on her hips. “Honestly, surface-doors. Always so… theatrical. Falling, glowing, doom-doom-doom.” She rolled her eyes. “The stories never mention how long it takes.”

“I only found it this morning,” Mara protested, more on reflex than anything. “It’s not like—wait. How did you—who are you?”

“Oh.” The girl straightened, remembering, perhaps, that other people might require introductions. “Liora of the Glass Tides. Princess of Pelagoria.” She pulled a face. “Unfortunately.”

She flicked her fingers, as if scattering the title away like stray droplets.

Mara’s brain, which had only just stopped shrieking about queens and bubbles, added princess to its crowded, blinking noticeboard. “I—um. Mara Bright. Of… the upstairs bit.”

“Of the Surface,” Liora translated with faint disdain, as if “upstairs bit” were a far superior term. “I know. You’re dripping land all over the place.”

“I am not dripping—” Mara started, then looked down.

She was, in fact, leaving small damp prints on the pale bench, and her shoes had collected fine grains of sand from the tidepool rim. A tiny pebble chose that moment to fall from the tread of one sole and ping gently off the floor.

Liora’s gaze followed it, then flicked back up to Mara’s face.

“See?” she said. “Surface. You all come down here shedding geography.”

Mara opened her mouth, uncertain whether to apologise on behalf of her species. “You said you were expecting me?”

“Not you, specifically,” Liora said. “But someone like you. A child from above. Door-fallen. Legend-flavoured.” Her eyes shone as she said it, as if the words themselves tasted good. “I’ve been watching the Door for years. Just in case.”

“Everyone keeps talking about doors,” Mara said. “Capital D doors. As if there’s… more than one?”

“There were,” Liora said. “Once. Now there’s this one. And it wasn’t supposed to open again. At least, that’s what my mother says. Which,” she added, with the swift, sideways glance of someone very used to situational disobedience, “means it definitely would.”

She glanced toward the big, official doors at the end of the hall, where the guards stood in their rigid positions, staring resolutely forward and pretending not to listen.

“You’ve met my mother?” Liora asked. “Tall, regal, draped in coral, looks like she’d apologise to you for drowning you?”

“Queen Nerissa,” Mara said. “Yes. She… asked a lot of questions. And then told me to sit.”

“That sounds like her.” Liora’s mouth crooked. “Everyone’s very agitated about you, by the way. It’s great. They keep trying to whisper, but the sound carries.” She wrinkled her nose. “And they won’t let me in on any of the good bits. ‘Not for the young, Liora’.” She imitated Nerissa’s cool, measured tone with unnerving accuracy. “‘Not your concern, Liora.’ ‘We mustn’t frighten you with politics, Liora.’ As if I’m not already frightened by having to attend Current Etiquette lessons twice a week.”

Mara blinked. “Current… etiquette?”

“Oh yes,” Liora said dryly. “How to bow at the correct angle to a delegation from the Eastward Gyres. Which side of your head to wear your coral when there’s a tsunami season. What to do if a current refuses to stop at a border. Very useful. Practically screaming with relevance.” She rolled her eyes toward the high, curving ceiling. “Whereas ancient prophecies involving mysterious children from beyond the sky apparently are not my concern.”

“Ancient prophecies,” Mara repeated weakly. “Involving… me.”

Liora’s gaze sharpened. “You came through the Queen’s Door,” she said. “Without a suit. Without a breath-stone. You shouldn’t have survived the Tunnel. And yet here you are, sitting on one of our least comfortable benches.” She shrugged. “So yes. Involving you.”

Mara felt a prickle run down her spine. “I didn’t ask to be a prophecy.”

“No one does,” Liora said matter-of-factly. “If they did, there would be forms and committees. And even more etiquette. Come on.”

She moved toward Mara with a quick, efficient stride that made the water still slick on her skin spatter delicately across the floor. Up close, Mara could see that Liora was about her own age, give or take a year. There was a faint crease between her brows that suggested she frowned at books a lot, and at adults even more.

“Come on what?” Mara said, as Liora reached out and caught her wrist, tugging.

“Before someone thinks of a Very Responsible Thing to do with you,” Liora said. “Like putting you in a room with no exits but teaching tapestries. Or handing you over to Professor Finn without supervision. You’ll drown in enthusiasm.” She shuddered theatrically. “No, thank you. I’ve waited too long for one of you to drop in just to let you be taken over by old people.”

Mara dug her heels in, more out of habit than conviction. “The guards will notice,” she hissed, glancing toward the far end of the hall.

Liora didn’t even look. “No, they won’t,” she said. “The panel’s shielded, and they’ve got their backs turned.” She flashed Mara a quick, wicked grin. “Trust me. I’ve been sneaking out of this hall since before I could swim a straight line.”

Mara had time to think, You probably still can’t swim a straight line, you’re too busy zigzagging, before a different, heavier thought dropped in behind her ribs.

If she stayed, she would sit and wait, while decisions were made in rooms where she was not allowed, about things that affected whether she went home or never saw the surface again. If she went with this strange, dripping princess, she might at least get some information—and possibly, if she was very lucky, some say in her own story.

“I am absolutely going to regret this,” she muttered, to herself more than anyone.

“Good,” Liora said cheerfully. “Regret means you picked the interesting path. Come on.”

She yanked lightly on Mara’s wrist. Mara slid off the bench, nearly catching her foot on a decorative swirl in the floor, and followed.

The carved coral guardians watched them go with unreadable, glossy eyes.

Liora pressed her palm against the shell-inlaid section of the wall again. Tiny, iridescent motes of light stirred under the surface at her touch, like schools of microscopic fish. The panel sighed open, the faint sound swallowed quickly by the hum of the hall.

“After you,” Liora said.

“But you—” Mara began. “You came out through there. Don’t you know—?”

“Of course I know. But you’re the one who fell through a door,” Liora pointed out. “You clearly have experience with dangerous thresholds. Consider this a practical exam.”

Mara shot her a look that said clearly We are going to talk about your sense of humour later, then ducked into the narrow opening.

The air inside was cooler, tinged with a stronger scent of minerals and the faint, metallic bite of worked shell. The passage—the word corridor felt too generous—was only just wide enough for Mara’s shoulders, its walls curving slightly inward, forcing her to hunch. A faint luminosity came from somewhere in the stone itself, the glow of creatures or crystals embedded within.

Behind her, the panel slid shut with a soft click. The throne hall and its watchful guardians were cut off as cleanly as if Mara had stepped out of a page.

For a heartbeat, the closeness of the space pressed in. Then Liora wriggled past her with the eel-like ease of someone used to small spaces and inconvenient physics.

“This way,” she said. “Mind your head. The palace was designed by people who thought children should fall in line, not run around in the walls.”

“That sounds familiar,” Mara muttered, ducking as the tunnel jogged sharply upward and then to the right.

The next few minutes were a blur of motion and stone.

The secret passages of Pelagoria were not, Mara discovered, a tidy network. They were more like the root system of an old tree gone half-feral: twisting, overlapping, occasionally doubling back on themselves as if they’d changed their mind mid-construction.

Sometimes the floor sloped gently; sometimes they had to scramble up what was essentially a set of rough-hewn steps, catching at small protrusions for balance. Twice, Liora took a sharp left that looked, to Mara’s eyes, exactly like a cliff face, and revealed at the last second that there was, in fact, a narrow, sideways slot that opened if you knew exactly which barnacle to press.

“Who built these?” Mara panted, after squeezing through a particularly tight kink that deposited her in a short, vertical shaft like the inside of a chimney.

“Depends who you ask,” Liora said, already halfway up, her fingers and toes finding holds that Mara’s eyes could barely register. “Officially, they’re maintenance channels. Unofficially, they’re the reason I still live. You can’t grow up in a palace and not develop emergency escape routes.”

“I meant—” Mara hauled herself up, her backpack catching on a projecting bit of shell. Liora reached down and gave it a corrective tug. “I meant… architecturally. Did you… grow them? Or… carve them?”

“A bit of both,” Liora said. “The first ones were fused from sand and shell with old heatstones. Then coral moved in. Then people moved in. Then I moved in.” She flashed a quick grin over her shoulder. “And any passage a child uses stops belonging to adults.”

They twisted around another corner. A faint murmur of voices filtered through the stone on one side, as if a group of people were holding a meeting only a few handspans away. The translation shell picked up fragments.

“…seal the Gate…”

“…the Lantern Whale’s last pass was late…”

“…you’d have us trust a surfacer—?”

Liora pressed a finger to her lips, eyes suddenly serious. She steered Mara away, down a steeper incline. The voices faded.

“Where are we going?” Mara whispered, partly because loudness felt disrespectful and partly because her lungs were starting to realise that Pelagorian air lacked some of the surface’s comforting density.

“Library,” Liora whispered back. “Mine. Mostly. The one no one wants to admit is there.”

“You have a secret library?” Mara said, unable to keep the envy out of her voice. “That’s not fair. I barely have a secret drawer.”

“You can visit anyway,” Liora said. “You’ve done the hard part. You fell out of the sky.”

They emerged at last into a space that felt at once larger and dimmer than anywhere they’d been since leaving the hall.

The passage ended abruptly in a rough opening. Beyond it, the world expanded into a cavern.

Mara stepped through—and stopped dead.

The library of whispers was carved into the inside of a hollow cliff that jutted out from Pelagoria’s main cluster. The air bubble here was narrower, closer; the outer wall was a broad curve of transparent shell, through which the sea loomed dark and near. The rest of the cavern was shaped from stone and coral, smoothed and hollowed and lined.

Shelves grew from the rock.

They rose in irregular tiers along the walls, curving with the cave, some jutting out like ledges, others recessed niches. Instead of wood, they were made from braided, pale coral and bands of thick, translucent shell, their surfaces polished to a satin sheen by many hands. Bioluminescent algae had been coaxed to grow along their edges, glowing in slow pulses of soft blue and green, lighting the space with a perpetual undersea twilight.

The shelves were full.

Not of books, precisely, but of objects that wanted very badly to be read.

There were flat tablets of stone etched with tiny, careful spirals of script, their lines inlaid with some faintly glowing substance. There were sheets of something like transparent paper made from dried algae, stacked and curled, their surfaces painted with swirling symbols that pulsed with their own light. There were loops of shell threaded together, each bead carved with minute dots and lines.

Clusters of glassy globes—no, not glass; some thicker, organic material like the museum’s lanterns—sat in groups, each cradling a swirl of dim, moving light. Thin ribbons of silvery metal hung from pegs, chimes that made no sound but shimmered with text-like patterns when they moved.

At the centre of the cavern, a wide, shallow basin had been hollowed into the floor and filled with still water. Above it, suspended from the ceiling by delicate strands of braided weed, hung a spiral construct of shell and stone, shaped like a nautilus unfurling. Tiny lantern-creatures lived along its inner coils, shedding a gentle, pearly glow.

The whole space murmured.

The sound was faint but constant: a susurrus of movement, the soft tick of things settling, the almost-voices of stored words seeping into the air. Sometimes it rose, like a breath, then faded again, as if the library were dozing and talking in its sleep.

Liora inhaled deeply, her shoulders loosening.

“Home,” she said under her breath, with a satisfaction Mara recognised instantly: the feeling of stepping into a place that fit you like an idea you’d had alone and then found someone had built.

“You… made all this?” Mara asked, incredulous.

“Not all,” Liora said. “It was here before I was born. But most people pretend it isn’t. Officially, all knowledge is stored in the Hall of Records.” She pulled a face. “Which is across from the Hall of Tedious Things and next to the Chamber of Arguments. So I found this instead.”

“How?” Mara asked.

Liora shrugged, moving toward one of the lower shelves. Her bare feet made no sound on the smooth ground.

“I was supposed to have a lesson with the Tidal Historian,” she said. “She fell asleep in mid-lecture. I went exploring. There was a draft. And a sound, like whispers. And a crack in the stone that someone had patched badly. After that, it was just… persistence.”

She ran her fingers affectionately along the edge of a shelf as she passed, as if greeting an old friend. The algae there brightened briefly under her touch.

“Mother doesn’t like it,” Liora added. “She thinks too many words in one place make waves. The Council would close it if they could find it. So it doesn’t exist. Except when I’m in it. And now when you are.”

Mara turned slowly, taking it in. Her fingertips tingled. “It’s… beautiful.”

“It’s an accident,” Liora said. “And a secret. And too damp for proper scrolls.” Her mouth twitched. “Which makes it perfect.”

Something bubbled at the edge of Mara’s hearing. She turned toward a shelf where small, clear jars were arranged in careful rows, each sealed with a waxed pinch of something dark. Inside each jar, a faint blue shape hung, like a miniature storm cloud.

“What are those?” she asked.

“Songs,” Liora said. “Mostly whales’. Some storm-voices. A few currents. Professor Finn got very excited when he discovered you could persuade sound to live in crystal. Everyone else got very concerned when he realised that meant arguments could be replayed forever.”

Mara moved closer. The nearest jar pulsed faintly, as if in time with some distant, remembered beat.

“Can I…?” She reached out, then caught herself. “Or will it explode? Or attract sharks?”

Liora huffed, amused. “They’re safe. Mostly. The lids are waxed shut. You have to crack the seal to let them out.” She picked up one of the jars, its contents swirling just slightly in response to the motion, and held it up to the light. “This one’s a lullaby, I think. Or a warning. It can be both.”

She set it back reverently. “Later,” she said. “First, I need to show you something else.”

She darted to a narrower shelf tucked into a crook of rock. On it rested a flat, circular object about the size of a large dinner plate: a disc of some translucent, pearly material, thin as shell but shot through with faint, swirling lines of colour.

When Liora touched the edge, it brightened.

Streams of light bloomed across its surface, rising up like smoke and then resolving into shifting lines and whorls in three dimensions. They hovered above the disc, forming a delicate, glowing model of something that looked at first like a map and then, as Mara’s eyes adjusted, like something stranger.

It was, she realised with a small, involuntary sound, the sea.

Not all of it, of course, but a section: an undulating plane representing the ocean’s surface, with faint, shimmering hints of landmasses at the edges. Below that, layers upon layers of curling lines in different shades of blue and green and faint gold looped and twined: currents, eddies, flows. Some moved rapidly, their light darting like quickfish; others turned ponderously, great, slow spirals.

Dots of pale light marked certain points: here a cluster, there a solitary shimmer. Tiny symbols glowed near some of them. The whole thing drifted and shifted subtly, never quite staying the same, as if it were a live feed from the idea of water itself.

Mara leaned in, eyes wide. “Is that…”

“Currents,” Liora said softly. “The ones near us, anyway. The shallow ones, the deep ones. The ones that circle, the ones that cut across and sulk. Professor Finn made it with a thousand little sensing shells and a lot of shouting. I… borrowed it.”

“Borrowed,” Mara repeated.

“He wasn’t using it,” Liora said defensively. “He was busy trying to teach a coral nursery the alphabet. This is important.”

Her finger traced one of the glowing lines that curved near the edge of the disc. It brightened under her touch, revealing a small, stylised shell symbol at one point along its length.

“Here,” she said. “This is Pelagoria. Our currents, our protections. The old songs say that as long as the Veil holds, the city stays hidden. Tides bend around us. Nets tear. Sonars fail. Doors stay shut.”

She flicked her fingers and another symbol appeared—higher up, toward the line representing the surface: a soft, pulsing dot.

“And this,” she said, “was the Door.”

“The tidepool,” Mara murmured.

“The Queen’s Door,” Liora corrected. “The one only she is supposed to be able to open. The one that used to be used for… exchanges.” Her eyes slid to Mara. “In the older stories. Back when we traded more than fear with the Surface.”

Mara thought of Captain Thimble Kelp’s battered museum, its walls pulsing under her hand. Of the dripping helmet and the map that had refused to stay still.

“There’s… another side,” she said. “Up there. It’s… attached to a room in a building. A… museum. On land.”

Liora’s voice quickened. “Is there a bell?” she asked. “A hanging rope? A ring of silver? A song written in a script you can’t quite read?”

“Um,” Mara said. “There’s a sign that says PRESS IF YOU MUST, but I think that’s just a bell.”

Liora shut her eyes briefly, exasperated and delighted at once. “Of course it is. Surface people are so dramatic.”

She opened them again. “Anyway. The Veil. It’s… complicated.” She chewed her lip, searching for the right explanation. “It’s a weaving of currents and old promises and… other things. It bends the water around us, hides us. The Queen and the Council say it is strong as ever. That we are safe. But…”

She hesitated.

“But what?” Mara asked quietly.

Liora tapped the glowing model. A few of the lines flickered, their light dimming for a heartbeat before returning.

“But there are shivers,” she said. “Little changes. Strange lag-times in the Lantern Whale’s calls. Old routes not holding as steady as they used to.” She nodded toward the far wall, where the sea pressed close. “And the Door opened when it should not. To someone it should not. I think… something is wrong.”

“Has anything… gotten in?” Mara asked. “Besides me, I mean.”

Liora shook her head. “Not yet. And if the adults have noticed anything, they aren’t saying.” Bitterness crept into her voice. “They say it’s nothing. That I read too much. That I take legends as if they were tide charts. That I make patterns where there are none.”

“That’s a lot of that they say,” Mara said.

“Exactly,” Liora said, sharp and pleased. “So I started collecting the things they didn’t want me to learn. Surface stories, old songs, fragments of treaties.” She gestured around at the shelves. “This is what they call forbidden. So I thought, It must be important.”

Mara’s mouth curved without her permission. “We have that on land, too,” she said. “If someone tells you not to read something ‘until you’re older,’ it usually means it has the good bits.”

“The good bits here are usually terrifying,” Liora said. “But also useful.”

She moved to another section of shelving. Long, flat pieces of shell leaned there, each etched with flowing script and small, careful illustrations. Liora pulled one free and laid it on a low, curved table grown from a protrusion of rock.

The script along its surface glowed faintly, like embers banked under ash.

“The Tale of the Twice-Born City,” she said. “The one I’m not supposed to know exists. The one that says the first Pelagoria sank, and then rose again somewhere no one could find. The one that mentions, in a footnote, the Promise of the Twin Horizons.”

“The… what?” Mara asked.

“Here.” Liora traced a line of text, and the translation shell hummed, obligingly weaving meaning into Mara’s understanding.

…when the water-sister and the sky-sister turn their faces in fear, a child from above and a child from below shall stand together in the place-between, seeing both ways. They shall mark the cracks in the glass tide and name the currents that forget their paths. Only through their joined eyes shall the Veil be mended, or else it shall tear and drown both worlds.

Mara’s skin prickled.

“That sounds…” She groped for a word that wasn’t ‘ominous.’ “…serious.”

“It’s a bad translation,” Liora said dismissively. “Professor Finn’s fault. He has very messy handwriting.” But her fingers lingered on the carved symbols, tracing them with a familiarity that spoke of many rereadings.

She looked up at Mara, eyes suddenly very bright, very intent.

“You fell through the Door the old songs talk about,” she said. “You’re a child from above. I’m a child from below. Half-below, anyway.” She flicked one of the small fins at her wrist. “We’re both… in-between.”

“I’m not in-between,” Mara protested. “I’m very firmly land. I get nosebleeds if I think about math too hard, I can’t swim in a straight line, and my mother thinks jellyfish are a political statement.”

“And yet, here you are,” Liora said. “Breathing our thin air. Standing in a place that doesn’t officially exist. Understanding me because the old translation net decided you were worth its trouble. My mother’s Veil let you through. The sea didn’t crush you. The Door held. Things that don’t happen, happened. That means something.”

Mara rubbed her arms, trying to chase away the goosebumps. “Where I come from,” she said slowly, “adults don’t believe in prophecies. They believe in… timetables. And test scores. And… recycling.”

“Where I come from,” Liora said, “adults say they don’t believe in prophecies, and then quietly adjust their entire foreign policy around lines in a song. They believe in currents, and treaties, and never, ever saying aloud that they are afraid.” She snorted softly. “I believe in patterns. And in being early to unpleasant truths.”

She straightened, suddenly brisk again. “Look. Whether or not you’re some Twice-Born Destiny-Child of the Sky, the fact is: the Door opened and the Veil is… itchy. Something’s wrong with our protections. If it fails, ships could find us. Nets. Drills. Poisoned rain. And if it fails big enough, it might not stop at us.”

“The sea could… drown the land?” Mara asked, quietly.

“The sea doesn’t hate the land,” Liora said. “It doesn’t love it either. It just… is. But when boundaries go wrong, everyone gets wet.” She met Mara’s gaze. “Your people don’t exactly have a good record with care.”

Mara felt her face burn. She thought of plastic washing up on their beach, of oil slicks she’d seen on the news, of the way rubbish bins along the promenade sometimes overflowed after tourist days, spilling wrappers into the wind.

“We’re not all like that,” she said, a little too fast.

“I know,” Liora said. “I’ve… read things.” Her mouth twisted. “And heard things. Some of the old stories say there was a time we traded songs and stories and… objects. Little strange things. There’s a whole section over there—” She jerked her chin toward a shelf where odd, familiar silhouettes lurked. “—of surface-things my ancestors thought were important enough to keep.”

Mara squinted. There was, unmistakeably, a rusty bicycle bell, a hairbrush with most of its bristles missing, a cracked snow globe with a faded, drowned-looking model of a city inside, and—she almost laughed—a fork.

“You hoarded our cutlery,” she said.

“It’s very good for catching slippery things,” Liora said defensively. “And we don’t have your sort of cheese. Anyway. The point is: our worlds used to touch. Then they stopped. The Veil thickened. The Doors sealed. The stories became forbidden. And now…” She spread her hands. “Now you. Here.”

Mara’s thoughts skittered like minnows. “Why me?” she blurted. “Why not some brilliant scientist? Or a… diplomat? Or at least someone who doesn’t trip over her own feet in gym class?”

Liora considered this with the seriousness of someone evaluating a tide’s mood.

“Maybe because you’re small enough to slip through cracks,” she said. “And stubborn enough to try. Big people get stuck. And they bring too many… things with them.” She flapped her hands in a vague gesture that encompassed bureaucracy, heavy boots, and poor listening skills. “You followed shells into a pool that was obviously wrong. Most surfacers would have taken a picture, posted it on… Flicker Snap or whatever you call it, and gone home.”

“Flicker Snap?” Mara said, despite herself.

Liora waved a hand. “I’m still working on my surface vocabulary. The point is: you’re the sort of person who goes where she’s not supposed to. So am I. That makes us useful.”

Mara looked at the swirling map of currents, at the glowing threads that pulsed and bent. At the point marked Pelagoria. At the faint, pulsing dot of the Door above it. At the lines that had flickered when Liora touched them.

Outside, beyond the shell wall, something vast and slow drifted past: a dark shape with speckles of light along its side. One of the lights flared brighter, then dimmed, like an eye opening and closing.

“The Lantern Whale,” Liora said, noticing her gaze. There was awe and affection in her voice. “He circles us. Sings to the Veil. Keeps it humming. He’s been… off, lately.”

“Off?” Mara said.

“His songs are late, or early, or… pitched wrong.” Liora’s brows knit. “You can feel it if you’ve listened to them enough. Most people don’t. They just say, ‘Oh, the tides are strange this season, how curious,’ and go back to complaining about algae in their filter-shells.”

Mara thought of Captain Thimble calling the storm unseasonable. Of the way the museum floor had seemed to breathe.

“What do you want to do?” she asked. The question surprised her as it left her mouth, but it felt right.

Liora’s eyes widened slightly, as if no one her age ever asked her that.

“Find the cracks,” she said simply. “Before something else finds them for us.” She gestured to the currents map. “If the Veil is fraying, it’ll show up in the flows. Tiny anomalies. Echoes where there shouldn’t be echoes. Fails to ripple. But I can’t see the surface currents as well as I’d like. Our sensors don’t reach up there easily. That’s where you come in.”

Mara blinked. “I don’t exactly have a pocket full of oceanographic equipment,” she said. “I have a notebook, three pens, a smushed cereal bar, and a phone my mum keeps threatening to take away.”

“Can your phone hear the sea?” Liora asked, dead serious.

“Not… usually,” Mara said. “It mostly hears my mother.”

“Pity,” Liora muttered. “Still. You can see things we can’t. From your side of the Veil. Strange storms. Odd tides. Door-behaviour. People-behaviour.” Her lips curled. “Surfacers are very loud. Patterns show up in your shouting.”

“And you can see things down here,” Mara said slowly. “Currents. Songs. Cracks. Grumpy whales.”

“Exactly.” Liora’s hand dropped to the glowing map, fingers splayed near the symbol for Pelagoria. “If we put what we know together… maybe we can see the whole pattern. Before it breaks.”

Mara chewed her lower lip.

“I’m ten,” she said. “I’m not… I’m not anyone important. On the surface, I mean. I’m just… Mara. I get told off for doodling in margins and leaving sand in my shoes. I’m not… chosen.”

Liora regarded her, head tilted, hair drifting gently as if underwater still decided it had claims on her.

“Down here,” she said, “I’m a princess no one really wants to listen to about the things I care about. Up there, you’re a girl no one listens to about the things you see. But the Door opened for you, Mara Bright from Above. The Veil twitched. The Whale sings wrong. My mother is afraid and won’t say so. That’s enough ‘important’ for me.”

The library hummed softly around them, as if in agreement.

Mara thought of being ushered into quiet corners while adults talked about climate and currents and “big issues,” as if her ears didn’t work if the words were over a certain length. Of seeing rubbish in the shallows and being told recycling was “being handled.” Of the way grown-ups liked their problems big and far away, not here and now and dripping brine on their tidy floors.

She looked at Liora: at the determined set of her jaw, at the flicker of nerves deep in her eyes that matched Mara’s own. At the mixture of fear and excitement coiled in her shoulders like a spring.

“Okay,” Mara said.

The word shook a little as it came out, but it was solid in her chest.

“Okay?” Liora echoed.

“Okay,” Mara repeated, firmer. “I don’t know how to fix… ocean physics. Or magical protective veils. Or whatever we’re dealing with. But I can… look. And listen. And tell you what I see up there. And… try not to drown.”

Liora’s grin unfurled slowly, bright as a rising lantern.

“Deal,” she said. She spat lightly into her palm and held out her hand.

Mara blinked at it. “Is that… is that a thing? Down here?”

“It’s a thing everywhere,” Liora said confidently. “Sworn on salt. Very binding. Very old. Very sticky.”

Mara wiped her own palm hastily on her jeans—because some habits were universal—and spat on it as well. Their hands met with an affectionate, damp smack.

A faint tingle ran up Mara’s arm, like static or the aftertaste of a good idea. The algae on the nearest shelf brightened for a heartbeat, then settled.

“Liora of the Glass Tides,” Liora said solemnly. “Princess of Pelagoria. Rule-breaker. Reader. Annoyance to elders.”

“Mara Bright,” Mara said, matching her tone as best she could. “Of… the upstairs bit. Question-asker. Door-faller. Perpetual detention risk.”

They held each other’s gaze for a moment that stretched and twisted like light through water.

Then Liora let go, wiping her hand on her tunic with only a brief wince at the smear.

“Right,” she said briskly. “Now that we’ve been extremely ceremonial, we can get to the good part.”

“The good part?” Mara said, flexing her tingling fingers.

“Questions,” Liora said, with relish. “So many questions. For instance: Is rain really as loud as the stories say? Is the sky always blue? Why do you put sharp things on your feet to walk on hard things? And why do you all insist on sleeping out in the open where anything could just fall on you?”

Mara snorted. “Is rain loud. You live under the entire ocean and you think rain is loud?”

“It sounds sharp,” Liora said defensively. “The drops. And the roof. We don’t have roof. We have… up.”

Mara perched on the edge of the rock table, drawn forward. “Fine. But I get to ask things too. Like: how do you not get lost when everything is blue? And how do you keep your hair from turning into a nest? And what does whale song actually… feel like?”

“Deal,” Liora said again. “We trade. A question for a question. Stories for stories. Surface for sea.”

They bent over the glowing map, heads close together, their voices threading through the soft murmur of the library.

As they traced currents with ink-stained fingers and argued in whispers about whether clouds were just floating algae or if Pelagorian jelly was better than peanut butter, the weight of prophecy and veils and failing protections did not vanish. It hovered at the edges of their awareness, like the vast shapes in the water beyond the shell wall.

But between them, in the narrow space carved out of stone and forbidden words, something else began to grow: a small, sturdy bridge of jokes and shared bewilderment and the extraordinary relief of being taken seriously by someone your own age.

Two children, one from below, one from above, bent over a map that showed neither world completely. In the faint glow of coral and thefted starlight, with the echoes of whale-song waiting in jars and old promises etched in shell around them, they started, in their own clumsy, determined way, to see the parts of the ocean neither the sea nor the land could see alone.

chapters.chaptershortdescription: Where Mara and Liora visit Professor Barnaby Finn, whose peculiar invention has started to malfunction and may be connected to the weakening of Pelagoria’s shield.
chapters.chapterdetails: Determined to prove that something is truly amiss, Liora sneaks Mara out of the palace bubble and into a quieter district of Pelagoria where odd lights blink from windows and strange contraptions hum under the watchful gaze of passing jellyfish. They arrive at a cluttered workshop in which bubbles drift like wandering thoughts and gears made of shell and pearl turn lazily in woven nets. Professor Barnaby Finn, halfway through calibrating a device that looks suspiciously like a teapot crossed with an octopus, nearly drops his tools when he sees Mara, then immediately asks if she’s willing to sign a waiver allowing for mild temporal confusion. Between his excited digressions, they learn that many years ago he helped Queen Nerissa construct the city’s great shield: an invisible barrier powered by currents and maintained by a vast, humming engine that subtly rearranges water itself. Lately, the engine has been glitching, creating unintended doors to the surface—such as the one in Mara’s tidepool—and momentary flickers in the dome that protects Pelagoria from storms and human eyes. Professor Finn shows them a display of wavering lines that represent the shield’s strength; they spike and dip like panicked fish. The professor, distracted by a sudden bubble-backfire, fails to notice the pattern, but Mara’s sharp eyes and Liora’s understanding of the currents reveal that something deep and ancient is straining against the engine’s rhythm—something as big as a mountain and as old as the first tides.
chapters.chapterText:
Pelagoria, Mara decided, was a city that liked to pretend it was calm.

From high up in the palace hall, looking out through the great curve of glass and coral, it had all looked serene: domes glowing softly, currents looping in graceful patterns, tiny fish slipping through bands of structured water as if they’d rehearsed their routes.

From down here, slipping between those patterns with Liora at her side, it felt different. Busier. Nervier. Like a pond that looked still until you stepped in and realised the whole thing was full of things darting just out of sight.

They had left the palace the official way this time—or at least, Mara assumed it was official, given the number of bows Liora got and the number of disapproving looks Mara attracted from people with very clean collars.

“Walk like you’re supposed to be there,” Liora had muttered as they passed through the coral arch into the wider city. “It confuses adults.”

“What if I’m not supposed to be here?” Mara whispered back.

“Then you should walk even more like you are,” Liora said. “Trust me. Authority hates confusion.”

Now they were well clear of the High Hall, moving through one of the upper districts that clung to the inside of the Pelagorian bubble like barnacles to a ship’s hull.

Here, the walkways were narrower, branching and looping without the stately curves of the palace bridges. The domes were smaller, clustered more tightly, their walls bearing the faint scuff-marks and algae streaks of everyday life. Lines of tiny, bobbing lantern-creatures hung across alleys. The distant hum of the palace machinery gave way to more local sounds: the hiss of water through pipes, the clatter of shell against shell from a workshop, the faint, echoing call of someone selling something that smelled strongly of brine and something only almost like garlic.

“We’re not going to be missed?” Mara asked, dodging a low-hanging strand of what might have been laundry and might have been experimental seaweed.

“Oh, we absolutely are going to be missed,” Liora said. “I left a note.”

“A note,” Mara repeated.

“Yes,” Liora said. “It says: ‘Gone to study. Do not worry. Not in danger (yet). Love, L.’ Very accurate.”

Mara considered this. “Will they believe you?”

“They will believe I went to study,” Liora said. “Which is true.”

A jellyfish the size of a carriage drifted past on the other side of the dome wall, its long, trailing tentacles streaming behind like the train of a very nervous bride’s gown. Its bell pulsed with a slow, steady rhythm. As it went by, the air in the district seemed to pause, watching.

“Why are they looking at us?” Mara murmured, aware of eyes tracking her from doorways and windows as they walked.

“Because you’re new,” Liora said. “And dry. And your hair is doing that surface thing.”

“What surface thing?”

“The…” Liora waved her fingers vaguely around Mara’s head. “The… halo. Like you stuck your fingers in a static eel.”

Mara clapped a self-conscious hand over her curls. Their brief, hurried journey through the palace and into the city had not improved them. Strands escaped her ponytail in all directions, drifting faintly in the thin air, refusing to decide which way was down.

“It’s not that bad,” she muttered.

“It’s loud,” Liora said, with the bluntness of someone who had grown up around people with very smooth hydrodynamics. “But it’s useful. If we get separated, I can just look for the cloud.”

Mara made a face. It was a good face. Unfortunately, a group of younger children, scaling a nearby railing like a school of monkeys chasing a particularly interesting current, saw it and burst into giggles.

“Surface,” one of them whispered, wide-eyed. “Look, look, she’s got no fins.”

“Her poor ankles,” another breathed. “So exposed.”

“Don’t stare,” an older woman hissed, dragging them back. “You’ll make the shield flicker.”

“That’s not how the shield works,” Liora said under her breath, with the long-suffering patience of someone who had explained this before and not been believed. “If staring broke it, the whole city would be in fragments.”

They turned down a narrower lane.

Here, the domes gave way to more irregular structures: little stacks of carved stone and fused shell, their edges softened by creeping coral. Odd lights blinked from round windows—colours that had no business being produced by anything natural. The hum in the air changed, became higher, chattier, broken into pockets. Mara could feel it in her teeth.

“Is this… a workshop area?” she asked.

“It’s the Tinker Quarter,” Liora said, with a peculiar mixture of fondness and exasperation. “Artificers. Mechanics. People who think ‘stable’ is an insult.”

A small bubble, no bigger than her fist, drifted past Mara’s face. It contained, impossibly, a tiny, slowly rotating cube of light. As she watched, the cube unfolded into a flower shape, then folded back into a cube again. The bubble bumped gently against her nose, decided she was uninteresting, and moved on.

“Professor Finn lives three bends down,” Liora said. “And if we’re very unlucky, he’s in one of his Focus Moods, in which case we may have to be loud. Or throw something.”

“I thought you liked Professor Finn,” Mara said.

“I do,” Liora said. “He taught me that you can boil water with pressure and that some currents can be tricked into looping on themselves if you compliment them enough. He also once accidentally flooded the Council Hall with coloured steam because he ‘slightly misjudged’ a thermal exchange.” She sighed, but there was admiration in it. “Come on.”

They rounded another curve, and there it was.

Professor Barnaby Finn’s workshop looked as if a thoughtful shipwreck had sprouted.

It bulged out from the side of a larger structure, its walls a patchwork of different materials: slabs of stone fused with patches of clear bubble-glass, ribs of coral stitched together with bands of metal that had no name in Mara’s vocabulary. Pipes of various widths emerged from its sides and dove back in, some gurgling, some quiet, some ticking faintly.

Above the wide, round doorway, a sign had been carved into a shell and bolted on at a slightly crooked angle. The flowing Pelagorian script shimmered faintly. The translation shell gave Mara: BARNABY FINN, CURRENTS ENGINEER, PROBABLE GENIUS. (APPOINTMENTS UNADVISED.)

“‘Probable,’” Mara said. “That’s… reassuring.”

“It used to say ‘Possible,’” Liora said. “He upgraded it after the shield went in.”

Two small bubbles hovered at either side of the door, glowing a gentle green. As Mara watched, one of them flickered, spitting out a crackle of blue light before righting itself.

“That’s not supposed to happen,” Liora muttered. “Good. We’re in the right place.”

She didn’t knock. She simply ducked her head and walked in. Mara, after a brief, resigned moment in which she accepted that her life had moved permanently into the column marked Unscheduled, followed.

The inside of the workshop was larger than it had any right to be, which at this point Mara suspected was just Pelagoria’s architectural style.

The ceiling was high and domed, its curve lined with hanging nets. In the nets, objects dangled: glass floats, gears, the occasional bewildered-looking shell. Bubbles drifted among them in slow, lazy currents, some tiny, some as big as Mara’s head. Each bubble held something: a small, ticking mechanism; a folded bit of algae-paper; a miniature lightning storm.

Workbenches grew from the floor in organic, uneven clusters, their surfaces an explosion of tools and half-finished contraptions. Coils of tubing snaked across the room, some transparent and full of water racing in different directions, others pulsing with light. Gears turned lazily in woven harnesses of kelp and thread, their teeth made of shell and pearl, their centres studded with little coral growths.

The air smelled of salt and hot metal and something else—sharp and tangy, like the moment you peel back the lid on a bottle of fizzy drink.

At the far end of the room, hunched over a contraption that looked, to Mara’s eyes, like a teapot that had been unfortunate enough to wander into a nest of octopi, was a man.

He wore a patched diving-suit of a sort Mara had never seen before. It looked like someone had decided a normal suit was insufficient and added extra bits whenever they thought of them. Plates of shell reinforced the chest and shoulders. Flexible bands of some rubbery material wrapped elbows and knees. Tubes sprouted from the back and arced overhead like a skeletal, translucent rucksack, ending in small, fluttering fans that whirred feebly.

His beard was magnificent.
