It floated around his chin in a cloud of white and grey, as if it had long ago given up trying to obey gravity and instead decided to stage its own weather system. Bits of something glinted in it: wire, perhaps, or small tools that had gotten trapped and been forgotten.

Mara had time to notice all of this because neither the Professor nor the beard were currently paying them the slightest attention.

“Now, now, just a little nudge,” he muttered to himself, bending close to the octo-teapot device. His fingers, long and stained with oil, adjusted a small coral dial. “If we can just get you to hum at the right frequency, my dear, you might finally understand Thursdays…”

The device—an elegant abomination of pearlescent metal and articulated limbs—made a noise like a kettle considering a scream, then released a small jet of glittering steam straight into his face.

Professor Finn reeled back, coughing, his beard briefly illuminated from within like a storm-cloud backlit by lightning.

“Ha!” he wheezed, blinking tears out of his eyes. “Progress!”

“Professor?” Liora said, loudly enough to compete with the general background hum.

He didn’t turn around. He waved a hand vaguely in their direction, nearly smacking a passing bubble and sending it wobbling uncertainly.

“Not now, not now, very busy, the tide is at a crucial angle and the cogs are sulking,” he said. “Leave any questions in the third drawer on the left, marked ‘Later.’ Or was it ‘Possibly Never’? I always forget.”

“Barnaby,” Liora said, with the patient force of someone who was used to navigating this particular storm. “You have a surfacer in your workshop.”

“Mm-hm,” Professor Finn said. “Very interesting, my dear, very interesting. I’ll have a look at it once I’ve—”

He froze.

Slowly, the man straightened. His beard puffed out in unconscious alarm, making his head briefly resemble a startled dandelion.

He turned.

His eyes were blue—not the sharp, sailor’s blue of Captain Thimble’s, but a milder, washier shade, like ink someone had tried to water down and then used anyway. They widened as they landed on Mara, taking in, in rapid succession: her hair, her clothes, the sand still clinging in stubborn specks to her shoelaces.

He dropped the tool he was holding.

It bounced off the workbench, ricocheted off a small gear assembly, and vanished into a cluster of tubing with a faint, metallic “ploink.”

“A surface child,” he breathed. “In… here.”

“Yes,” Mara said, because there seemed to be no point in argument. “Sorry about the… mess?”

“The mess is mine,” he said absently, then, with a sudden, jarringly bright grin: “Marvelous! Welcome! Don’t touch anything that looks like it might object, and if you feel a sudden urge to sneeze backwards, duck.”

Mara blinked. “I—what?”

“Barnaby,” Liora said, stepping between them before Mara’s brain could dissolve. “Focus.”

“Oh, it’s you,” Professor Finn said, noticing her belatedly. “Hello, Princess. How are your currents? Still rebellious?”

“Always,” Liora said. “And it’s Liora, not ‘Princess.’ And this is Mara. She fell through the Queen’s Door this morning. Nearly drowned in narrative complications.”

“Did she?” Professor Finn said faintly. “Excellent. Terrible. Terribly excellent.” He scrubbed at his face, leaving a smear of something metallic across his cheek. “Has Her Majesty…?”

“She’s asking questions,” Liora said. “And not telling me the answers. So I’m asking my own. Starting here.” She waved a hand at the cluttered workshop. “With you. And your… things.”

Professor Finn beamed. “My things! Yes. Most of them work. Some of them work as something else. A few of them refuse to work unless you don’t want them to. Which is a philosophical achievement, really.”

“We think something is wrong with the shield,” Liora said, cutting through his enthusiasm with the precision of a scalpel. “The Veil. The city’s protections. The Lantern Whale’s songs are off, the currents are twitchy, and a Door opened for someone it shouldn’t have. You helped build the shield. If it’s breaking, I thought you might notice before anyone else stops pretending it’s fine.”

Professor Finn opened his mouth. Closed it again. His gaze flicked to Mara, to Liora, back to Mara.

“Did you,” he said slowly, “by any chance, sign a waiver before coming here?”

“A what?” Mara said.

“A waiver,” he repeated. “A formal acknowledgment that whatever happens in my general vicinity is both temporally and narratively unstable and that you accept the risk of mild confusion, occasional déjà vu, and the very remote possibility of being in two places at once for up to three seconds.”

“No,” Mara said. “Should I… have?”

“She’s ten,” Liora said. “She shouldn’t have to sign anything.”

“Everyone should sign waivers,” Professor Finn said seriously. “Life is very badly signposted. Still. We’ll proceed without, but if you find yourself remembering things that haven’t happened yet, do let me know. It would be terribly useful.”

He wiped his hands on his patched suit, leaving twin streaks of oil, and then clapped them together briskly.

“The shield,” he said. “Ah. The Veil. The Great Hush. Our shared delusion of safety. Yes. You think something’s wrong with it.”

“We know something is wrong with it,” Liora said. “The Door opened.”

“Yes, but doors open,” Professor Finn said. “That’s what they do. It’s in the job description.”

“They don’t open on their own,” Liora said. “Not that Door. Not after… what happened.”

Professor Finn’s face shuttered, briefly, at that, his eyes going distant.

“No,” he agreed quietly. “Not after that.”

He shook himself, beard fluffing, and pointed at Mara.

“And you, young…?”

“Mara,” she supplied. “Mara Bright.”

“Miss Bright,” he said. “You fell through the Door. Unprotected.”

“Yes,” Mara said. “It wasn’t really my idea.”

“They rarely are,” Professor Finn said. “Doors can be very pushy. How did you breathe?”

Mara hesitated. “I… just did,” she said. “The water felt… different. Not like normal water. Softer. Or… friendlier. It didn’t go up my nose. Much. I could hold my breath for longer than usual. And when I…”

She gestured at the floor, miming a vague plummeting motion.

“…arrived, there was air,” she finished lamely. “In the bubble. And it wasn’t… drowning air. It was okay.”

Professor Finn stared at her as if she’d just casually recited the formula for untangling currents.

“Remarkable,” he murmured. “I always suspected there might be self-adjusting properties in the threshold matrix…”

“Barnaby,” Liora said again, more sharply.

“Right, right.” He rubbed his hands together, brisk now. “The shield. The Veil. The thing what keeps us out of sight and out of mind. You are quite right, Your… Liora. I helped Her Majesty construct it. Or rather, I helped build the machine that keeps it humming. Madam Ocean did the rest.”

“Madam…?” Mara said.

“The sea,” Liora and Professor Finn said together.

“Oh,” Mara said. “Her. Yes. I’ve heard about her.”

“She has opinions,” Finn said gravely. “The shield is a negotiation. We ask the sea to bend around us in certain ways. She agrees, mostly, as long as we don’t break the old rules. No nets, no hooks, no noisy propellers. No calling attention. In return, she lets the Veil sit in her currents and redirect prying eyes.”

“And the engine?” Liora said.

“Ah.” Professor Finn’s face lit. “The engine is my bit.”

He gestured expansively at a large, partially obscured shape occupying the back corner of the workshop. Until he moved, Mara had thought it was simply another haphazard mound of equipment. Now, as he cleared a path with surprising agility, she saw it for what it was.

For a certain, slightly alarming value of “what it was.”

The Veil engine looked like someone had taken the idea of a clock, a watermill, and a glassblower’s studio, thrown them into a whirlpool, and then built whatever had clumped together at the end.

A broad, circular base of fused sand anchored it. From that base, several thick, curved columns of translucent material rose, not straight but spiraling gently, like the bones of some enormous shell. Between these columns stretched membranes of water held in impossible shapes: sheets that hung without falling, twisted tubes that looped in and out of each other, all shot through with threads of light that pulsed in slow, intricate patterns.

Around and through these water-forms moved gears of various sizes, their teeth made of shell, their centres crystallised into strange, shimmering densities. Some turned steadily, others ticked forward a tooth at a time and then paused, as if thinking. Tiny, bell-like chimes were attached at intervals; when a gear completed a circuit, it nudged one, producing a soft, clear ring.

Above it all, a sort of crown of branches arced, made of braided coral and thin rods of metal that glowed faintly. They dipped into the hanging water-planes here and there, pulling little streams out and redirecting them.

It all hummed—a low, complex tone that made Mara’s ribs buzz. It was not a machine for making anything as mundane as power or heat. It seemed to be reshaping something more fundamental.

“Behold,” Professor Finn said, with the pride of someone introducing a slightly unruly pet. “The Current Harmoniser. The Veil Engine. The Great Big Thing That Goes Hummmm.”

Mara stepped closer. The hairs on her arms stood up. The air around the engine felt thicker, like it had been folded a few extra times.

“How does it… work?” she asked, mesmerised by the slow pulse of light through the hanging water. Tiny motes—sand? air?—sparkled within it.

“In theory?” Professor Finn said. “Beautifully.”

“In practice?” Liora asked.

“Temperamentally,” he admitted. “It reshapes currents at the smallest level—just enough to create a sort of… edgeless edge around us. It persuades water molecules to remember different paths. It whispers to turbulence and says, ‘Not here, thank you, go bother a cliff instead.’ It is very polite. Mostly.”

Mara watched one of the hanging sheets of water. As she stared, its surface shivered, then briefly showed a reflection that was not of the workshop: a grey, rain-dark sky; a row of breaking waves; the suggestion of a distant shoreline.

Then it smoothed again, the image dissolving.

“That looked like the surface,” she blurted.

“Yes, yes, it does that,” Professor Finn said. “Leakage. Echoes. Perfectly harmless. Usually. Though it does confuse the cleaning staff.”

“Leakage?” Liora repeated, incredulous. “You built a machine to hold back the entire Outside and you’re okay with it… leaking?”

“Well, you can’t have a barrier without a bit of bleed,” Finn said. “Boundaries are messy things. But lately…” He frowned, rubbing the bridge of his nose. “Lately, it has been… more enthusiastic.”

He shuffled over to a nearby bench and rummaged among stacks of algae-paper and little discs. After a moment, he produced a flat panel studded with small, iridescent shells.

He propped it on a slanting stand and tapped one shell. The surface of the panel rippled, then blossomed with a series of lines.

At first, Mara thought they were random squiggles. Then her brain recognised the shape of a graph: time along the bottom, something else up the side. Several lines undulated across it, each in a different faint colour—blue, green, pale gold. They rose and fell with a certain rough regularity.

“This is the Veil’s output,” Finn said, warming to his subject. “Each line represents a different aspect of the shield. Density. Phase-hum. Emotional tenor of nearby currents. The usual.”

Liora gave him a look that said very clearly that nothing in that sentence was usual.

“For years,” Finn went on, tapping one section of the graph where the lines jogged along with mild, predictable squiggles, “it has been wonderfully boring. A few little spikes when there’s a storm. A dip or two when Madam Ocean has a sulk. Nothing alarming. But in the last few months…”

He pointed to a section nearer the right-hand edge.

The lines there were not calm. They spiked up and down, some in tall, narrow leaps, others in wide, uneven waves. There were places where two lines crossed that had not intersected before. A faint dotted band at the top—some threshold—quivered, occasionally brushed by a jump from below.

Liora sucked in a breath. “That’s… bad,” she said. “Isn’t it?”

“Oh, well, ‘bad’ is such a strong word,” Professor Finn hedged. “I prefer ‘energetic.’ Or ‘expressive.’ Or ‘statistically interesting.’”

“When did it start?” Liora demanded.

Finn scratched at his beard, dislodging a small spring that pinged onto the floor and rolled away in a sulky spiral.

“Approximately… nine Whale-cycles ago,” he said. “Possibly ten. My notes are a bit… damp.” He flapped a hand at a nearby pile of algae-sheets covered in tiny, spidery writing. Some were indeed smudged, as if someone had taken them for a swim.

“Nine cycles,” Liora said. “That’s when the Lantern Whale’s songs started coming late.”

“Is it?” Finn said vaguely. “Oh, how synchronised of him.”

“And about when Madam Ocean began having… moods,” Liora added. “More storms. Unseasonal ones. And Captain Th—” She caught herself. “And some surface people started noticing.”

Mara thought of Captain Thimble Kelp shaking his head at the unseasonable storm. Of the way the museum floor had seemed to breathe under her hand.

“You don’t think that’s… connected?” she asked.

Finn opened his mouth to say something reassuring and meaningless. Liora, watching him with narrowed eyes, cut in.

“Show her the last door-event,” she said.

Finn winced. “Is that necessary?”

“Yes,” Liora said. “Or we can let her drown slowly in lack of context.”

Finn sighed, the sound rattling his tools on their hooks. He tapped another shell on the panel.

A new line bloomed across the graph, this one in a sharper, angrier red. It was flat for a time, hugging the bottom. Then, abruptly, it shot up, slashed jaggedly across the others, and held there for a worrying stretch before dropping back.

“That,” Finn said, “is your tidepool.”

Mara stared. “That’s… when I fell?”

“That’s when the Door opened,” Finn said. “Properly. Without a key. Without my… coaxing. It’s supposed to be a controlled aperture. The engine knows its song. The Queen knows hers. This—” He tapped the spike. “—is not controlled.”

“And you still called it ‘leakage’?” Liora demanded.

“I was hoping,” Finn said weakly, “if I used a nice, small word, the problem would feel obliged to be nice and small.”

Mara leaned closer. Her eyes traced the lines, the peaks, the dips. She frowned.

“Have you noticed,” she said slowly, “that the spikes aren’t random?”

“Hmm?” Finn said.

“They’re… bunched,” Mara said. “Look.” She pointed. “Here. And here. And that one.” Her finger hovered over several clusters where the red line—door-activity, she assumed—leapt, each cluster roughly the same distance apart.

“And between them,” she went on, “these…” She touched the blue and green lines, which, between the clusters, rippled in a subtle, almost wave-like pattern. “…do this. Like they’re… being pulled. Or… pushed from underneath.”

Professor Finn squinted, leaning so close his nose nearly brushed the panel. Several of the shells flickered, indignant.

“Intervals,” he murmured. “Regular-ish intervals. I did wonder about that. I thought perhaps my measuring shells were having a little joke. They do that sometimes. They have a poor sense of humour.”

Liora’s hand darted in from the other side. Her finger traced a different set of marks: faint, almost lost in the clutter of the graph.

“Here,” she said. “The Lantern Whale’s songs. Recordings from the listening shells outside the dome. See? They repeat every cycle, but lately…” She ran her finger along a section where the marks were smeared, drawn out. “Lately they come early. Or late. Or… doubled.”

Mara saw it, then: how the smeared whale-song marks lined up, roughly, with the red door-spikes and the wobbles in the other lines.

“It’s… like something is… nudging,” she said, groping for words. “From… beneath all of it. Like there’s a… a big… thing—”

“Technical vocabulary,” Liora muttered approvingly.

“—turning on its side,” Mara finished. “Or… shifting its weight. Every time it does, the shield… jumps. The doors flicker. The Whale… sings funny. And on the surface…”

She thought of storms, of odd tides, of Captain Thimble muttering about Madam Ocean being in a mood. Of the Museum under her hand, the slow pulse she’d felt.

“...things feel… wrong,” she finished.

Professor Finn’s face had gone very still.

“You think something is pushing against the Veil,” he said. Not mocking. Not dismissive. Testing the words like a wire.

Liora nodded, sharp and sure. “Something deep,” she said. “Deeper than us. Older than the Engine. Old as the first currents.”

“As old as the first tides,” Mara said, the phrase from the prophecy-shell coming uninvited into her mind. “As big as a mountain. Maybe bigger.”

Professor Finn’s hands twitched, as if wanting something to hold on to and finding only trailing tubes.

“There are… things,” he said slowly, “in the deep trenches. Older than cities. Older than stories. We feel them in… omissions. Places the Whale won’t sing over. Areas Madam Ocean steers us gently away from. They rarely move. When they do…” He swallowed. “We get… legends. Of waves where there should be calm. Of holes in the sea.”

“Could one of them be… restless?” Liora asked.

“Or waking up?” Mara said.

Finn shot her a look that was part alarm, part delight, part professional irritation at the narrative escalation. “Let’s not say ‘waking up’ in front of the machinery,” he said hastily. “It gets ideas.”

“But if something that big is shifting,” Liora said, “it would… strain everything. The Veil. The currents. The Door. Your engine.”

“And if the engine tries to… compensate,” Mara said, watching the graph, “it might… open the wrong… bits. Doors. Cracks. Echoes. The tidepool. Maybe the… museum on my side.”

“Museum?” Finn said sharply. “What museum?”

Mara blinked. “On the surface,” she said. “There’s a little… place. Kelp & Curiosities. Captain Thimble Kelp runs it. He—”

She stopped.

Professor Finn’s eyes had gone very, very round.

“Thimble Kelp?” he whispered. “Wooden leg? Beard like a particularly stubborn wave? Smells faintly of stories and guilt?”

“Yes,” Mara said, startled. “You know him?”

Finn made a noise that was probably meant to be a dignified harrumph and came out as a strangled wheeze.

“I might,” he said, “have met him. Once. Or twice. Or sufficiently often to regret it.”

“He’s got a helmet,” Mara blurted. “An old diving helmet. It’s… dripping. All the time. And the water around it feels… like this.”

She gestured at the engine, at the humming air.

Professor Finn closed his eyes briefly, pinched the bridge of his nose again, and muttered something in Pelagorian that the translation shell rendered as, “Of course he does.”

“Oh,” Liora breathed. “Oh. The old stories say there was a first… exchange. A first door. Between here and… a ship. A captain. A promise.”

“And some of us,” Finn said, without opening his eyes, “were foolish enough to help build it.”

Silence settled for a heartbeat, heavy as deep water.

A bubble drifted alongside Mara’s head. Inside it, a tiny, silent thunderstorm flared and faded, oblivious.

“So,” Mara said quietly. “You think… whatever’s pushing… might find its way through there. Through my side. Through his… museum. Through the tidepool.”

“And through here,” Liora said.

“Maybe,” Finn said. “Possibly. Probably. It depends.”

“On what?” Liora asked, a dangerous edge in her voice.

“On whether we can… retune the Engine,” Finn said. “So it hums with whatever is moving, instead of against it. Like… like shifting your weight with the wave, instead of bracing.” He gestured, off-balance. A small spanner fell out of his beard with a clink. “If we resist too hard, we might… crack. If we don’t resist at all…”

“We get nets and storms and drills in the dome,” Liora said flatly. “And a deep thing in our kitchen.”

“And on my side,” Mara said, throat dry, “we get… floods. Weird storms. Shorelines moving. People not understanding why the sea is suddenly… somewhere else.”

They looked at each other, the three of them, standing in the humming, cluttered workshop: the professor with his traitorous engine, the half-sea princess with library ink still faintly staining her fingers, the surface girl with sand in her laces.

Outside, beyond the workshop walls, a flicker of shadow slid over the bubble. The light in the room dimmed for a heartbeat, then brightened again. Somewhere far above, the Lantern Whale sang a note that was almost the right pitch and then, disconcertingly, wasn’t.

“Right,” Professor Finn said briskly, as if a decision had been presented and he’d chosen the option marked Dangerous But Interesting. “We shall have to fix it, then. Before anything terrible happens. Or at least before anything irreversibly terrible happens.”

“You sound very calm about that,” Mara said.

“Oh, I’m not calm at all,” Finn said cheerfully. “I am absolutely terrified. But terror is an excellent motivator. We’ll need data. And patterns. And more waivers.” He pointed at the graph. “You two clearly see things I’ve… been skimming over. So. You will help. Yes?”

Liora’s chin lifted. “Obviously,” she said. “It’s my city.”

Mara’s heart thudded hard enough to make her feel slightly ill. The idea of being anywhere near the engine while it deliberately adjusted itself to a moving, possibly ancient trench-creature was… not comforting.

Then she thought of the tidepool’s glow, the way it had pulled at her. Of Captain Thimble’s warning: Some doors stay open even when we pretend they’re shut. Of her mother rinsing dishes at the sink, oblivious to the fact that the water in the pipes might be listening.

“It’s my… shore,” she said, surprised at the fierce protectiveness in her own voice. “My… upstairs bit. If this goes wrong, it goes wrong there, too. So yes. I’ll help.”

Professor Finn beamed, relief and delight cracking his face into a mess of laugh-lines.

“Splendid!” he said. “Wonderful! Utterly irresponsible, but in the very best way. We’ll recalibrate the Engine. We’ll map the anomalies. We’ll hum along with the Whale until he stops sulking. And you—” He pointed at Mara. “—will go back and forth. Up and down. Through the Door. Bring us tales of strange storms and odd tides and any peculiar behaviour on the part of kettles.”

“Kettles?” Mara said.

“Anything that boils unexpectedly is suspect,” Finn said gravely. “Also any clocks that run backwards, maps that refuse to sit still, or adults who admit they’re afraid.”

“That last one might be the rarest,” Mara said.

“Precisely,” Finn said. “And you—” He turned to Liora. “—will keep your ears on the currents. The Whale. The little shivers in the Veil. Your mother will not thank you. The Council will absolutely not thank you. I shall almost certainly be banned from formal events, which is a mercy. But we may, if we are very careful and slightly lucky, keep everyone from being squashed by something larger than their comprehension.”

“Fine,” Liora said, with the grim satisfaction of someone who has finally been given permission to do exactly what she was going to do anyway. “We’ll need more charts. And access to the Listening Shells. And a way to talk across the Door that isn’t just hoping it opens at convenient times.”

“I can build something,” Finn said immediately, his fingers already twitching, eyes going distant in the way that meant some new, terrible machine had just been born in his head. “A… communicator. A Current-Phone. A Message Mollusc. Something portable. With bells.”

“Nothing with bells,” Liora and Mara said together.

“Fine,” Finn sighed. “No bells. Spoilsports.”

Mara looked back at the wavering lines on the panel.

Behind them, through the clear patch of wall over the Workshop’s door, the dim outline of the Lantern Whale passed again, his flank aglow with gentle lights. One of them, near what might be his head, flared a little brighter as he went by, like a wink.

The graph’s lines wobbled in time with his passing.

Something was pushing against the edges of the world. An ancient engine hummed, trying to keep its promises. A city held its breath, pretending to be calm.

Mara, who had fallen through a door in a tidepool that led downward instead of in, felt a weight settle around her shoulders. It was not light. But it fit, in a strange way, like a backpack she had decided she wanted to carry.

“Okay,” she said again, quietly, into the humming air. “We fix it.”

No one—not Professor Finn with his impossible machine, not Liora with her forbidden library, not Mara with her stubborn, questioning brain—noticed that one, thin, hairline crack had appeared near the very top of the graph, just grazing the dotted threshold and then vanishing.

But the engine felt it.

Far below, in a trench that had forgotten the touch of light, something vast rolled slightly in its sleep and listened, for the first time in a very long time, to the sounds of children planning to change its sea.

chapters.chaptershortdescription: Where Mara, Liora, and Professor Finn travel to the ocean trench to seek the wisdom of the Lantern Whale and witness the damage that fear has done.
chapters.chapterdetails: With the Queen reluctantly granting them a supervised expedition—on the strict understanding that they will not, under any circumstances, wake anything large—Mara and Liora ride in one of Professor Finn’s eccentric submersibles, a bubble-boat that paddles itself with fan-like fins and complains in a squeaky voice whenever the pressure increases. As they descend into the dim blue depths, the familiar bustle of Pelagoria fades into silence broken only by distant calls and the crackle of shifting rock. The world darkens until it feels like drifting inside a folded blanket, and then, far ahead, soft lantern-lights bloom: a vast shadow edged with bioluminescent glow, moving with the weight of centuries. The Lantern Whale glides into view, its colossal eye reflecting the tiny vessel like a spark. Through a mixture of translated whale-song, flickering light patterns, and the quiet patience of ancient things, the Whale reveals that the shield-engine’s constant hum is drowning out an older harmony—the natural song of tides and migration paths that the deep ocean follows. Pelagoria’s fear of the surface has grown so strong that they tightened the shield too much, locking currents in unnatural patterns and hurting creatures that depend on them, including the Whale itself. The engine’s malfunctions, and the accidental doors, are the sea’s way of pushing back. Faced with the damage done by well-intentioned isolation, Mara feels an uncomfortable pang as she thinks of fences, borders, and closed bedroom doors on land, while Liora struggles with the idea that her people’s safety may have come at too high a cost.
chapters.chapterText:
The submersible looked, in Mara’s considered opinion, like someone had persuaded an oversized soap bubble to swallow a mechanical crab and then strapped umbrellas to the result.

It waited for them in one of Pelagoria’s lower harbours, cradled in a pocket of air that bulged out from the city’s main dome like a blister. The harbour itself was a shallow bowl hollowed into the inner wall, lined with smooth, worn stone. Water lapped gently at the lower edge, where the air ended and the true sea began, its surface forming a soft, shimmering curve.

The bubble-boat—because that was what Professor Finn resolutely called it—rocked faintly on an invisible axis, half in air, half nestled against the water’s skin. Its main body was a clear, rounded sphere big enough to hold three or four people who were willing to be on very familiar terms with each other. Around its waist, a belt of metal ribs clung like a girdle, studded with control levers and a few worrying patches of hand-soldered something.

From the sides sprouted fins: wide, fan-like constructs made of layered, translucent material that reminded Mara of the undersides of certain jellyfish. At the rear, a larger pair stretched and flexed, stirring the water with slow, experimental strokes. Every time the fins moved, the boat emitted a faint, reedy wheeze, like an asthmatic accordion.

A hatch set into the top of the bubble stood open. Professor Finn crouched beside it on a little platform, fussing with a bundle of tubes that ran from the bubble’s belt into a nest of valves and dials. His patched diving suit was sealed this time, helmet tucked under one arm, its glass faceplate fogged around the edges with his breath.

Behind them, Queen Nerissa’s presence made the air in the harbour feel thinner.

She stood at the edge of the dry stone, robes falling around her in measured ripples, coral crown catching the filtered light. A cluster of guards ringed her at a respectful distance, tridents held upright, their pale blades almost delicate against the curve of water behind.

“This is folly,” she said, and made it sound like a simple fact, not an argument. “Spectacular folly.”

“Yes,” Professor Finn said cheerfully, not looking up. “But productive folly, we hope. And it’s the only way to talk to him properly.”

Nerissa’s gaze slid to her daughter.

Liora stood straight, bare feet planted firmly on the damp stone, hands clasped loosely behind her back in an attempt at appearing less like she was about to explode with restless energy. Her scales caught the light along her arms. Her expression said: I know you are the Queen. I also know you are not going to stop me.

“You touch nothing that glows without asking,” Nerissa said to her, tone clipped. “You do not stray from the vessel. You will listen when Professor Finn says we must rise. You will not—”

“—wake anything large,” Liora finished, rolling her eyes. “Yes, Mother. You’ve said.”

“I will say it as often as I must to make the point bed in,” Nerissa snapped, then caught herself, smoothing her voice. “Liora. This is not a story. There are things in the deep you have never seen and should never wish to. The Whale is not the only ancient there. And even he is not always… safe.”

“I know,” Liora said, and for a second some of the brittle humour dropped from her voice. “But he’s hurting. I can hear it in his songs. If our Veil is part of that hurt, don’t we owe it to him to listen?”

Nerissa’s jaw worked. The muscles in her throat shifted, betraying words unsaid. Then she lifted a hand and brushed a stray tendril of hair back from Liora’s cheek, fingers lingering for a heartbeat against the line of faint scales.

“If he calls,” she said softly, “answer. If he turns away, you do the same. You are not there to fix him. You are there to learn.”

Liora nodded, serious now. “Yes, Mother.”

Nerissa’s gaze moved to Mara.

Mara fought the urge to shuffle her feet. She had the unnerving sensation of standing in the beam of an extremely powerful moral lighthouse.

“You,” Nerissa said, “owe me three explanations, two apologies, and at least one report.”

“I… can start on the report?” Mara offered.

One corner of the Queen’s mouth twitched, very slightly. “Finn will see that you are briefed on the necessary safety charms,” she said. “You will not attempt to leave the vessel. You will not attempt to touch the Whale’s lanterns. You will not attempt to… negotiate with anything.”

“Absolutely not,” Mara said, because even her curiosity flinched at the idea of trying to bargain with something the size of a small mountain.

“And Mara,” Nerissa said, voice dropping low enough that the guards politely pretended not to hear. “If you see anything that feels… wrong… in a way you do not have words for yet, you tell me. Whether my Council thinks it relevant or not.”

Mara blinked. “You… want my… opinion?”

“I want your eyes,” Nerissa said. “They have not learned yet how to look away.”

She hesitated, then added, “My people’s fear weighs on this city like extra water. Sometimes I cannot tell where it has bent my sight. You have not been here long enough to share our… blind spots.”

Mara thought of how adults on the surface sometimes asked children what they thought and then smiled indulgently and went on ignoring them. This sounded different. Less like performance, more like need.

“I’ll tell you,” she said. “If I… notice anything. Even if I can’t explain it very well.”

“Imperfect words are better than silence,” Nerissa said. “Go.”

She stepped back as Professor Finn straightened, satisfied with whatever last-minute tinkering he’d inflicted on the bubble-boat.

“All right!” he said, helmet under one arm, eyes bright. “Boat’s sealed, fins are flapping, Voice Modulator is—” He paused, frowned at a small panel, and hit it with the heel of his hand. A faint crackle answered. “—mostly fine. Everyone in.”

Liora hopped lightly onto the little platform and swung herself down through the open hatch with an ease that made Mara’s knees hurt just to watch. Mara, less water-bred and more accustomed to things like stairs, clambered after, accepting Professor Finn’s steadying hand as she lowered herself into the bubble.

The inside of the submersible was as cramped as it had looked. A curved bench circled the inner wall, padded in patches, scuffed in others. In the centre, a post rose up from the floor, sprouting levers and a wheel and what appeared to be an entire cluster of tiny, colour-coded valves with labels like DO NOT TOUCH and REALLY DO NOT TOUCH in Professorial scrawl.

The transparency of the walls made Mara’s stomach flip. There was something unnerving about being able to see, all at once, the harbour stone beneath their bubble, the curved air–water boundary ahead, and the darkening water beyond that.

Professor Finn followed them in, slightly less gracefully, and pulled the hatch shut over his head. A series of bolts snicked into place with a snug, final sound.

“Breathing?” he asked.

Mara inhaled experimentally. The air was cool and a bit damp, faintly tinged with oil and metal and the indefinable smell of enclosed spaces.

“Breathing,” she confirmed.

“Annoyed?” Liora added.

“Moderately,” Mara said.

“Excellent,” Finn said. “Baseline conditions established.”

He twisted a dial. Something thumped quietly beneath their feet. The bubble rocked. The fan-fins outside flexed and spread, their shadows rippling over the harbour floor.

Mara swallowed as the world outside began to move.

The stone lip of the harbour slipped upward in her field of view; the curving interface of water rushed closer. For a disorienting instant, it was as if they were plunging toward a mirror of themselves.

Then the bubble-boat met the water.

There was no splash. Instead, it was like being wrapped in a cool, firm skin. The thin shell of air clung to them inside their clear globe; outside, the world blurred for a second as they passed through. The sounds of the harbour—voices, footsteps, the distant rumble of machinery—muffled abruptly, replaced by a quieter, thicker silence, punctuated only by the faint hum of the boat’s mechanisms.

The light changed.

Pelagoria’s lower dome fell away above them, its graceful architecture shrinking as they descended. The city lights turned from individual glows to a hazy, luminous smear, like a bioluminescent galaxy pinned to the underside of the ocean’s skin.

Beyond that halo, blue deepened around them. Not the friendly, airy blue of sunny days, but a denser, cooler shade. It thickened with every meter they dropped, turning from turquoise to indigo, from indigo toward ink.

The fan-fins paddled with steady, measured strokes. Their faint, breathy wheeze filled the bubble like nervous whistling.

“Professor?” the boat said in a small, squeaky voice.

Mara jerked. “Did… it… just…?”

“Oh, yes,” Finn said, flicking a switch. “Meet Bubbles.”

“Please don’t call me that,” the boat said, in tones of weary resignation. “It is not dignified.”

“We are descending, Bubbles,” Finn told it. “Do let me know when the pressure makes you uncomfortable.”

“I am already uncomfortable,” Bubbles said. “You have wedged three people and a week’s worth of poor decisions inside me and are now taking me somewhere dark.”

“It complains,” Finn explained to Mara. “It helps regulate the air. If it stops complaining, tell me immediately. It will mean something has gone terribly wrong.”

“Good to know,” Mara said faintly.

Outside, the world dimmed further. The last of Pelagoria’s light receded behind them, leaving only a soft, general glow above. The water itself grew darker, not because it wasn’t there before, but because Mara’s eyes, limited surface things that they were, failed to parse its depth.

They passed through layers.

Here, a zone of hazy particulates that glimmered briefly in the sub’s own faint light, like dust motes in a sunbeam. There, a band of clearer water, colder, that made the bubble’s skin creak audibly. The pressure gauge—a cluster of concentric circles painted on the inner wall, with a little arrow that wobbled as they descended—began to creep upward.

“Eeeeee,” Bubbles said.

“That is not a helpful diagnostic noise,” Finn said. “Use your words.”

“The outside is getting… heavy,” Bubbles said. “Squashy. I do not like squashy.”

“You’re holding perfectly,” Finn said, tapping a reassuring gauge. “Structural integrity is at ninety-eight percent.”

“What happened to the other two percent?” Bubbles demanded, offended.

“Existential dread,” Finn said promptly. “Quite normal at this depth.”

“The light’s going,” Liora murmured, leaning forward, palms pressed to the inside of the bubble. Her hair floated around her head, framing her face in dark cloud. “Look.”

Mara looked.

Above them, the vague brightness that marked Pelagoria’s region thinned, scattered by distance and particulate. Below, a different kind of darkness gathered: not empty, but full. Full of water, of pressure, of the endless slow movements of things that never saw the sun.

Shapes appeared at the edge of perception.

A long, pale form slipping past: a fish with too many teeth and no interest in their little bubble. A cluster of tiny specks blinking on and off, like fragments of a broken constellation drifting on an unseen current. Once, far to the right, something enormous and indistinct rolled in the gloom and vanished, leaving behind a swirl of silt that drifted lazily for long minutes.

The deeper they went, the more vivid the small lights became. Strange jellyfish pulsed with internal phosphorescence, trailing threads that glowed faintly green. Some cratered creature on the seafloor flexed, its rim studded with tiny lanterns that flickered in irritation at the disturbance.

“How deep are we?” Mara asked, trying not to press too hard against the glass. It felt like leaning on the skin of something breathing.

“Past the city’s comfort,” Finn said. “Beyond the reach of most of our swimmers. Into the long-fall region. The trench itself is… further yet.”

“Further?” Bubbles squeaked. “We are already at ‘absolutely not recommended.’ The gauge says so. Look.”

The arrow on the pressure dial trembled near a band that Finn had, unhelpfully, marked with a little skull and a note that read: PROBABLY FINE, BUT.

“We’re still within your design limits,” Finn said. “I gave you an extra margin. For personality.”

“I do not want a personality,” Bubbles said. “I want a nice, shallow puddle and perhaps a quiet life as a decorative aquarium.”

Liora made a small sound that might, in less terrifying circumstances, have been a laugh.

“Look,” she said again, but this time there was awe threaded through the single word.

Ahead, the darkness changed quality.

It was subtle at first: a kind of faint, velvety softening in one direction. Then, as the bubble-boat paddled onward, small, floating points of light began to appear at the edge of the gloom.

They were different from the scattered glows they’d been seeing. These were larger, more deliberate, spaced with intention. Each one burned a soft, milky white with a faint halo of other colours—pale blue, sea-green, the occasional soft rose.

They hung in the water in loosely parallel lines, curving gently with some vast geometry Mara couldn’t yet see. More and more of them appeared as they moved closer, until an entire wall of twinkling lights floated in front of them, like a Milky Way turned sideways and submerged.

“Lanterns,” Liora whispered. There was reverence in her voice. “His lanterns.”

The bubble-boat slowed, fins folding in with a soft hiss. Finn adjusted a lever, eyes narrowing. He said something low and wordless that was half request, half greeting.

Something enormous moved in the dark.

It wasn’t a sudden motion. It was more like the shifting of a hillside, the slow, almost imperceptible adjustment of something that had spent a very long time not needing to go anywhere.

The lines of lights swung, subtly, as if attached to the flanks of a vast, turning body.

Then he was there.

The Lantern Whale slid into their limited field of view like an eclipse.

Mara had seen whales in pictures. She had a vague idea of their size. None of that had prepared her for this.

He was colossal.

Not just in length—though that was impressive enough, his body stretching away into the dimness both ahead of and behind their bubble—but in presence. He filled the water around them with slow, massive certainty. His head was broad, his jawline curved, his mouth a long, shadowed line. His skin was a dark, almost black blue-grey that drank in what little light reached it, the ridges and scars along his flanks smoothed by time.

Down his sides, along the gentle arc of his back and the thick base of his tail, ran rows of lanterns.

They weren’t actual lanterns, of course. They were living tissues, bioluminescent organs embedded in his skin, each one a gently glowing node. From a distance, they looked like strings of floating orbs half-wrapped around a mountain. Up close, Mara could see that each had a slightly different hue and pulse, like individual thoughts.

His eye was the size of Mara’s outstretched arm from fingertip to shoulder. It glimmered as it turned toward them, a deep, dark iris ringed with a pale blue halo. For a moment, their little bubble-boat was reflected there, a tiny, trembling spark in the dark mirror.

Mara’s breath caught.

“Hello,” she whispered, entirely without meaning to. The word fogged the inner surface of the bubble in front of her.

The Whale’s presence pressed against her mind not as sound, not quite as thought, but as a slow, enveloping awareness: like lying very still under blankets and feeling the house breathe. There was weight in it. Age. The patient, long-viewing eye of something that had watched continents crack and currents learn their routes.

Then, through the translation shell that Nerissa had anchored around Mara’s hearing, through a filter of distorting water and complicated physics and Finn’s humming machinery, came a sound.

It started so low she felt it more than heard it.

A deep, thrumming note rolled through the water, through the bubble, through her bones. It climbed, slowly, carrying harmonics with it like trailing fish, until it hovered just at the edge of her hearing. There, it broke into a pattern: a sequence of rises and falls, long and short, threaded with subtle changes in timbre.

“They are small,” said the translation net in Mara’s mind, draping meaning over the whale-song like a subtitle. The voice it chose—because somehow it had to choose a voice for something this vast—was deep and resonant, but slowed, as if each word took time to arrive.

“Hello, old friend,” Professor Finn said quietly, pressing his palm against the inside of the bubble.

The Whale’s lanterns nearest them brightened slightly, then dimmed, like an eye narrowing in recognition.

“Maker of humming,” the translated voice said. “Child of coral and clever fingers. You have brought… others.”

The lanterns along his flank rippled in a slow wave. Two in particular near the midline flared and dimmed in a pattern.

“Name-lights,” Liora whispered. “He’s asking who we are.”

She pressed her own hand to the bubble, a handspan from Finn’s. The Whale’s nearest lanterns bloomed in a matching configuration, lines of light connecting them briefly like a diagram.

“Liora of the Glass Tides,” the net interpreted. “Half-swimmer. Half-walker. Quick tongue. Sharp ears.”

Liora flushed. “He remembers me,” she whispered, eyes wide.

Mara, heart thumping, reached out her own hand.

The Whale’s gaze—if that’s what it was, that steady, unsettling sense of attention—rested on her. For a moment she felt impossibly small, a dot on a dot on the skin of a bubble hanging in his field of view.

Then the lights near his head kindled, flickering in a new pattern.

“Sky-breath,” the voice said. “Door-fallen. Bright-eyes. Question-heart.”

Mara’s throat tightened.

“I’m… Mara,” she said, voice small in the bubble. “From… above. From… the shore.”

The Whale’s lanterns glowed, a soft, almost amused pulse.

“Above,” he repeated, the concept pulled slowly through the heavy medium of his understanding. “The up-water. The place of hard air and sharp sun. I remember. Long ago.”

His great body shifted, muscles like underwater hills rolling under his skin. The water around them thickened with the slow turbulence.

“You come… deep,” he said. “Deeper than your kind should. You come with the hum-maker and the half-child. You come on the Queen’s thread. Why?”

Liora shot a glance at Finn. Finn nodded slightly, encouraging.

“We think something is wrong with the Veil,” Liora said. “With… your… paths.”

She fumbled, searching for words that would carry. “The shield that makes us… hidden. The humming shell around Pelagoria. We think… it is hurting you.”

The Whale’s lanterns dimmed.

A silence rolled out from him like a tide withdrawing.

“When the hum began,” he said, after a long beat, “I learned its rhythm. I bent my songs around it. The small ones”—a flicker of light near his tail, perhaps indicating fish, or currents, or both—“learned its edges. It was… strange. But not… pain.”

He rolled slightly, exposing more of his flank. Some of the lanterns there were not smooth. A few glowed irregularly, edges blurred. One patch of skin was paler, marred by a faint, jagged line where no light shone.

“Then the hum… grew,” he said. “Louder. Tighter. It did not flow with the long songs of the deep. It… pulled. It turned… this way.” One of the patterns along his side shifted, showing spirals flattening into forced arcs. “Currents that should curve… were straightened. Paths that should wander… were bound. The little ones… lost their ways.”

Mara imagined shoals of fish suddenly finding their migration routes blocked or twisted. Eggs laid in the wrong places. Feeding grounds missed. Whales arriving where krill no longer gathered.

“Some of us,” the Whale went on, “pushed against it. We sang twice, thrice, louder. We made our own… hum. Madam felt it. She is not… gentle when irritated.”

His lanterns flickered, a faint, rueful pattern that the translation net rendered as a puff of wryness.

“She pushed… back,” he said. “She took the hum-maker’s song”—a tilt of his massive head toward Professor Finn—“and shook it. Doors that were shut… rattled. Cracks… remembered they were cracks. The long sleep of some things… creased.”

Mara thought of the tidepool door, of the way the engine in Finn’s workshop had started to leak little images of the surface. Of the hairline crack that had appeared near the top of the Veil graph no one had noticed.

“Is she… angry with Pelagoria?” Mara asked, before she could stop herself.

The Whale’s eye glimmered.

“Madam does not… anger as you do,” the voice said. “She does not wish ill. She wishes… balance. She wishes… movement. Your city asked to be still. To hide. To bind its edges so tight that nothing could get in. Or out.”

His lanterns flared, then dimmed, in a pattern Mara felt more than understood: the sense of something squeezed too hard.

“The Veil… is fear, made into current,” he said. “Fear of hooks. Of poison. Of… forgetting. It hums always now. It hums so loud that the old songs… fray.”

“The old songs?” Liora echoed, frowning.

“The songs of tides,” the Whale said. “Of seasons under water. Of where the warm streams run and the cold rise. Of when the little fish become big. Of when the storms roll long. We sang them together, long ago. The great ones, the small, Madam, the Stone. You—we—” A complicated wash of tones that the net struggled to translate. “—your people—used to add your own noise. Boats. Nets. Laughing at the sky. We… listened. We moved. We changed. Then you… stopped.”

“We hid,” Liora said softly.

“Yes,” the Whale said. “You wrapped yourselves in a humming cloak and said, ‘We will not be seen. We will not be touched. We will not be… hurt.’ But the hum does not care why it sounds. It only cares that it is loud.”

He shifted again. As his vast tail unfurled briefly in the gloom, Mara’s stomach swooped; the sense of scale made the bubble feel suddenly very, very small.

“The little ones…” His lanterns along his flank flickered weakly in one section, their glow uneven. “Some do not find the places they remember. Some… do not remember. The great ones…” A deeper pulse rolled through the water. “We feel… wrong. Like swimming with half a song. Like turning in a current that has forgotten how to turn.”

Mara’s chest hurt. “You’re… in pain,” she said.

“There is… ache,” the Whale agreed, in the careful way of someone who does not like to use the words hurt and I in the same sentence. “But more than that, there is… thinness. The world is… thinner where the hum rubs. Threads wear. Doors… remember. Things below… stir.”

He let that last word hang.

Liora’s fingers tightened where they gripped the inner surface of the bubble. “And the Door that Mara fell through?” she asked. “That was… the sea’s doing?”

“Madam’s,” the Whale said. “And yours.”

“Ours?” Mara said. “We didn’t… I mean, I did follow it, but—”

“You hummed,” the Whale said. “You, bright-eyes. Question-heart. When you put your hand on the wall of the half-city on the shore. When you touched the old helmet. When you stepped into the Door in the small-pool. You hummed with us. You did not know. Your hum is… young. But it is… loud in its way.”

Mara remembered the museum’s pulsing wall under her palm. The drip from the helmet. The way the tidepool had seized her hand and gently, inexorably, pulled.

“So I… made it worse,” she said, with a horrible little twist in her stomach. “I… made the cracks… crackier.”

“You made them… seen,” the Whale corrected. “Fear binds. Curiosity… loosens. Both are needed. If only one sings, the sea… limps.”

Liora’s face was pale, even under the soft blue light of the lanterns.

“We did this,” she whispered. “Our Veil. Our… fear. To stay safe from the Surface, we hurt… all of this.”

She gestured, helplessly, at the surrounding dark: at the faint glows of distant creatures, the slow drift of particles, the invisible but ever-present movement of water itself.

“We asked to be hidden so hard that the sea bent,” she said. “And now… everyone else pays for it.”

Mara thought of fences on the surface. Of neighbours putting up higher and higher hedges to avoid having to talk to each other over the back fence. Of borders drawn on maps that sliced through rivers and migration routes and people’s lives because someone far away had been frightened of mixing.

She thought of her own bedroom door, shut tight when she was angry or scared, the way the air in her room had grown stale and thin when she stayed inside too long.

“My people… build walls,” she said, quietly. “Sometimes for good reasons. To keep out… war, or storms, or bad ideas. Sometimes just because they’re scared. They always say it’s safer. But the walls… do things. They change… everything around them. People can’t get to food. Or to each other. Or to… safety. And sometimes the people who built the walls end up trapped behind them.”

She swallowed. The words felt heavy. No adult back home had wanted to hear this kind of thing from a ten-year-old. They’d said things like, It’s complicated, dear. As if complication canceled consequence.

“We thought we were protecting ourselves,” Liora said. “From hooks. From nets. From oil. From… surface greed. And we did. But we hurt you. And all the others.”

The Whale’s lanterns shimmered.

“Fear is a wave,” he said. “It rolls. It hits one shore. It rebounds. It hits another. If you build a wall, the wave does not stop. It breaks… differently.”

Mara pictured it: a high concrete barrier on a beach, waves slamming against it, water spraying up and sideways, eating away at other parts of the shore.

“You must… soften the hum,” the Whale said. “Loosen the cloak. Let some songs through. Or Madam will tear it for you. And when she tears, she does not… mend with care.”

Mara shivered.

“How?” Liora asked, voice rough. “If we loosen the Veil, the Surface will see us. They’ll send ships. And nets. And… drills. And garbage.”

“Some will,” the Whale said. “Some will not. They are… many. They do not hum all the same. You cannot… hide forever. Even at the bottom, we hear their… thunder. Feel their… heat. They melt the ice-songs. They thicken the currents with… trash. Your cloak hums… louder with fear. Their boats… scrape louder with greed. The songs… clash. The sea cannot… carry both without… splitting.”

Finn winced. “That’s… roughly what the graphs say,” he admitted. “In fewer metaphors and more terrifying numbers.”

Mara pressed her forehead against the inner wall of the bubble, closing her eyes for a moment.

She saw, in the dark behind her eyelids, the lines on Finn’s paneled graph wobbling, intersecting, spiking. The smeared whale-song marks. The red door-spikes. The dotted threshold.

“How bad is it?” she asked. “The… tearing.”

The Whale was quiet for a long time.

“There are… places,” he said at last, voice lower. “Where warm meets cold… too sharply. Where the currents… whirl without… reason. Little fish gather… and find nothing. Great ones follow… paths that end in… heat. The ice-songs… at the top grow thin. The deep… grows hungrier.”

He shifted, and for a moment their bubble drifted over the edge of something.

Mara’s stomach swooped again. She opened her eyes.

The seafloor, which had been a reasonably comforting, if distant, presence beneath them, fell away.

The trench yawned.

It was not a neat valley. It was a rent. The ground sheared downward in jagged steps and broken shelves, vanishing into black that swallowed even the Whale’s lantern-glow. Faint flashes of light winked in that depth—isolated, stubborn, like stars glimpsed through storm-cloud.

The edges of the trench were not smooth. In some places, rock had slumped, forming landslides of rubble that poured partially into the darkness. In others, walls jutted out in sharp, layered cliffs. Here and there, Mara saw cracks in the rock, thin lines of faint, sickly green glow seeping out, like bruises.

A low, constant crackle reached them, even through the insulating skin of the bubble. It sounded like glass being very slowly, very insistently strained.

“The Stone… complains,” the Whale said. “Pressure… moves. Heat… seeps. Old… things… stir.”

“Please stop saying that,” Bubbles whimpered quietly.

Finn adjusted a lever with shaking fingers. “We’re not going any closer to the bottom,” he said firmly. “Queen’s orders. My orders. The Stone’s strong suggestion.”

Mara could feel it, though: an enormous presence below. Not the Whale. Something… broader. Slower. Like an old thought at the back of the sea’s mind, turning.

Her skin crawled. Every instinct screamed that she was somewhere she was not meant to be, hanging in a fragile sphere above a hunger too big for the word.

“Do not wake,” the Whale said, and for the first time there was something like fear, clean and sharp, in his ancient voice. “Do not call. Do not… name.”

“We won’t,” Liora said, hoarse. “I promise. We came to listen. Not to shout.”

The Whale’s lanterns along his flank softened.

“You listen,” he acknowledged. “You ask. That is… new. Once, your people shouted from ships and… did not hear. Now you hide and… do not see. Both are… dangerous.”

He tilted his vast head slightly, regarding their tiny bubble. “Half-child,” he said to Liora. “Glass-Tide. You walk in two hums. You can… carry songs between. Sky-breath,” he said to Mara. “Door-fallen. You touch walls and they… answer. You can… hear cracks.”

Mara’s hand tightened involuntarily around the strap of her backpack. Somewhere up there, in a museum held together by dust and narrative momentum, there was a wall that had pulsed under her palm.

“Maker of humming,” the Whale said to Finn. “You tied your clever machine to Madam’s skirts. You hear her… tug. You must… loosen your knots. Or they will… snap.”

Finn swallowed, Adam’s apple bobbing under his beard. “I built the Engine to protect us,” he said, almost to himself. “To keep ships from finding us. To keep… another Thimble from… stumbling in. I didn’t… mean…”

“Intent is a small fish,” the Whale said. “It can be eaten by… larger ones.”

Mara winced. The image lodged itself too neatly in her imagination.

“So we… change it,” Liora said, fierce now. “We… tune it differently. Softer. So it hums with your songs, not over them.”

“You talk to your Queen,” the Whale said. “Tell her… the cloak is too tight. Tell her… hiding has a cost. She knows. She does not like to… know. You hum in her ears.”

“I’m good at humming in people’s ears,” Liora muttered.

“And you,” the Whale said to Mara. “You go… up. Watch the sky-water. Listen to the storms. Watch where the shore… moves. Tell the hum-maker… and the Queen-child. Tell the half-city man with the wooden leg.”

“Captain Thimble,” Mara said.

“Yes,” the Whale said. “He hums… guilt. It is… heavy. He may… help, if he… sings differently.”

Mara thought of Thimble’s face when he’d seen the dripping helmet in the museum. The locked, guilty muscles around his eyes. The way he’d pulled her hand from the wall.

“We’ll… tell him,” she said. “If I can get back. If the Door—”

“The Door… remembers you now,” the Whale said. “It will not… forget quickly. Madam likes… pattern. You are… a pattern.”

Mara wasn’t entirely sure she liked the sound of that, but the alternative—never reaching her shore again, never warning anyone up there—was worse.

“We’ll… try,” she said. “To fix it. To… loosen the cloak. Without…” She glanced down at the trench, where the darkness felt like a held breath. “…without tearing it.”

The Whale’s eye watched her for a long, long moment.

“Small promises are better than… large lies,” he said. “You are… small. Your promise… fits.”

Mara couldn’t tell if that was comforting or not.

“Time,” Bubbles whispered urgently. “Please say we have had enough of this. The pressure is… a lot of pressure.”

Finn checked a gauge, then another. His brow furrowed.

“He’s right,” he said reluctantly. “We can’t stay at this depth much longer. The hull’s fine, but the air mix… isn’t happy. And I’d rather not find out what happens to the translation net if we all pass out.”

“Then go,” the Whale said. “Up… and out. Do not… be slow. The Stone… shifts.”

As if in agreement, a faint tremor ran through the water. Far below, in the trench’s throat, a small cascade of gravel avalanched off a ledge and disappeared into the black.

“Right,” Finn said, flipping a series of switches with fingers that shook only a little. “Retract fins. Trim ballast. Bubbles, up, please.”

“With… absolute… pleasure,” Bubbles said fervently.

The fan-fins flexed and angled. The bubble-boat shuddered, then began to rise.

The Lantern Whale drifted alongside for a few heartbeats, his lanterns pulsing slowly. For a moment, their tiny sphere and his vast bulk were level, eye to eye.

“Remember,” he said, voice following them up through the dark. “Fear that forgets… to listen… is as dangerous as… greed that forgets… to share. The sea holds… both. You must… teach it… a new… song.”

Then he rolled, huge body corkscrewing with lazy grace, and glided off along the edge of the trench, lanterns marking his path like a string of floating moons.

The bubble-boat climbed.

The darkness thinned by imperceptible degrees. Faint hints of blue seeped back into the black. The crackling of strained rock faded, replaced by the more familiar susurrus of open water.

Mara realised she’d been clenching every muscle in her legs. She forced them to unclench, one by one, feeling as shaky as if she’d run a race.

Her head buzzed—not just from the odd air, but from the weight of what they’d heard.

We did this. We hurt him. We hurt all of them.

Liora stared up at the dimming glow of the Whale’s lanterns, her jaw tight.

“I thought hiding was the only way to keep us safe,” she said quietly. “Us, Pelagoria. From your kind.”

Mara flinched, but Liora shook her head, eyes still on the water above.

“I still… don’t trust the Surface,” she said. “Not all of it. Not the big ships and the people who dump things in rivers and the ones who think the sea is a bin.” A wry, bitter twist pulled at her mouth. “But… I didn’t think about… everyone else. The fish. The… kelp. The… Stone.”

“The Whale,” Mara said.

Liora’s voice cracked, just for a syllable. “Him,” she said. “We tied ourselves in a knot and choked his song.”

Mara thought of the fences around fancy houses on the cliffs above her town, shutting out wind and view, throwing their own small climates onto the beach below. The way her school’s rules sometimes hurt the kids they were meant to protect more than the ones they were protecting them from.

“We do that too,” she admitted. “On land. We build things to keep ‘bad stuff’ out and then pretend there’s no cost.” She chewed her lip. “And people who say, ‘Maybe this isn’t great’ get called… dramatic. Or told they don’t understand. Because they’re kids. Or because it’s ‘complicated.’”

Liora huffed. “They say that here, too. ‘Complicated.’ ‘Ancient agreements.’ ‘You’re too young.’” She flicked a tear angrily from the corner of her eye. In the thin air, it glistened for a second on her scale-dusted cheek before dripping onto her tunic. “Well. The sea didn’t think we were too young to listen.”

Mara swallowed. Her chest felt too full.

“Maybe… that’s the point,” she said. “We’re not… carrying all the old… fear yet. Or the old… excuses.”

Liora glanced at her, a quick, sharp look that said, without words, I am both terrified and glad you’re here.

“Professor?” Mara said, turning to Finn. His hands moved automatically on the controls, but his eyes were far away, replaying graphs and whale-song and old decisions.

“Yes?” he said absently.

“You built the Engine,” she said. “To protect Pelagoria. You didn’t… mean to…” She gestured downward, taking in trenches and currents and lantern-scars. “But you did. What are you going to do?”

Finn’s beard fluttered as he blew out a long breath.

“I am going to apologise,” he said. “First to the Queen. Then, if I can bear it, to the Council. Then, perhaps, to the Whale, though I suspect he already knows I am sorry.” He adjusted a valve with more tenderness than before. “And then I am going to change my machine. Not because all fear is foolish. Some of it keeps us from putting our hands in fires. But because I have been… listening only to one fear. The fear of being seen. I have not listened enough to the fear of… breaking what we sit in.”

He looked at Mara. Really looked, seeing not just the land-child who had blundered into his city but someone the Whale had named.

“And I am going to ask for help,” he added. “From a half-child and from a door-fallen bright one. Because clearly my generation’s very careful, very reasonable solutions have… problems.”

The bubble-boat shuddered softly as it passed through another thermocline. Bubbles of some gas fizzed and popped against its skin, tiny fingers tapping.

Ahead, high above, a faint glow strengthened: Pelagoria’s lights, smudged but real, like a cluster of candles in a far window.

“I don’t know how to tell my mother,” Liora said abruptly. “That her cloak is strangling her Whale. And her sea. And… maybe her chances of ever trusting the Surface again.”

“Carefully,” Finn suggested.

“Loudly,” Mara said.

Liora snorted, half-laugh, half-sob. “Both,” she decided. “Definitely both.”

Outside, as they rose, shadowy shapes peeled away from the trench’s edge, dispersing into the higher water. A school of small, bright fish spun around the bubble-boat in a quick, curious spiral before zipping off to some appointment with a safer current.

Far below, the trench yawned, unbothered by three small hearts beating hard in a fragile sphere.

The sea held its secrets. But now, at least, it had shared one of them.

As Pelagoria’s halo swelled ahead, Mara pressed her hand once more to the inside of the bubble. She thought of the museum wall under her palm, of the Whale’s old, vast voice in her bones, of Nerissa’s tight jaw when she said the word safe.

“We broke your song,” she thought downward, toward the fading lantern-glow. “We’re going to try to fix it. Even if it scares us.”

The water around them hummed, just a fraction, as if in answer.

Whether that was Madam Ocean’s approval, the Engine’s malfunction, or her imagination, Mara couldn’t say.

But as the bubble-boat paddled up toward the city of glass and currents, carrying with it the weight of what they’d seen—a wounded Whale, a strained Stone, a shield that strangled the very sea it asked for shelter—she knew one thing for certain:

Doors, once opened, did not like to close again. Not properly. Not if they’d seen there were other ways to be.

And somewhere above, on a storm-prone shore, a shabby museum waited, its walls full of old hums and its keeper full of old guilt, both of them about to find out that hiding from the deep was never as simple as it looked on a map.

chapters.chaptershortdescription: Where a gathering storm on the surface mirrors the growing instability of Pelagoria’s shield, forcing Queen Nerissa to face old fears and long-buried promises.
chapters.chapterdetails: As the explorers return to Pelagoria, the water around them churns with unusual turbulence, jolting the submersible and rattling Professor Finn’s inventions off their hooks. Above the city, the surface boils with a powerful storm: waves pound against the invisible dome, lightning flares like angry camera flashes in the sky, and for brief, terrifying moments, the shield turns visible—an enormous shimmering bubble that any ship might notice. Inside the palace, alarms ring in resonant tones as cracks of light flicker through the outer membranes of the city, sending panicked inhabitants racing for shelter. Queen Nerissa stands at the top of Pelagoria’s central spire, watching as the shield writhes like a net tangled around a struggling giant. Whispered reports confirm what the Whale suggested: the engine is conflicting with the natural pulse of the ocean, amplifying the storm rather than softening it. Old memories rise in her mind—of surface sailors who once visited, of peaceful exchanges turned sour by greed and fear, of a desperate decision to cut the two worlds apart. When Mara and Liora present the Lantern Whale’s warning, the court erupts in argument, some demanding the engine be made stronger, others insisting they leave Pelagoria altogether. Nerissa realizes that either choice, made in haste and fear, could destroy her people. The storm outside batters the dome in time with her racing heart as she contemplates a third path: one that will require trusting a surface child and her own restless, hybrid daughter.
chapters.chapterText:
The bubble-boat hit the turbulence like a toy in a washing machine.

One moment, they were rising in a relatively dignified manner, Pelagoria’s hazy glow expanding above them, the dark weight of the trench receding below. The next, the water around them clenched.

A sideways shove grabbed the submersible and flung it half a body-length to the left. Mara’s shoulder slammed into Liora’s; Liora’s elbow smacked into the central post; Professor Finn, who had not yet invented a safety harness he trusted, bounced off the interior of the bubble with a muffled “oof.”

Outside, the water boiled.

It wasn’t the usual, stately shift of a current deep below. This was choppier, less… polite. Dancey little whirlpools snapped into being around them, their edges marked by furious bands of bubbles. The light from Pelagoria’s distant dome lurched up and down as if on loose strings.

“Eeep,” Bubbles said, in a tone that did not inspire confidence. “No. No, thank you. I do not like this. I did not sign up for this.”

“You didn’t sign up for anything, you were assembled,” Finn grunted, grabbing a lever and shoving it hard to the right. “Adjusting pitch. Hold on. Don’t—”

The sub lurched again, this time up and back. Something thudded against the outer shell—a rock? A startled fish with poor reflexes?—and rattled the metal ring around them.

Glimmers of light flickered at the edge of Mara’s vision—not from above, but from the side, where there shouldn’t have been anything but darkness and the occasional, respectful glimmer of jellyfish.

“What is that?” she gasped.

Liora, one hand clamped white-knuckled around a pipe, twisted to look. Her pupils, already dilated in the low light, widened further.

“The Veil,” she whispered. “It’s… showing.”

Mara pressed her forehead against the inner wall of the bubble, squinting through the churning water.

For a heartbeat, the space around Pelagoria was no longer invisible.

An enormous, shimmering film bulged through the murk: the outline of the city’s protective shell, usually intangible as temperature, now lit up like a soap bubble catching a flash. It encased Pelagoria in a huge, imperfect sphere, its surface striated with lines of force that reminded Mara disturbingly of the Whispering Map in Liora’s library—currents drawn in frantic, overlapping loops.

Where the storm-warped water above hammered down, the shield thickened visibly, flaring with pale, blue-white light. Lightning from the surface—thin, vicious jabs of brilliance—stabbed into that light and jerked sideways, running along the bubble’s outside like spilled electricity along a wire.

The whole immense dome quivered.

“Professor…” Mara began.

“I see it,” Finn said grimly. He twisted three valves in quick succession. The engine’s hum—normally so deep and steady Mara barely noticed it—had climbed into an angry, mid-range whine. Through the hull, she could feel tiny vibrations ratcheting up, like a kettle being boiled past boiling.

“Bubbles,” Finn said carefully, “how are your seals?”

“Very, very concerned,” Bubbles said. “The outside is pulling one way and the humming is pushing another. I feel… elongated.”

Another jolt hit them, this one more of a twist than a shove. The sub rolled thirty degrees. Liora slipped, catching herself at the last second on a protruding brace. Mara’s backpack, for the first time in its life, achieved a sort of sideways flight, smacking Finn in the hip.

“Up,” Finn muttered. “We need to get inside that mess before it decides we don’t belong.”

The fan-fins strained, flared, beat harder. The sub nosed upward like a very determined bubble in fizzy drink.

Through the chaos, the city grew: the smudge of Pelagoria’s lights resolving into individual domes, bridges, towers. Along the outermost curve, Mara could see faint cracks of brightness racing like lightning along the line where the protective membrane met the rock. Pieces of the city’s architecture itself—the outer coral ridges, the highest walkways—glowed at the edges, thin and strained.

The storm over the surface—that far, unseen drama—was pounding its opinions straight down through miles of water, and the Veil, instead of softening, was… grabbing.

“It’s amplifying,” Finn said under his breath. “Of course it is. Stupid, beautiful machine. It’s pushing back so hard it’s singing the storm louder.”

“The Whale tried to tell us,” Liora said through her teeth. “The hum’s wrong.”

“Can we get through?” Mara asked. “The shield—”

As if in answer, a section of the shimmering bubble near them shimmered more violently, its surface thickening into a milky film. For a split second, Mara thought they were going to slam straight into it.

At the last instant, the film… parted.

The bubble-boat shot through a brief, circular opening, like a fish darting through a net’s torn ring. Light bent oddly around the edges; Mara’s stomach swooped again, that Door-feeling back for a heartbeat.

Then they were inside.

The churning at least changed flavour. The water between the Veil and the city was still rough—shaken by the storm pounding above—but it no longer tried to twist them in three directions at once. The fan-fins relaxed by a fractional degree. Bubbles’ voice dropped half an octave from sheer, shaking relief.

Inside the dome, Pelagoria was in motion.

The graceful loops of traffic Mara had seen before—people drifting along air-bridges, fish weaving through water-tunnels, small maintenance submersibles trundling about their business—had dissolved into something closer to purposeful chaos.

Lanterns along streets and in domes flickered as the power grid, such as it was, tried to cope with the Veil’s tantrum. Alarm-shells hung from arches shrieked in long, sobbing tones, their sound echoing weirdly through the water and air. From where their sub approached one of the lower harbours, Mara could see small figures—Pelagorians—racing along walkways, some diving in coordinated groups into water-tunnels, others shepherding clusters of children into deeper buildings.

“They’re heading for the inner vaults,” Liora said, voice tight. “Storm-shelters. For if the dome… breaks.”

Mara swallowed. “Has that… ever happened?”

“Not entirely,” Liora said. “Not here. Not yet.”

The engines whined as Finn coaxed Bubbles toward the harbour intake.

Inside the palace, the alarms sounded different.

They were deeper there, each slow toll of the massive warning-shells reverberating along the coral ribs of the High Hall and down into the foundations. Queen Nerissa stood at the very top of the palace’s central spire, just below the highest bulge of the dome, her hands braced on a rail grown from coral, watching the sky above the sea boil.

From here, the storm felt almost close enough to touch.

Waves, swelled and sharpened by wind, hurled themselves against the invisible barrier. Each impact sent a shudder down through Pelagoria’s shell, visible from the inside as a brief, bright flare along the curved ceiling. Sometimes the Veil yielded a little, dimpling inward, then pushing back out with a rebound that made the water within heave.

Lightning stitched the dark sky beyond, line after jagged line splitting cloud and air. Every time it struck, the point of impact on the Veil flared like a camera flash reflected in glass, scattering spiderwebs of light along the entire surface.

For years, the shield had been the city’s quiet, unseen blessing. Its presence felt only by those who listened, its workings known in detail to only a handful of engineers and a Queen who had signed the old agreements with salt on her fingers.

Now, under the assault of a storm that would, once, have been simply part of the sea’s temper, it was visible. Obvious. A bubble in the middle of the deep, filled with stolen air and stubborn fear, outlined again and again by the sky’s anger.

Nerissa’s heart thudded each time the Veil’s surface flashed.

If any ship passed overhead now—any trawler, any drilling platform, any cruise liner packed with people taking pictures of waves—the bubble would be unmistakable. An enormous, shimmering lens in the water. The perfect, glittering target for curiosity and greed.

Old memories rose, unbidden, riding the thunder.

She smelled, suddenly, tar and pitch and the sharp, dry smell of canvas, layered over the salt. Heard laughter in a language she had once spoken fluently, shouted over the slap of waves against wooden hulls.

Stood again on the deck of an old ship, her fingers webbed for swimming and ink-stained from recording new agreements, watching a man with a ruddy, windburned face and eyes the colour of winter sky grin at her over a crate of strange, glittering trinkets.

“We trade in stories,” Captain Alder Bright had said then, his teeth bright in the lamplight. “Yours from below, ours from above. Value for value, promise for promise. No nets. No hooks. No cages. That’s the bargain.”

She’d believed him. For a time, he’d made good on it.

Then had come other captains.

Nerissa’s fingers tightened on the rail until the fine scales along their backs rasped faintly against coral.

She remembered the slap of a net breaking the surface near the first Door, years later, full not of fish but of gasping, struggling people dragged up from a flooded coastal village. Remembered pulling them free, one by one, promising temporary shelter, sanctuary, while the sea raged above.

Remembered the clutter of surface objects that had followed: more crates, more tools, more “gifts.” Plastic that didn’t rot. Shiny things that tumbled into gullies and stayed. Oil, leaked and left.

Remembered the first time a child from above had asked, voice quavering, if they could stay in Pelagoria forever, because the land felt unsafe now. Remembered finding out later that a few had not gone home at all, having slipped into depths they didn’t understand, chasing magic instead of learning to swim.

Remembered arguments in the Council Hall that had lasted days. The word contamination thrown back and forth like a weapon. The word invasion spat like a curse. The word protect whispered like a prayer.

Remembered, finally, standing where she stood now, watching another storm slam the surface above, and saying the words that had cut a whole world off.

“No more doors.”

Thimble Kelp’s ship had been the last to come that way. The last to pass freely through. The last to see Pelagoria openly.

She had watched him go, jaw clenched, heart pounding, listening as Finn’s newly-constructed Engine spun up into the soft, humming barrier that had hidden them ever since.

Now, the Engine’s hum was fighting the sea instead of dancing with it.

Alarms from below—a different tone, sharp and insistent—cut through the groan of worked water.

“Your Majesty!” A voice at her shoulder, breathless. Nerissa turned.

Tideglass, her Captain of the Guard, stood there, scales along one cheek still spattered with droplets from the hurried swim up. Their fin-crest lay flat against their skull, a sure sign of strain.

“The lower harbours report structural stress along the western arc,” Tideglass said. “Some of the older coral is… complaining. We’ve sealed three intake tunnels as a precaution. The first inner vaults are full. There’s… some panic.”

“‘Some,’” Nerissa repeated, dry.

“We’re redirecting flow away from the pressure points as best we can, but there are… odd echoes,” Tideglass went on. “The currents don’t… listen properly. Like they’re hearing two songs at once and can’t decide which to follow.”

“Finn’s Engine,” Nerissa said.

“Yes,” Tideglass said. “The hum doesn’t match the storm’s… beat.”

Another flash, another shudder. Down along the city’s outer skin, one of the visible cracks of light—thin fractures in the membrane’s usual silence—flickered wider for a terrifying instant, then narrowed. She saw tiny silhouettes darting along a nearby walkway, hurrying past.

“If we strengthen the Engine, amplify the Veil,” Tideglass said, “we might… ride it out. Make the dome harder. Less… yielding.”

“Or we might tear more cracks,” Nerissa said, “by pulling harder against the wrong rhythm.”

Below, in the palace, a chorus of voices rose—a low, anxious rumble.
