“They’re waiting,” Tideglass said quietly. “For you.”

Nerissa took a breath of the thin, strained air inside the dome.

“It is what queens are for,” she murmured. “To be looked at while the walls shake.”

She turned from the storm.

The High Hall was not as she’d left it.

Pelagoria’s ruling chamber, carved into the very heart of the palace, usually held itself with a certain solemn, quiet grandeur. Coral pillars arched up into a ceiling alive with muted bioluminescence. The wide space before the throne-platform gave room for debate, for discussion.

Today, it was a tidepool of barely contained chaos.

Councilors clustered in knots, robes rustling, coral ornaments clacking faintly as they gestured with more passion than dignity. A few had abandoned the usual formal coral crowns for practical caps or head-wraps more suitable to emergency swims. The air was thick with overlapping complaints, proposals, fears.

As Nerissa stepped down toward her seat, the sound swelled, then broke over her like surf as the councilors surged toward the centre to be heard.

“—must increase power to the Engine—”

“—shut down all outer currents, treat this as a siege—”

“—this proves the Veil is failing, we must evacuate to the deep vaults—”

“—leave Pelagoria?” Someone’s voice, high, shocky.

“No one is suggesting—”

“We must shut all Doors,” another insisted. “That child from above—”

“Mara Bright,” Nerissa said, and the name cut clearly through the babble.

The hall stilled, just for a beat, as everyone remembered that she knew it. That she had spoken with the bright-eyed trespasser from the storm’s between-space.

Queen Nerissa walked the last steps to her throne without hurry, despite the storm raging above and the fear swirling below. She took her seat, the living coral subtly shifting to support her as if sensing the weight she carried.

The murmurs resumed, but lower now, as currents of protocol reclaimed some of the flow.

“Bring them in,” Nerissa said. Her voice carried easily, no need to raise it; the hall was designed to let the Queen’s words reach every corner.

The great doors at the far end swung open.

Professor Finn entered first, beard slightly askew, suit damp in patches that suggested he’d forgotten to dry thoroughly after disembarking. He looked more rattled than Mara had ever seen him, but there was a set to his jaw that said he’d grown tired of apologising only in his head.

Liora walked beside him.

Her tunic clung damply. Her hair, still faintly buoyant from the thinner air, drifted around her shoulders. Lines of tension bracketed her mouth, but her chin was high, her eyes steady. The jellyish smudge of worry on her brow had been joined by a harder, sharper resolve.

Mara came just behind them, tiny compared to the arching coral and towering councilors, her trainers leaving faint wet marks on the stone.

The chamber’s reaction to her was audible.

A hiss here, sucked in between teeth. A mutter there. The word surfacer threaded through the whispers in a dozen worried intonations: accusation, fear, grim satisfaction that their warnings about surface entanglements had been right all along.

“Silence,” Nerissa said, not loud, and the word dropped like a stone into the hall’s water, sending stillness rippling out.

Finn bowed with a kind of lopsided dignity, as if he were used to standing in front of hostile committees and had long ago decided embarrassment was a waste of time. Liora inclined her head, enough respect shown, no more. Mara hovered, unsure of the correct protocol, then settled for a small, awkward nod.

“The Lantern Whale has spoken,” Nerissa said. “You have heard him. Report.”

Finn cleared his throat, glancing once at Mara and Liora as if drawing courage from their smaller, stubborn forms.

“The Whale confirms what my instruments hinted and what my conscience has been trying to say louder for some time,” he said. “The Engine—the Harmoniser—my… machine—is in conflict with Madam’s natural rhythms. Where it should bend with the storm, it is bracing. Where it should soften, it is… sharpening.”

A murmur of alarm, indignation, I-told-you-sos washed around the chamber.

“It was meant to protect us,” Finn said over the swell, his voice sharper than usual. “To make it harder for ships to see us, for sonar to ping us back, for drills to burrow near. It did that. It did it well. But it did more. It made the currents forget some of their own paths. It sang too loud. The Whale’s lanterns bear the scars.”

A flicker, unbidden, of the glowing sores along that ancient flank passed behind Mara’s eyes.

“The storm above is worse because of us?” one councilor demanded, scandalised. “We are—what—insulting the weather now?”

“The storm would be there regardless,” Finn said. “The Surface has become… very good at stirring the sky. But our Veil—my Engine—is taking what should be a rolling blow and turning parts of it into a direct… punch.”

“Technical term?” Tideglass muttered.

“Regrettable metaphor,” Finn said. “The pressure on certain points of the dome is… amplified. That’s why you’re seeing cracks of light where you never have before.”

He gestured upwards. As if on cue, as if the sea itself appreciated good timing, a deep boom rolled through the hall. Light flashed along the dome’s curve, filtered through layers of water and shell, turning the ceiling briefly into a flickering second ocean.

“And the Door?” an old councilor with a particularly elaborate collar said. His voice shook more with outrage than age. “The surfacer-girl’s fall? Also this Engine’s fault?”

Mara colour-spiked—from shame, from anger.

“The Door opened because the hum pressed too hard on Madam’s patience,” Finn said. “And because the Queen’s fear—that we would be found, invaded, hurt—was woven tight into the workings. We pulled too hard on the sea’s fabric. It… pulled back. Finding the old weak spots. The old… promises.”

He looked at Nerissa as he said that last word.

In her throne, Nerissa’s fingers tightened imperceptibly. Old promises. Made in storms like this, with hands that had held ropes worn by generations of sailors and fins that had traced the edges of maps now buried under decisions.

“And what did the Whale say?” Tideglass asked. Their voice was less accusing, more tautly curious. “Straight, Finn. No… metaphors.”

“He said the Veil is fear made into current,” Liora said, stepping forward before Finn could soften it. Her voice shook, but with outrage, not nerves. “He said our cloak is too tight. That we are choking his songs and the sea’s. That hiding has a cost the deep is paying for us.”

Gasps. One of the councilors half-rose, then sat again as if the floor had moved.

“He said,” Mara added, not sure if it was allowed for her to address an entire underwater government but deciding this was not the time to worry about etiquette, “that fear that doesn’t listen is as dangerous as greed that doesn’t share.”

A beat of stunned silence followed. The translation net, bless it, delivered her mangled translation of whale-poetry with a strange, solemn weight.

“And that,” one councilor said acidly, “is exactly the sort of thing a child would find profound.”

Mara’s heart hammered. She was about to mumble something defensive when Nerissa spoke.

“And what would you call it?” she said, eyes on the councilor. “Comfortable?”

The man shut his mouth.

Mara’s spine uncurled a fraction. Liora’s shoulder bumped her own, a tiny, conspiratorial nudge.

“The Whale also said,” Finn put in, “that if we do not alter the Engine’s song, Madam Ocean will do it for us. And when she tears, she does not… mend with care.”

“Then we must strengthen it,” someone burst out—Councilor Virel, whose family had lost two cousins to a trawler net generations ago and had never let the story silt over. “More hum. More power. If the sea pushes, we push back. Better a few cracks than open rifts. Better strain than invasion.”

“And if the Engine tears the Veil wide open?” a younger councilor shot back. “If a storm like this one rends our cloak and shows us to every ship above? We sit here arguing theoreticals while the Surface drops nets straight through our ceilings.”

“We could move,” an older woman said unexpectedly. Heads turned. She stood near one of the lower arches, her coral crown askew, eyes distant. “Abandon Pelagoria. Go deeper. Away from the storms. Away from the lanes. Find a quieter hollow. There are trenches unclaimed. Grottos Madam has not yet lent to cities.”

Mur-mur- ripple. The idea spread through the hall in a low, uneasy wave.

“Leave our home?” Tideglass said, more wounded than angry. “The coral we’ve grown for generations? The maps our grandparents etched? The doors—that we sealed at such cost?”

“Would you rather be found?” the older woman snapped. “Pulled out by hooks, your air stolen, your children gawped at behind glass—”

“You speak as if that is already happening,” someone else cut in.

“It happened,” the woman retorted. “Once. Twice. How many times do we test their greed?”

“Enough,” Nerissa said, and the word had weight.

The hall fell quiet again. Outside, lightning stitched another jagged seam in the upper world. The boom rolled through the water a breath later, the dome’s shell shuddering minutely. The light along its inner surface flickered, lingered, then faded.

Nerissa let the silence stretch for a beat longer, long enough for the weight of the storm to press down on every mind in the room.

“We have two doors before us,” she said. “One swings into greater isolation. Strengthen the Engine. Thicken the Veil. Pull tighter on Madam’s currents until she slaps us away. We may buy ourselves years. A generation. Perhaps two. At the cost of the Whale’s song and the sea’s patience.”

She inclined her head toward the older councilor who’d suggested flight.

“The other door swings into flight,” she went on. “Abandon Pelagoria. Flee deeper. Wrap ourselves tighter in the dark. Trust that depth and distance will do what diplomacy and listening have not. Pray that the Surface never drills that far. That the old things in the trenches do not wish to… notice.”

Her gaze travelled the room. Many wouldn’t meet it. A few held firm.

“Either way,” Nerissa said softly, “we are choosing from fear. Closing our hands until we crush what we hold.”

The floor beneath Mara’s feet vibrated slightly; a hairline crack of light flickered briefly in one of the High Hall’s side walls where the living shell met older stone. A child’s muffled whimper, quickly hushed, came from a cluster of families sheltering near an inner arch.

Nerissa’s jaw worked.

“I chose fear once,” she said, more to the ceiling than the crowd. “On a night like this. After a storm like this. When ships had come too often and too hungry. When hooks had dipped into our corridors and oil had smeared our schools. I chose to close the doors. To hum louder than the sky.”

Her eyes flicked to Finn. To Liora. To Mara.

“And I would still close those particular doors,” she added. “I do not regret stopping the nets and the cages. But I regret that I stopped listening as well. That I took my fear of what the Surface might do and wove it into every current around our city. I forgot that the sea does not stop at our walls. That our safety cannot be welded on top of everyone else’s without… cost.”

She looked at Mara fully now.

“You came through Madam’s anger and the Engine’s stubbornness,” she said. “You breathed where you should have drowned. You listened where many of my own people would have shut their ears. You have seen both worlds in a way none of us has for a long time.”

Mara’s throat closed. Every eye in the chamber seemed to shift, however slightly, in her direction.

“I am ten,” she wanted to say. “I still mix up my long division. I spent an entire week last year convinced a shadow on my wall was a ghost.”

Out loud, what came instead was, “On the surface… storms are getting worse. My mum says it’s… climate change.” The translation net stumbled slightly over the unfamiliar term, rendering it in Pelagorian as “sky-water sickness.” “The sea’s… higher. Sometimes. Colder. Sometimes not. Everyone keeps saying ‘we’ll adapt.’ But we… don’t. Not really. Not yet. We just… talk about it. And build more walls. And buy more… stuff.”

She swallowed.

“When I saw the Veil from outside…” She groped for words. “It felt… like one of our walls. But made of… worry. Huge. Bright. Saying ‘keep out’ so loudly that it… hurt. Not just… up there. Here.” She put a hand on her chest. “And the Whale… he’s… caught in it. Between our fear and their… noise.”

She met Nerissa’s gaze and, because the storm had already torn so much open, said the thing no adult at home would have wanted to hear from a child.

“If we keep pretending we’re the only ones in danger,” she said, “we’re going to break everything.”

A slow intake of breath moved through the room like a small tide.

Liora stepped up beside her, shoulders brushing. “We can’t make ourselves safe by making the sea sick,” she said. “We can’t hide by tying the currents in knots. The Whale said we should soften the hum. Loosen the cloak.”

“And let ships find us?” Virel demanded, half-risen again. “Let drills pierce our domes? Let curious surfacers poke their fingers into every bubble we’ve grown?”

“Maybe some will,” Liora said bluntly. “Maybe we’ll have to push some back. But we can’t decide they’re all the same just because some of them brought nets.” Her voice cracked a little. “If we do that, we’re not better than the ones who looked at us and saw… monsters to catch.”

A few councilors flinched. Others stiffened.

“We need a third path,” Finn said quietly into the charged silence. “Not stronger hum. Not deeper hiding. Something… less simple. More tiring. Like most good solutions.”

Nerissa’s lips quirked despite the tension. “Spoken like a man whose inventions never do what they’re told,” she said.

“Madam will not let us pretend she is a wall we can simply lean against harder,” Finn said. “We must… retune. Speak with her instead of shouting over her. Turn the Engine from a barrier into… a translator.”

“And risk opening doors again,” the older councilor murmured.

“Yes,” Finn said. “Properly. Not just where they crack on their own. Controlled openings. With rules. Agreements. Songs. The way you did… before we shut everything.”

Nerissa’s mind flickered back, unbidden, to Captain Alder Bright’s earnest face. To Thimble’s younger eyes, full of stories and nervous wonder as he’d first stepped through the shimmering Door into Pelagoria’s High Hall.

To the day she’d told him not to come back.

She remembered the look in his eyes then: not just fear, not just betrayal, but hurt. The particular pain of having a door shut in your face by someone you’d thought of as a friend.

“How did that go?” someone scoffed. “Your ‘agreements.’ Our ‘diplomacy.’ Hooks, again. Poison, again.”

“We picked the wrong people,” Nerissa said, the admission scraping her throat raw. “We listened to the loudest captains. The richest traders. The ones with the biggest ships. We did not listen to children, or… quiet inventors, or… librarians with bad habits.”

Her gaze slid briefly toward Liora’s secret spoiling shelves.

“We made deals with those who wanted glitter, not balance,” she went on. “And when it went wrong, we decided all Surface was… wrong. I am tired of declarations made from hurt and fear and… preciousness. We have no more time for that.”

Thunder muttered faintly overhead, its sound thickened by water and architecture. The next strike of lightning made the Veil’s ceiling flare almost continuously for a heartbeat, outlines of coral towers thrown into stark relief against the sudden brightness.

“If we keep humming the way we have,” Nerissa said, “we will tear something that cannot be easily patched. If we fortify the Veil out of panic, we may save ourselves from being seen and doom others to storms they cannot outrun. If we flee to the trenches, we will trade one kind of risk for another, deeper and less… negotiable.”

She looked at Mara. At Liora. At Finn.

“And if we do nothing, if we let old fear and new storms grind against each other unchecked…” She spread her hands. “We leave our fate to Madam’s exhaustion.”

A low, bitter laugh from someone at the back. “Queens are for choosing when the sea refuses to be simple,” they muttered.

“Then I will choose this,” Nerissa said.

The hall tightened, waiting.

“We will weaken the Veil,” she said, and the words dropped like a stone into still water, sending shockwaves out. “Not tear it down. Not yet. But we will loosen the knots we tied in Madam’s skirts. We will retune the Engine to hum with the Whale’s song, not over it. We will let some currents through. Let some paths return.”

Cries erupted—half protest, half exclamation.

“Your Majesty—!”

“Madness—”

“Inviting—”

“Listening,” Nerissa cut across. “And in return, we will ask something of the Surface.”

A snort. “Ah yes. I’m sure they’ll be very eager to sign treaties drawn in algae.”

“They did, once,” Nerissa said. “And broke them. We broke ours too. We all carry that failure. But I would rather attempt a new promise, with new people, than drown quietly under the weight of my old ones.”

Her eyes fell to Mara again.

“Some surfacers are trying to mend their sky-water,” she said, quieter. “To fish differently. To poison less. To listen. Most of them are ignored. Or treated like children in a room full of frightened elders.” Her mouth twisted. “I know what that feels like.”

Soft, bitter agreement murmured through the hall, especially from the younger councilors.

“We will not open Doors without conditions,” Nerissa continued. “No nets. No hooks. No walls pushed outward. We will not offer ourselves as a sanctuary for those who wish to escape the consequences of their own harm while continuing to harm. But we will find people—few at first, carefully chosen—with whom to share hums. Stories. Perhaps even maps.”

A ripple of horror at that. Maps were powerful. So were shared songs.

“And who will you trust to choose these surfacers?” Virel demanded. “To stand at the Door and judge hearts? You? The man who built the humming wall? The princess who sneaks into forbidden libraries?”

“No,” Nerissa said. “I will ask those who are already walking on the edges to do it.”

Her gaze settled fully on Mara and Liora, as if drawing a line of light between them.

“A child who has seen the shoreline of both worlds,” she said. “And a child of mine who walks in both waters. They will hum where we cannot. They will see cracks we overlook. They will make mistakes,” she added, before anyone could accuse them for her. “So will we. But they will not be weighted by the same old fears. And they have already done what none of us dared: talk to the Whale and admit we were wrong.”

Mara’s heart pounded so hard she could feel it in her gums.

“I—I don’t know anything about treaties,” she blurted. “Or… diplomacy. Or… fixing an entire ocean.”

Nerissa’s mouth softened, just a fraction. “Nor did I, when I signed my first one,” she said. “I learned. Badly, at times. You will not do this alone. You will carry questions to your world. We will listen to your answers. Liora will carry ours to you. Professor Finn will make sure his machines whisper instead of shout.”

“And if the Surface doesn’t listen?” someone asked. “If they laugh at a child with salt on her shoes?”

“Then we will know,” Nerissa said. “Truly. And we will choose from truth, not old stories and old hurt. Maybe we will decide then to make the Engine a wall again. Maybe we will leave Pelagoria. But at least we will have tried a third path. Not just cowering behind the first wall we built and praying it does not crack.”

A crack of light flickered along the hall’s side, brighter this time. Tiny chips of old calcified coral dusted down into the air like very slow snow. A child coughed.

Nerissa stood.

Outside, the storm still battered the Veil, but there was a subtle difference in its rhythm now. Whether Madam had tired a little, or whether something in Finn’s recalibrations—he had, Mara realised with a start, been turning small wheels and muttering equations under his breath throughout—had already begun to tug the Engine’s song into a slightly new key, she couldn’t say.

“We do not have the luxury of time for perfect solutions,” Nerissa said. “We only have decisions. This is mine. We loosen. We listen. We trust, carefully. We ask the Sea’s forgiveness and our children’s help.”

Her gaze rested, last, on Liora.

The girl met it steadily, brown eyes ringed with the faintest hint of salt-irritation from deep-water pressure and deeper conversations.

“You will have to go up,” Nerissa said, and the words cost her. “Properly. Through a Door we choose. Not tumbling through a storm’s tantrum. You will breathe their air. See their sky. Judge their… hums for yourself.”

Liora’s throat worked. For a heartbeat, Mara saw the flicker of a younger Liora in her face: a child staring up at the shimmering distortion of the surface from just under the waves, wanting and fearing in equal measure.

“Yes,” Liora said. “I will.”

“And you,” Nerissa said to Mara. “Will come back. Not just to visit. To carry what you see to us. To be answerable to both. That is… a harsh ask of a child. If you say no, I will not blame you.”

Mara’s mind flashed, for a moment, to her kitchen table. To cereal. To homework. To her mother’s anxious texts. To Captain Thimble’s cluttered museum, its walls full of ghosts and its owner full of regrets.

To the Whale’s great eye, full of patient ache.

To the storm thundering above them, gnawing at the edges of the bubble they all sat in.

“If I say no,” she said slowly, “I’ll still know. About… all this. I’ll still see… storms and rubbish and fish where they shouldn’t be and… cracks.” She swallowed. “And I won’t be able to… not… do anything.”

She took a breath, thin but steady.

“So… yes,” she said. “I’ll… try. To go back and forth. To… tell you what I see. To tell them what you say. Even if they… don’t listen. Even if I’m… just a kid with sandy shoes and weird friends.”

Liora’s hand found hers and squeezed, hard enough to hurt.

“And I,” Liora said, “will… annoy whoever needs annoying on this side. Including you, Mother.”

Nerissa almost smiled. “That,” she said, “I never doubted.”

The hall breathed.

Outside, a particularly savage wave crashed against the Veil. Light flared all along the dome. For a moment, the shield’s shape was perfectly visible from within: a vast, perfect sphere of trembling brilliance, encasing their city like a drop of air in an oceanic throat.

Then—instead of rebounding harshly as before—the shimmer seemed to… shiver. The flaring smoothed, just a fraction. The afterglow lingered in a softer pattern.

Finn stared up, his engineer’s mind already breaking the sight into pulses and diagrams.

“Did you…?” Mara began.

“I… tweaked,” he admitted. “Ever so slightly. Turned a few knobs in the direction of… listening, rather than resisting. If Madam approves, she may let the Engine sing a little less off-key.”

As if in answer, a different sound rolled faintly through the hall.

Not thunder. Not alarms.

A long, low chord, deeper than any instrument Pelagoria owned, vibrated along the dome’s ribs: the Lantern Whale, far below, testing the new shape of the Veil’s hum.

The note wobbled, just a little. Then steadied. It didn’t match, not yet. But it grated less.

Mara felt it in her bones.

Nerissa closed her eyes for a heartbeat.

“When the storm passes,” she said, opening them again, “we will count the cracks. We will mend what we can. Professor Finn will dismantle half his Engine and rebuild it with more humility.” A small, pained noise from Finn. “Liora will begin preparing an expedition to the surface. With safeguards. With songs. Not in secret this time.”

Her gaze fell, one last time, on Mara.

“And you,” she said. “Will go up when the Door is ready. Tell your people that hiding from them broke more than they know. Ask them what they are willing to… loosen.”

Mara pictured herself standing on the wet stones outside Kelp & Curiosities, rain plastering her hair to her forehead, Captain Thimble’s sign creaking overhead. Pictured walking into a town meeting, or a classroom, or a living room, and saying, The sea is angry and it’s our fault and also there’s a whole city down there. Pictured the faces. The laughter. The disbelief. The fear.

Then she pictured doing none of that. Letting the storm cut new paths every year. Watching the Veil crack a little more each season until one day it didn’t hold at all.

“I’ll… start with one person,” she said. “Someone who… already hears… weird things. And go from there.”

Liora’s lips quirked. “Professor Finn’s right,” she murmured. “You’re terrifying. In a good way.”

The storm above continued its tantrum.

But somewhere between its fury and the strained patience of the deep, something had shifted.

The Veil no longer thought only of being a wall. The Engine no longer insisted on shouting. The Queen no longer clung quite as hard to the first, tight choice she’d made in fear. And two children—one with ink on her fingers and scales on her skin, the other with salt in her shoes and questions in her throat—stood together in the place between, feeling the cracks and plotting, in their stubborn, hopeful way, how to turn them into doors.

Outside, lightning flared again.

For a moment, high above, any ship that happened to pass would have seen it: an enormous, shimmering bubble in the deep, flickering like a lantern struggling in the wind.

Then the light softened, blurred, and the bubble’s outline blurred back into water.

Not hidden.

Not yet exposed.

Poised on the brink of something new.

chapters.chaptertitle: The Plan That Isn’t Sensible (and Therefore Might Work)
chapters.chaptershortdescription: Where Mara, Liora, and Professor Finn hatch a risky plan to retune the shield-engine using stories, songs, and surface knowledge instead of more power.
chapters.chapterdetails: Gathered in Professor Finn’s workshop with rain-dimmed light filtering through the water above, Mara doodles swirling lines on a scrap of algae-paper, trying to imagine the shield as something alive rather than a wall. Liora, tapping a rhythm with her tail against the floor, mimics the patterns of the Lantern Whale’s song that still hum in her bones. The Professor, meanwhile, attempts to brew tea in a kettle that doubles as a pressure gauge, causing it to whistle anxiously whenever anyone suggests something dangerous. Piece by piece, they build an idea: instead of strengthening the shield by brute force, they can widen it, transforming it from a rigid barrier into a permeable veil that bends but doesn’t break, letting currents and certain creatures flow through while still cloaking Pelagoria from harmful eyes. To do that, they’ll need to retune the engine using not just mechanical adjustments but layered patterns—stories encoded as rhythms, whale-song woven with human lullabies and merfolk chants, all synchronized with the beating hearts of the city’s inhabitants. Mara offers a surface perspective, describing wave patterns and weather cycles she’s seen from above, while Liora translates these into the language of currents. The result is undeniably absurd, wholly unapproved, and full of elements that could misfire spectacularly, prompting Professor Finn to declare it “technically unsound, morally ambiguous, and therefore, in my professional opinion, our best option.”
chapters.chapterText:
Professor Finn’s workshop had a particular way of reacting to bad weather.

On calm days, its nets of tools and half-finished contraptions swayed gently, their shadows rocking on the walls like quiet thoughts. The bubbles that drifted up from floor vents glowed politely. The big engine in the corner hummed at a contented, background sort of pitch.

Today, with rain hammering the surface far above and the whole of Pelagoria wrapped in that strange, storm-tinged half-light, the workshop fidgeted.

The nets creaked. Spoons clinked against beakers without being touched. Bubbles drifted in from nowhere and burst against shelves with faint, disgruntled pops. The Veil engine’s hum wobbled occasionally, like a singer testing different notes under their breath.

At the centre workbench, Mara hunched over a sheet of algae-paper, pencil gripped so tightly her knuckles had gone pale.

The paper smelled faintly of brine and old leaves. Its surface had a slight give, a texture her pencil caught on in tiny, satisfying snags. She had already filled most of it with loops and lines: a tangle of curves that crisscrossed in rough circles, arrows slipping between them.

It had started, sensibly enough, as a diagram.

Now it looked more like the inside of a seashell if seashells could have nervous breakdowns.

“I keep drawing walls,” she muttered, half to herself. “Even when I’m trying not to.”

Liora lay on her stomach on the floor nearby, propped up on her elbows, legs raised behind her. In the thin air of the workshop, the fins along her ankles drifted lazily. She tapped the tip of her tail—really just the last, more flexible bit of her spine, edged with delicate fin—against the floor in a slow, repeating rhythm.

Thump, pause, thump-thump, longer pause. Thump.

“I’m not hearing walls,” she said. “I’m hearing… roofs. Over our heads. Too low.”

Thump, thump.

Professor Barnaby Finn, across the room, was trying to make tea.

This would have been fine, except that the device he was attempting to boil water in also happened to be a pressure gauge.

It looked like a copper kettle someone had crossbred with a barometer and then entangled in a nest of brass coils. A narrow glass tube ran up one side, filled with a pale, viscous liquid that rose and fell according to some principle only Finn trusted. Thin wires sprouted from its base and vanished into a tangle of instruments.

Whenever the conversation veered toward anything even slightly dangerous, the kettle let out an anxious little squeal of steam.

At their last mention of “loosening the shield,” it had shrieked like a panicked beetle and tried to climb off the stove.

Finn caught it deftly, set it back down, and patted it with one gloved hand. “None of that,” he said. “We’re all anxious. You are not special.”

The kettle burbled resentfully but stayed.

Mara chewed on the end of her pencil, studying her messy, looping lines.

“On the surface,” she said, slowing her words until they came out in something like order, “we build sea walls.”

Liora craned her head to look. “Those are literal walls?” she asked. “Not yet another metaphor?”

“Literal,” Mara said. “Concrete. Big blocks. They stick out into the sea or run along the shore. To stop waves from eating the land. To keep towns from flooding. Or to keep stupidly expensive houses from… falling in.”

Liora resumed her tail-thumping, thoughtful. “Do they work?”

“Sometimes,” Mara said. “Sort of. For a while. But the waves don’t stop. They just bounce off. Or go around. Or find somewhere else to hit harder. So… we move the problem. We don’t… solve it.”

She jabbed the paper with her pencil. “I keep thinking of the Veil like that. A bigger and bigger wall. But the Whale said that just… makes the waves... weird.”

Finn, who had been fussing with a valve, nodded absently. “Reflected energy,” he said. “You shove the force away, it comes back at you from another angle. Hydrodynamics. Politics. Same problem. Different lecture.”

“So maybe,” Liora said slowly, “we stop trying to block everything. And… start trying to… shape it.”

She rolled onto her back, staring up at the workshop’s domed ceiling, scales along her cheekbone catching stray workshop light.

“It’s like… current etiquette,” she went on. “Those awful classes. When a strong current comes through a corridor, you don’t just slam a gate in its face. You guide it. You redirect. You give it somewhere to go that won’t knock over all the children.”

“You do slam gates sometimes,” Finn said. “When those children have snuck unsupervised into the turbine galleries.”

“Hypothetically,” Liora said, with the reflex of someone who had, in fact, done exactly that. “But mostly you… bend. You don’t just… stop.”

Mara frowned at her drawing. She began sketching again, not the straight, thick line she’d used before to show the Veil’s edge, but a series of looping, overlapping arcs.

“Like… curtains,” she said slowly. “Not a brick wall. Lots of… layers. They move. Air can get through, but not… everything. And they can… billow when the wind hits, instead of… cracking.”

Finn, curiosity piqued by the absence of squealing from the kettle, wandered over to peer at her paper.

“What’s that?” he asked.

“The Veil,” Mara said. “If it wasn’t… one big… hard thing.” She pointed at the outermost line. “This is what you’ve got now. A… shell. If the storm pushes, it has to hold. Or it breaks.” Her fingers traced the concentric, more flexible rings she’d doodled. “But if it was more like… I don’t know. A… net. Or a jellyfish bell. Layers. You could… let some of the storm through. Bleed it off. Instead of… taking it all here.”

The kettle gave an alarmed “wheeeeep” at the word bleed.

“Yes, yes, yes,” Finn said, ignoring it. “A permeable barrier. A… semi-permeable membrane.” His eyes lit the way they did whenever biology snuck into engineering. “Filters instead of walls. Letting in what we need, pushing out what we don’t.”

He tapped the paper. “But how would it know the difference between a… safe current and a dangerous one? Between a friendly dolphin and a trawler?”

Mara’s pencil hovered. “That’s… the problem,” she admitted. “We’d need… rules. Patterns. Something that tells the Veil ‘this kind of movement is okay, this isn’t.’”

“Language,” Liora said.

They both looked at her.

She sat up, tail curling under her, that inward-listening expression on her face again. The one she’d worn when they’d first stepped into her Library of Whispers. As if half her attention was on something no one else could hear.

“The Whale… spoke about songs,” she said. “The way currents know where to run because they’ve always run there. Because something sang them that way. His songs. Madam’s. Ours, once.” Her tail flicked against the floor, faster now, matching some remembered pulse. “The Veil’s just… another song. Right now it’s… shouting one word: NO. Over and over. At everything.”

Mara winced. She could almost hear it: a constant, droning note that didn’t care what it was drowning out.

“What if we taught it… more words?” Liora mused. “Different rhythms. Codes. Ways to say… ‘let this through, hide that; bend here, hold there.’”

“Stories,” Mara said, almost at the same time.

Finn raised his eyebrows. “Stories?”

Mara flapped her pencil, trying to catch the idea as it tried to flee.

“On land,” she said, “when we… don’t know what to do, or how to be… with something big, we… tell stories about it. We have… weather-lore. Sailors’ sayings. ‘Red sky at night, shepherd’s delight.’ ‘Mackerel scales and mare’s tails make lofty ships carry low sails.’”

The translation shell tangled itself briefly, struggling with the idioms, then draped a version of them over Liora and Finn’s understanding as: red-sky calm-warning, fish-cloud caution, lower your fins when the high-wind shapes appear.

“We… encode patterns,” Mara said. “In words. In… songs. So you don’t have to know… the meteorology. You just… feel the proverb and act. What if the Veil’s… instructions… weren’t just numbers in your engine, Professor? What if they were… patterns. Rhythms. Stories. Like… teaching it cultural etiquette instead of just… physics.”

The kettle gave a low, uncertain whistle, as if torn between warning and curiosity.

Finn’s beard fluffed. “You want to… program the shield-engine with… folk wisdom.”

“Is that bad?” Mara asked.

“It’s… gloriously bad,” he said. “Deeply suspect. Elegantly foolish.”

Liora’s eyes glittered. “It makes sense,” she said. “Our engine’s already… humming. Madam’s already… singing. The Whale’s… complaining in chords. If we keep treating the Veil like a… machine in a box, we’ll keep… scraping against them. But if we treat it like… another voice in the choir…”

“We weave its hum out of… songs,” Finn finished, half to himself. “Layered patterns. Structural as well as narrative. The Engine would still shape currents, but instead of a blunt ‘push everything away from the bubble,’ it would… listen. It would… harmonise. Or try.”

His hands were already moving, grabbing a scrap of algae-paper of his own, scratching circles and notes onto it: a schematised Veil, the Engine, the Whale, Madam Ocean herself sketched as a spiralling, central arrow.

“We already know certain songs affect local currents,” Liora said. “The Tide-Callers do it. They sing into the stones. The old work crews used to chant while laying coral. Professor, you told my class once that the first Engine prototype only started working when someone”—she coughed delicately; everyone in the room knew it had been Finn himself—“swore at it in three different dialects and a minor key.”

“I maintain that was coincidental,” Finn said. “But yes. Sound matters. Not just pressure. Not just flow. Meaning, perhaps, in a way we don’t quite… quantify yet.”

Mara looked back at her mess of curls and loops.

“We could… start small,” she said. “Not rewriting the whole Veil at once. Just… some parts.” She circled one section of her doodled ‘curtain.’ “Here. The layers… nearest Pelagoria. Instead of just saying ‘no,’ they could say… ‘slow.’” She drew tight little loops. “They… tangle fast things. Blunt impacts. But…” She left gaps. “They don’t… trap. They just… delay. Spread.”

“You’re describing a… boundary layer,” Finn murmured. “Viscous drag. Turbulence damping. That we can do. That’s… already in the Engine. But you want it to… change based on… what’s hitting it.”

“Like a story reacting to who’s listening,” Mara said. “You don’t tell a three-year-old the same ghost story you tell a teenager. If you’re… kind.”

Liora grinned. “So we teach the Veil to… tell different stories to different things. If it hears the pattern of a trawler’s propellers, it sings one way. If it hears… the Lantern Whale’s song, or… friendly fish, it sings another.”

Finn’s eyes lit properly now, the way they did when nine impossible concepts finally linked into something mathematically juicy.

“A pattern-recognition layer,” he said. “An acoustic signature filter. We’d need… listening shells embedded along the outer membrane. To hear. To classify. To feed that into the Engine. And the Engine would need a… new library of responses.”

He looked around his chaotic workshop as if expecting a library to materialise out of guilt.

“You have a library,” Mara said promptly. “Liora’s. Full of… forbidden stories and old songs.”

Liora sat up straighter. “We could… use the coded shells,” she said. “The ones with recorded chants. Whale-songs. Current-calls. The ones you said we weren’t meant to crack open without a grown-up.”

She folded her arms. “You count as a grown-up. Sort of.”

Finn spluttered. “Those are… untested. You can’t just… pour random cultural artefacts into a sensitive machine.”

“You already did,” Liora pointed out. “You poured your fear of nets and your mother’s anger and everyone’s caution into it. You just didn’t admit that’s what you were doing.”

The kettle let out a long, mournful keen. Finn swatted its spout until it subsided.

“All right,” he said. “Point taken. The Engine is already full of stories. They’re just… all one kind. ‘Hide.’ ‘Repel.’ ‘No.’” His mouth twisted. “We need… more complicated ones. ‘Not here.’ ‘Not that.’ ‘Slow down.’ ‘Come in, but gently.’”

Mara’s heart thumped, excitement battling terror.

“We could… encode them,” she said. “Like… knots. Sailor’s knots.” She’d seen a book in Thimble’s museum once, full of diagrams: bowline, clove hitch, reef knot. Each with its little song to remember it by. “On land, we used to… memorise things with… rhymes. Liora can… translate into current patterns. You can… turn those into… gear timings. Water pulses.”

“Oh, can I?” Finn said. But he didn’t sound affronted; he sounded intrigued. “We’d need… stable anchors. The Engine’s main gears. They hum at fixed frequencies.” He tapped the air as if plucking invisible strings. “We can overlay other rhythms on that. Liora, the Whale’s last song—can you remember its… contour?”

Liora closed her eyes. Her tailtip flicked, then began tapping again.

This time the rhythm was more complex: long pulses, short pulses, a rising pattern, a long held beat. Her fingers joined, drumming on the floor in a syncopated counterpoint.

The workshop seemed to lean in.

Mara felt the shape of it in her chest. Not as clearly as the Whale’s song in the trench, but a ghost of it. Her heart wanted to follow it, slotting its own lub-dub into the spaces between.

Finn’s hands twitched, mapping the rhythm unconsciously. “Good,” he murmured. “Yes. That… there. If we feed that through the Engine’s primary valves instead of the current flatline… the harmonics would shift. The hum would… match more of Madam’s background song. The Veil might… stop fighting quite so hard at the edges.”

“And if we weave in…” Liora groped for a word. “…home-songs.”

Mara blinked. “Home-songs?”

“The chants we use when we lay coral,” Liora said. “The ones the builders hum when setting stone. The lullabies mothers sing to make babies sleep through storm surges. The patterns our hearts already know.”

She thumped her tail again. For a few beats, the rhythm changed: gentler, rocking. Mara thought of someone swaying in shallow water with a child in their arms.

“We could… synchronise,” Finn said slowly. “Use the Heartstones.”

“The what?” Mara said.

Finn pointed at the floor. “Every major structure in Pelagoria has a Heartstone,” he said. “A chunk of thick, resonant coral fused into its foundations. It carries vibrations. It lets us know if something is… wrong. Cracks. Strains. Extra weight.” He tapped his own chest. “We can… monitor them. In theory.”

“In theory?” the kettle asked shrilly.

“In theory and practice which is ongoing,” Finn corrected. “What if, instead of just listening for damage, we sent rhythm down?” His eyes gleamed. “We could… cascade. Start the new hum in the Engine. Feed it into a few key Heartstones. Let the city’s own… footsteps reinforce it.” His gaze slid to Liora. “And their… heartbeats.”

“You want the whole city to… sing the shield into a new shape,” Liora said, half-marvelling, half-horrified. “At once.”

“Yes,” Finn said. “Briefly. Carefully. With supervision.”

“That’s… impossible,” Bubbles quavered.

“Good,” Finn said. “Impossible things are where all the interesting mistakes live.”

Mara’s pencil moved almost of its own accord, adding to the loops on the page: tiny, repeated motifs. She found herself humming under her breath, a snatch of a tune her mother used to sing washing dishes when storms rattled their windows.

She didn’t even realise she’d done it aloud until Liora said, “What’s that?”

Mara stopped. “Oh. Just… a song. My mum’s.”

“Words?” Liora asked.

Mara flushed. “It’s silly,” she said. “It’s about… rain. And… cups of tea. And… staying inside until the worst blows over.”

“The Veil likes that,” Finn observed. “Too much.”

“It’s not just that,” Mara protested. “It’s… about… how storms pass. How… you’re still there after. How the same roof that keeps the rain out… also keeps you in.” She struggled. “We could… use that. Inverse it. Teach the Veil… that letting some things through… is part of… not breaking.”

Liora’s eyes softened. “Sing it,” she said.

Mara grimaced. “Absolutely not.”

“Just a bit,” Liora cajoled. “For… pattern. I won’t tell anyone your voice cracked.”

“My voice does not crack,” Mara said, stung. “It… squeaks. Occasionally. In dignified protest.”

Finn, already at a nearby chalkboard, scribbling new equations that looked suspiciously like music notation, said absently, “We don’t need pitch. We need rhythm. Words. The structure. We can… abstract.”

Mara stared at the algae-paper, mortified. Then she remembered the Whale’s lanterns, the lines of strain along his flank. The thin crack of light that had opened near the top of Finn’s graph.

“Fine,” she said.

She sang.

Her voice came out small in the big, cluttered workshop, but steady. The words were simple, the melody lilting: an old tune, passed down through kitchens and damp coat stands, meant to make scrubbing plates feel less like labour and more like a spell.

Tip-tap on the window, rain on the glass,  
Boil up the kettle, let the dark clouds pass.  
Roof over, floor under, walls standing fast,  
Storm in the doorway, you can’t come in last.

She faltered, cheeks heating. “It gets… sillier after that,” she muttered.

But Liora was already tapping the rhythm with her tail, brow furrowed. “It’s… like our storm-lullabies,” she said. “Different notes, same… shape.” She tapped out a counter-rhythm, fitting it against Mara’s beats. “If we… lay this under the Whale’s song… here…” She marked a point on Finn’s chalkboard with one finger. “Where his long note dips. The Veil might… rock instead of… brace.”

Finn added another line of marks. “Rocking is good,” he said. “Structures that rock don’t crack as easily as ones that insist on being still. Madam likes rocking. The Engine can… be taught.”

The kettle gave a low, doubtful hiss. Finn flipped its little lid up and down as if shushing a toddler.

“So,” Mara said slowly, looking from board to paper to Engine. “We… retune the Engine to hum a pattern that… includes the Whale’s deep song, our… home-songs, my… storm-song. We feed that through the Heartstones. The city… responds. For a while. Enough to… change the Veil’s… shape.”

“And we build into that hum,” Liora added, “a set of… listening rules. The Engine’s… pattern-recognition. Stories about… what’s safe and what isn’t. We use your scary graphs,” she nodded at Finn, “to tell it when the Lantern Whale is… near, so it opens. When trawler-sounds appear, so it… thickens. When storms slam down, so it… yields at the top and… holds at the bottom.”

“Yielding at the top,” Finn repeated, scribbling furiously. “Yes. Let some energy pass through. Dissipate. We can… bleed it sideways, around the city. Make the Veil… bulge instead of… crack.”

The kettle squealed at bleed again. He silenced it with a firm twist of a valve.

“There are… problems,” Bubbles piped up, voice tinny from a nearby speaker shell. “Major flaws. Catastrophic holes. You are all pretending not to see them.”

“Go on, then,” Liora said. “Be the sensible one.”

Bubbles huffed. “Fine. First: Professor Finn’s Engine is… twitchy. You tune it wrong, it might… hum off-key, confuse Madam, and tear the Veil anyway. Second: you’re talking about synchronising an entire city’s… heartbeats. People might not… cooperate. Or they might, and it might still… misfire. Third: you intend to pour unknown sonic patterns from untested cultural archives into a device currently preventing several million tons of water from sitting on your heads. Have I missed anything?”

“Only that we’ll be doing all this… while the Surface continues to throw storms at us and trawlers at the Whale,” Finn said. “Small footnote.”

“Exactly,” Bubbles said. “This is not… sensible.”

“Good,” Liora said again. “Sensible is what got us here.”

Mara stared back down at her paper. Her swirls and loops looked less ridiculous now. Messy, yes. But… alive.

“It is… risky,” Finn conceded. “Yes. We are proposing to replace a relatively stable, if harmful, wrong thing with a possibly unstable, possibly less harmful, possibly differently wrong thing. From an engineering standpoint, this is… a nightmare.”

He straightened, chalk clenched in one hand, algae-sheet in the other. His beard haloed out around his face like a cloud of startled thoughts.

“From a moral standpoint,” he said, “we are already doing harm by—” He waved vaguely upward. “—squeezing the sea. Doing nothing is a decision too. A very safe-feeling one with very unsafe consequences. More power, more hum, more of the same is… worse. Leaving is… worse in a different flavour. So.” He slapped his algae-sheet down on the bench. “We arrive at… this.”

He gestured to Mara’s drawing, to Liora’s remembered rhythms, to the chalkboard spiderweb of equations and arrows.

“Technically unsound,” he said, with a kind of reluctant admiration. “Morally ambiguous. In violation of at least four Council edicts and probably two natural laws.”

He smiled then, a crooked, bright, reckless thing.

“And therefore,” he concluded, “in my professional opinion, our best option.”

The kettle, perhaps sensing the shift from hypothetical danger to chosen risk, let out one last feeble whistle and then, astonishingly, settled.

Mara felt the idea—the Plan That Wasn’t Sensible—solidify in her chest.

It was absurd. Of course it was. They were going to fix a failing ocean shield by teaching it to sing better. They were going to ask a whole city to trust them long enough to let their heartbeats be used as tuning-forks. They were going to poke at Madam Ocean’s patience with a bunch of stories and hope she appreciated the effort.

But the alternative was to sit there while the Veil tightened and the Whale winced and the storms pounded and the cracks widened.

“I’ll… have to go home,” Mara said, the thought falling into place with a weighty inevitability. “Soon. To… watch. To see if the surface… changes. If the storms feel… different. If the tidepool Door… behaves.”

“And to bring us… new stories,” Liora added. “Sky-patterns. Those… proverbs. ‘Mackerel scales.’ ‘Mare’s tails.’ The way the wind smells before a storm. We don’t… have that up here.Our Veil needs that… perspective.”

“And I will need,” Finn said, “to make the Engine… receptive. To build in the listening shells. To talk Queen Nerissa into letting me take apart my own greatest achievement in front of the entire Council. Preferably without being exiled to the outer algae farms.”

“And I,” Liora said, “will need to talk the city into… helping. Library-smugglers. Tide-callers. Mothers with lullabies. Grumpy elders who know old work songs. We’ll need them all. Or the Heartstones will just hum with… nonsense.”

Mara’s pencil drew one more line: a simple, connecting one between two loops. It was a clumsy little stroke. But it bridged the gap.

Her own fear sat beside her curiosity, not gone, but… reorganised.

“I’ll do it,” she said. “I’ll… go back. And come down again. And tell you what I see. And tell… them… about you. The Whale. Madam. The Veil. Even if they… laugh.”

“They will,” Liora said. “Some of them.”

“Some of them won’t,” Mara said. “Some… will hear. You said so yourself. They don’t all hum the same.”

“Nice phrase,” Finn murmured. “Must steal that for a paper.”

The workshop seemed, in some small, indefinable way, to approve.

The Engine’s hum smoothed just a fraction, as if encouraged by the promise of new songs. The bubbles drifting along the ceiling slowed their nervous popping. The kettle stopped whistling entirely and released, at last, a small, apologetic puff of steam that smelled faintly of over-brewed tea.

Rain still pummelled the world above. The Whale still glided along the edges of trenches, feeling the strain in his lanterns. The Veil still shuddered under storm-strikes.

But here, in a cluttered room full of half-built things and too many ideas, three unlikely conspirators had chosen a path that was neither more wall nor simple flight.

They would widen.

They would weave.

They would ask a humming machine and a stubborn sea to learn a new kind of story—one made of lullabies and weather-sayings and whale-chants and the shaky, unapproved conviction of a child from above and a child from below that safety built only on fear could never really hold.

“Right,” Finn said briskly, as if they had just agreed on something minor, like dinner. “First step: test. Small-scale. We find one Heartstone, one little corner of the Veil. We try humming at it differently. See if it… ripples. No citywide catastrophes until at least the second trial. Agreed?”

“Agreed,” Liora said.

Mara swallowed. “Agreed.”

Bubbles sighed dramatically. “If I explode, I’m haunting all of you,” it said.

“You’d have to queue,” Finn told it. “Now. Who knows a good storm-lullaby in nine-eight time?”

Liora’s tail began to tap again. Mara found herself humming. Finn reached for his tools.

Outside, the sea rolled and rumbled. Inside, three hand-hewn hearts and one semi-sentient bubble of engineering started, in their own small, not-at-all-sensible way, to retune the hum of a city.

chapters.chaptershortdescription: Where the entire city participates in a daring ritual to reshape the shield while Mara balances between two worlds.
chapters.chapterdetails: On the day of the recalibration, Pelagoria grows strangely quiet, as if the ocean itself is holding its breath. Queen Nerissa stands before the great shield-engine, a towering spiral of shell, metal, and living coral that glows with contained stormlight, her robes trailing like waves in a tidepool. Citizens gather in concentric circles around the central plaza, some wary, some hopeful, all casting curious looks at the lone surface child standing beside the Queen and her daughter. Following Finn’s intricate instructions, technicians adjust valves and current-channelers while the Lantern Whale drifts slowly overhead, its lanterns dimmed to a solemn glow. Liora begins the ritual, her clear voice singing an old Pelagorian melody that speaks of home and hidden harbors; Mara joins in with a land lullaby her mother used to hum during thunderstorms, the unfamiliar syllables twining with the mer-song like two currents merging. The Whale’s deep calls vibrate through the water, shaking loose bits of sand and fear, and soon the whole city adds its voice—humming, chanting, tapping rhythms that skip across shells and stones. The engine shudders, flares too bright, then begins to pulse in a steadier, warmer pattern, its energy stretching outward in spiraling filaments instead of spiking against the storm. For a moment, everything hangs in a delicate uncertainty: Mara feels as if she is standing on a tightrope between ocean and sky, belonging to neither and both. Then the pressure eases, the storm’s fury softens into heavy rain, and the shield settles around the city like a flexible, invisible cloak that breathes with the tides.
chapters.chapterText:
Pelagoria had never been this quiet.

Even on the calmest days, the city carried noise the way waves carried light: the tick of workshops, the rush of water through channels, the rumble of distant pumps, the overlapping murmur of thousands of voices layered over the constant, low heartbeat of the sea.

Today, it felt as if the ocean had inhaled and forgotten how to exhale.

The great central plaza, usually a place of bright chaos—market stalls spilling shells and woven weed, children chasing flickerfish in the narrow water-lanes, elders arguing amiably over currents and recipes—had been cleared.

No stalls, no stray nets, no banners hawking smoked eel or glimmer-pearls. Just the smooth, pale floor of fused sand, swept so clean it looked almost new, and the people of Pelagoria standing around its edge in wide, careful rings.

They weren’t pressing forward, the way surface crowds did in Mara’s world when something big was about to happen. There was distance between them, small gaps like breaths left between words. But there were a lot of them. Their presence filled the plaza more than any stalls could have.

Mara stood beside Queen Nerissa on the lowest step of the plaza’s raised central platform, with Liora on Nerissa’s other side and Professor Finn a little behind, shifting from foot to foot in nervous, off-beat time.

From here, the circles of people looked like ripples.

Closest to the platform: guards in pale, scaled armour, Captain Tideglass at their head, tridents butt-down, faces set in the careful neutrality of people determined not to admit they were afraid. Behind them: technicians and engineers with tool-belts slung low, their fingers twitching, eyes fixed on the machine that towered behind Nerissa. Beyond that, in widening rings, the regular citizens—shopkeepers with calloused hands, builders with coral dust in their hair, fishers with gill-scars along their wrists, children pressed against parents’ sides.

Faces lifted toward the platform: wary, hopeful, resigned, skeptical. And here and there, little gleams of something sharper. Curiosity. Defiance. The same things that hummed under Mara’s own skin.

They were all looking at the same focal point.

The shield-engine.

Mara had seen it before in Finn’s cluttered workshop, squeezed against the back wall like some overgrown, sulking pet. Here, in the open air of the plaza, given room and a proper foundation, it was magnificent and terrifying in equal measure.

It spiraled up from a broad base of fused sand and coral, like a giant shell unfurling. Its main ribs were thick arcs of translucent material, curved around a central column of braided shell and metal. Between the ribs hung membranes of water held in impossible sheets and twisting tubes, shot through with soft, restless light. Gears turned slowly within those watery curtains—some as small as Mara’s thumb, others the size of cartwheels—shell teeth glinting, centres pulsing with captured glow.

Coral grew along its spine, not as decoration but as living conduit. Tiny polyps opened and closed in waves, tasting the air, feeding on light. Thin veins of metal, etched with runes that glowed faintly, wrapped around those coral outgrowths, binding the biological and the mechanical into a single, uneasy whole.

At the very top, a crown of delicate branches arched outward, each tipped with a cluster of listening shells—little spirals like cupped ears—angled toward the dome above, toward the unseen storm.

The whole thing thrummed.

Not yet the great, over-loud hum that had strained the Whale’s lanterns, but a low, unsettled vibration. Caged stormlight flickered along its membranes, flashes of too-bright white caught and softened as they ran through spirals and tubes.

Nerissa stepped forward. Her robes, layered in soft greens and sea-blues, flowed behind her like gentle backwash between rocks. The coral of her crown had been braided with strands of duller, matte twig-coral today—less ornamental, more grounding.

She laid one hand on the Engine’s lowest rib.

The flickering light steadied, just a fraction.

“All right,” Professor Finn breathed, barely audible over the soft, collective rustle of the crowd shifting. “She likes you. That’s… something.”

Mara’s fingers ached with the urge to draw—this whole scene, the Engine’s towering spiral, Nerissa’s small, steady figure before it, Liora’s tense shoulders, the wide rings of people—but there was nowhere to put pencil or paper. She curled her hands into fists at her sides instead, ink-stains and salt-crystals pressing into her palms.

Above them, beyond the clear curve of the dome, the sea moved.

They could see it through the shell overhead: a huge, uneven weight of darkened water, streaked with pale, agitated curls. Occasionally, the far-off flash of lightning turned the whole membrane briefly into a mirror, showing back the city’s own upturned faces.

Farther out, beyond even the dome’s reach, a faint, slow-moving constellation of lights drifted along the deep—the Lantern Whale, keeping station near the Veil’s outer edge. His lanterns were dim today, their glow banked to a solemn murmur.

He was watching.

Mara could feel it, not with eyes or ears but with that new, taut sense in her bones she was only just beginning to understand: the awareness of something vast, patient, and currently very intent, hanging out in the dark like a thought at the edge of words.

Queen Nerissa lifted her hand from the Engine and turned to face the crowd.

“People of Pelagoria,” she said.

She didn’t shout. She didn’t need to. The plaza was built to carry her voice—stone and coral and water cooperating to pass the sound along, softening it without ever letting it fade.

“You know why we are here,” she went on. “You have felt it. In your walls. In your bones. In the Whale’s song. The Veil that has hidden us for a generation is straining. The storms above grow sharper. The deep below grows… restless.”

A murmur, low and uneasy, rippled through the rings.

“We built this Engine,” Nerissa said, resting her hand once more on the spiral of shell and living coral, “to keep us safe. We asked Madam Ocean to let us hum along her skirts instead of being swept with every tide. We asked the Lantern Whale to turn his songs around us instead of over us. We wove our fear of nets and cages and poison into its workings. And it did what we asked.”

She paused. The words hung, dense as water.

“But fear does not know when to stop,” she said softly. “It sings the same note until it drowns all others. It has made the Veil too tight. It has hurt those we did not mean to hurt. It has begun to crack the very shell we live in.”

Her gaze moved across the crowd. Mara followed it, seeing the flickers of guilt, of grief, of stubborn denial.

“Today,” Nerissa said, “we will loosen it.”

That word—loosen—landed like a dropped weight. Shoulders tightened. Fins twitched. Someone at the edge of one ring hissed, “Foolish,” under their breath.

Nerissa heard it. She inclined her head slightly.

“Perhaps,” she said. “Perhaps this is foolish. But I have seen what our cautious wisdom has brought. I will take a foolish hope over a careful collapse.”

She stepped aside then, gesture subtle but unmistakable, making space at the front of the platform.

Liora swallowed, throat bobbing.

Mara felt, absurdly, like someone had just shoved her out onto a stage with no script. Her palms went damp.

Professor Finn cleared his throat and stepped forward just enough to be seen by the technicians clustered nearest the Engine.

“Right,” he said, voice pitching up awkwardly at the first syllable before he wrestled it back down. “You all know your stations. Outer valve circle—you’re on intake modulation. If you see pressure spikes, you bleed them sideways, not down. I don’t care what your uncle taught you; today we’re not treating problems like enemies to punch.”

A ripple of strained laughter. The tension in the nearest ring eased by a hair.

“Inner shell-tuners,” Finn went on, “you listen for Madam’s reply. If she shoves, you… say ‘thank you’ and move with it. Do not attempt to out-stubborn the sea. She has more practice.”

“Heartstone team,” he said, nodding toward a group of stolid-looking builders across from him, each with a long, thin metal rod strapped to their backs like a lance. “You know where you’re going. When I signal, you plant those rods on your assigned stones and hold them there. Doesn’t matter what it feels like. Doesn’t matter if your teeth rattle and your ears buzz. That’s the point.”

“What if we pass out?” someone called.

“Then you’ll be unconscious and I’ll be annoyed,” Finn said. “Try not to. Breath-stones are ready if anyone gets too… poetic.”

“Everyone else,” he said, sweeping an arm to take in the concentric rings, “you’re chorus. Think of this Engine as a very large, very temperamental instrument, and yourselves as its… tuning forks.”

A few children in the second ring looked instantly delighted by the idea of being trusted to vibrate on purpose.

“You all know songs,” Finn said. “Work chants. Lullabies. Tide-calls. We’re going to give the Engine some of those patterns, instead of just numbers and ‘NO.’ Don’t worry if you’re not ‘good singers.’ The sea does not care if you are on pitch. It cares if you are… earnest.”

He glanced sideways at Mara, at Liora.

“And we have… new patterns to add,” he said. “From above. And from between.”

Nerissa touched his arm lightly. “Begin,” she said.

He nodded once and stepped back, leaving the front of the platform fully to Liora and Mara.

Liora exhaled.

“I hate being watched,” she muttered out of the corner of her mouth.

“Same,” Mara said. “On land, I hide behind bookshelves.”

“We’ll have to build more bookshelves after this,” Liora said. “For hiding. And storing complaints.”

She stepped forward.

The plaza held its breath.

Liora drew in a long, steadying inhalation, filling lungs that had never known air alone until Mara arrived. Her fingers curled and flexed at her sides, as if unsure whether to reach for stone, for water, or for a hand.

Then she sang.

The first note fell into the silence like a drop into still water.

It was clear and low, not the high, bright tones Mara had heard in some Pelagorian songs. It sat in Liora’s chest and ribs, a sound that belonged as much to bone as to throat. It swelled, carrying easily across the plaza, up into the dome, down into the ground.

The melody that followed was old.

Mara could feel that, even without knowing the words. It moved in slow arcs, dipping and rising with the laziness of a noonday tide. There were strange intervals—notes that didn’t quite fit Mara’s ear, held a hair longer than she expected, slipping into others by narrow, sliding steps. But there was also a familiarity there, like the way waves always, eventually, returned to shore.

The words, translated by the net, brushed against Mara’s mind like seaweed in a gentle current:

Stone below me, salt around,  
Walls that grew from empty ground,  
Harbour hidden, harbour home,  
Where the lost and tired come.

Fins that folded, feet that slipped,  
Lanterns hung in currents’ grip,  
Here we anchor, here we hide,  
Here we breathe between the tides.

The Engine’s hum responded.

It didn’t change entirely; this was no instant transformation. But it… noticed. A faint overtone crept into the low thrum, a new note that lined itself up under Liora’s, trying to match and not quite knowing how.

The listening shells along the Engine’s crown tilted imperceptibly toward her.

Mara’s chest ached.

She thought of her own home: not a carved coral dome in an impossible bubble, but a semi-detached house with peeling paint and a temperamental boiler, three streets back from the sea. The smell of damp towels, toast, and recycled air. The little square of garden where nothing quite grew the way the seed packet promised.

Her mother at the sink, sleeves rolled up, humming—always humming—under her breath when storms rattled the windows. The tune had never had proper words. Sometimes it picked one up for a verse or two; sometimes it was just nonsense, vowel sounds wrapped around breathy consonants.

Safe in. Rain out. Kettle on. Walls hold.

Mara swallowed.

Liora glanced at her, a flick in her gaze that said, It’s your turn.

Mara opened her mouth.

The first sound stuck.

Her throat, traitorous, went dry. Her tongue felt thick. For a heartbeat, all she could think of was the circle of faces, the weight of the entire city’s attention, the absurdity of singing a kitchen-lullaby into an ancient, humming machine in a place no one she knew above would believe existed.

She almost stopped.

Then she remembered the Whale’s lanterns, scarred and uneven. The thin crack of light that had crept up Finn’s graph. The way Nerissa had said, I want your eyes. Because they haven’t learned yet how to look away.

She thought of her mother’s hand on her back during thunder, smoothed in time with that silly little song, and of how storms had seemed less huge when her fear had something small and human-sized to hang on to.

She sang.

Her voice was thinner than Liora’s, higher, with that slight rawness of a child’s voice not yet settled. It wobbled on the first note, then found its footing.

She didn’t think about how it sounded. She thought about her kitchen table. About rain on glass. About the way light flickered on wet pavement.

“Tip-tap on the window, rain on the glass,” she sang into the humming air. “Boil up the kettle, let the dark clouds pass…”

The words felt strange here, where there were no windows in the surface sense, no kettles (unless you counted Finn’s complaining contraption), no sky to see clouds through. Strange—but not wrong.

She kept going.

Roof over, floor under, walls standing fast,  
Storm in the doorway, you can’t come in last.

Her melody braided around Liora’s.

At first, they jostled.

The two tunes were not written to sit together. One had grown from underwater lungs and the push and pull of tides; the other from radiators and the thrum of rain on thin glass. Their rhythms didn’t match; their intervals tugged at each other.

Then Liora, ears sharp, adjusted.

She bent her melody, just a little, sliding one held note down by a half-step to meet Mara’s rising one. Mara, hearing that, changed the length of her next phrase, shortening it to leave Liora’s line room to unfold under it. They wove.

Two currents, different temperatures, meeting.

The Engine’s hum shifted again.

It was more noticeable this time, enough that the nearest technicians glanced up from their valves in instinctive alarm. Finn flapped his hands at them—keep going, don’t panic—and they turned back, hands trembling only a little more as they adjusted flow at his shouted numbers.

Above, outside the dome, the Whale sang.

His call rolled down through the water, through the Veil, through the bubble of air. It hit the plaza floor like a slow earthquake, fine grains of sand lifting in tiny jumps before settling again. The coral pillars around the rim vibrated visibly.

It wasn’t a song in the sense of tidy, surface tunes with verses and a chorus. It was more like a paragraph you felt in your bones.

It was old. It tasted of ice ages and drowned forests. It moved in great, slow arcs, some notes so low Mara felt them in her marrow before she heard them as sound. No translation net tried to turn it into words this time. It was too broad for that.

The Engine took that deep note and wrapped it around Liora’s and Mara’s thinner ones.

Its membranes of suspended water shuddered, then began to pulse in time. The light threads within them swung out of their previous rigid pattern, re-mapping themselves along new spirals. Tiny, suppressed flares of stormlight that had been building at certain junctions found new routes, oozing sideways into looping channels instead of jumping straight down.

“Heartstones!” Finn cried, voice cracking. “Now!”

Around the plaza, the builders moved.

They broke from their ring, hurrying off down side corridors and into the city’s underpassages, long rods over their shoulders. Mara knew, from Finn’s frantic, chalk-scribbled map in the workshop, where they were going: key points in Pelagoria’s foundation. The cores of the biggest coral towers. The deep, fused nodes under the palace. The original stone in the first-built dome.

Each Heartstone was a thick lump of dense coral and mineral, grown and carefully hardened where loads met: silent, steady recorders of strain and rhythm. Today, they were about to become speakers.

Technicians fed new lines—thin strands of shell-wire and listening tubes—from the Engine’s base into those same conduits, linking the beating core of the machine to the city’s bones.

Liora’s song lifted. Mara’s circled under it. The Whale’s thrummed through both.

And then, from the circles, other sounds joined.

A woman near the front of the second ring, hands calloused from years of knotting nets, began to hum: low, tuneless at first, then resolving into the lilting cadence of an old work chant.

A child, clutching a parent’s hand, started tapping their feet on the fused-sand floor in a steady, two-beat rhythm. Another picked it up, then another, until a soft, syncopated patter underpinned everything, like distant, controlled rain.

An elder with a voice like cracked shell launched, without apparent warning, into a tide-call: the deep, repetitive phrases used to persuade stubborn cross-currents to shift during construction. His neighbours, after a moment’s startled hesitation, joined in, their voices rolling along the ring, imperfect but united.

The sound rose.

It wasn’t beautiful in any tidy, choir-trained way. It was too layered, too full of individual quirks. Some people were out of tune. Some couldn’t hold a pitch if it had handles. Some only hummed, others chanted words Mara didn’t know. A few clapped, hands smacking against scaled arms in off-beat emphasis.

And yet, as more voices came in, the whole became something… right.

The plaza floor vibrated. The coral pillars thrummed. Dust flaked gently from old cracks as new patterns of vibration slid into them.

Deep in the city’s foundations, the Heartstones woke.

At first, they shuddered, disconcerted. They were used to being receptors, not transmitters. The steady, ever-present tremor of the sea’s weight, the occasional sharp jab of impact, the slow drag of stress moving through rock—that was their familiar song.

Now, through the rods pressed against them by the builders’ sweating hands, a different hum came. Layered. Complex. Full of human-scale patterns.

The stones took it in.

A note from the Engine’s reshaped hum. A line from the Whale’s song. A fragment of Liora’s harbour-melody. A bar of Mara’s rain-lullaby. A hundred, a thousand small, imperfect human vibrations.

Then, obedient to the purpose they’d been grown for—carry movement, report strain—they pushed it outward.

Up through coral, down into old rock, sideways along the curved base of the dome. Into the legs of tables and the frames of doors, into the stone steps of staircases and the ribs of arches. Into the floors where children’s bare feet felt it and laughed, and where elders’ chairs rocked gently with it.

“It’s in,” Finn whispered, eyes bright, hands hovering over the Engine’s main control levers like a conductor waiting for the right moment to bring in the brass. “Come on. Come on, you stubborn beauty. Take it.”

The Engine shuddered.

For a second, it did entirely the wrong thing.

Its internal light spiked, not sideways but straight up. The membranes of held water flashed near-white, every gear’s teeth lit as if backlit by lightning. The hum jumped a whole octave, becoming a thin, keening whine that set Mara’s teeth on edge.

Several of the nearest technicians flinched, hands jerking back from hot valves. A few of the children in the outer rings clapped their hands over their ears, faces screwing up.

The Whale’s lanterns, visible through the dome above, flared sharply, as if in pain.

“No,” Liora gasped, her song stumbling.

Mara’s voice thinned.

The Engine whined higher. One of the membranes bulged outward in a sudden, alarming swell, its surface crawling with froth like a panicked wave trapped in glass.

“Finn!” Tideglass barked. “Shut it down!”

“Wait,” Finn said hoarsely, every muscle in his body taut. “It’s… overshooting. It’s… looking for the pattern. If I cut it now, it will snap back too hard.”

The plaza’s sound faltered.

People’s voices hitched, caught between instinctive silence—be quiet, something is about to break—and the knowledge that the whole point of this was not to cower.

Mara’s throat felt like she’d swallowed a handful of dry sand. She forced out the next line of her lullaby anyway, voice cracking on the second syllable.

“Storm on the doorstep, you can’t come in last…”

Her mother had always made a joke of that line. Had pulled a face at the door, as if scolding a wet dog. Mara tried to put that into the sound: the faint, ridiculous defiance of trying to boss around something much bigger than you for the sake of making your child laugh.

Liora caught it.

Her own melody, which had almost dropped away, swelled again—not louder, but… deeper. She reached back into that place where songs and promises touched and pushed more of herself into it.

“Harbour hidden, harbour home,” she sang, voice rough now. “We are not your nets to close.”

The Whale answered.

His next call rolled down like a boulder. It started low, then stepped up—not in the smooth, sliding way of before, but in rough, deliberate intervals. Three pulses. A pause. Two more. He was… counting, Mara realised dimly. Marking out beats for them.

The Engine hit its peak.

Light poured through its membranes, bright enough that Mara had to squint. For a terrifying heartbeat, it seemed every element was going to tear free: water-sheets bursting, gears spinning out of alignment, coral cracking.

Then, with a convulsive shudder that ran from its base all the way up through its listening-shell crown, it… let go.

The hard, piercing whine broke apart.

In its place, a lower, more complex chord bloomed. It wasn’t one note. It was many, layered: a deep, steady vibration that owed as much to rock as to machinery; a mid-range pulse with a rhythm suspiciously like the tide-call the elders were chanting; a higher, wavering line that bore an unmistakable echo of Liora’s melody and Mara’s kitchen-song tangled together.

The membranes of water relaxed.

They didn’t go flat—they rippled. The bulged one drew back, its surface smoothing like a frightened creature being coaxed down from a panic. Light no longer jagged through them in harsh, straight paths. Instead, it moved in spirals, in looping curls, in little branching filaments.

Those filaments shot outward.

Not in spikes, not in single, brittle lines, but in a network. They flowed along the shell-wires to the Heartstones, into the coral, into the arching bones of the dome. They pushed outward, through, around.

Up above, along the inside of the Veil, the change became visible.

Before, during storms, the shield’s reaction had been harsh: sudden flares where lightning hit, narrow streaks of over-brightness racing in straight lines across its surface, small, tight points of pressure where water slammed.

Now, when the next wave thudded against the dome, the light that marked the impact spread more evenly. Instead of a single sharp flare, a broad, softer glow rippled out in rings from the point of contact. The dome bulged inward slightly—yielding, not cracking. The next lightning stroke’s energy streaked along gentle curves instead of jagged paths, bleeding into wider arcs that faded rather than piling into stress points.

Mara felt the pressure that had been building behind her eyes ease, just a fraction, like a headache finally beginning to unclench.

The plaza heard it too.

Their humming changed—not to something new, but to something less strained. Where their voices had been tight, forced up in defiance, they loosened. Some people even smiled, incredulously, as the vibration running up through their feet and into their ribs shifted from anxiety’s brittle buzz to a steadier, warmer hum.

Liora’s song settled into the new chord like a bird folding into a new, better-fitting nest. Mara found, to her own astonishment, that her voice had stopped wobbling. She let it slip into harmony—third above here, unison there, guessing and adjusting in clumsy, earnest stabs.

The Whale’s lanterns along his flank brightened—not in that alarm-spike way, but in a gentler, more diffuse glow, like embers being breathed on.

He called again.

This time, there was no edge of flinch in it. The chord rolled through the city, through Mara’s bones, through the Engine, and back out into the Veil. The folded storm above snarled, but its teeth met something that did not shatter.

For a few moments that felt stretched-out and thin, like the surface of the tidepool Door just before it had grabbed her, Mara existed in two places at once.

Part of her was here: on the damp, slightly sticky step of the plaza platform, surrounded by a ring of people whose lives depended on a hum she was helping to shape, lungs working hard in the thin air, throat sore, ears full of new chords.
